commands.tooltip: Halts any in-progress rollout, so new pods stop being created mid-change. Useful when you want to apply several changes and let them roll out together. Resume with kubectl rollout resume deploy/web.

commands.desc: Resume a paused deployment rollout
commands.tooltip: Continues a rollout paused with kubectl rollout pause deploy/web. Any pending pod template changes apply now. Check completion with kubectl rollout status deploy/web --timeout=120s.

commands.desc: Scale a deployment to three replicas
commands.tooltip: Sets the web deployment's replica count to 3, and the deployment controller creates or deletes pods to match. Scaling down deletes pods, so stateful workloads need careful handling. For automatic sizing, use kubectl autoscale deploy/web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70.

commands.desc: Update a deployment's container image
commands.tooltip: Changes the image of the container named web to nginx:1.26, triggering a rolling update. The deployment's old replicas are replaced gradually, so the service stays up. Watch the rollout finish with kubectl rollout status deploy/web --timeout=120s.

commands.desc: Edit a deployment in your editor
commands.tooltip: Opens the deployment's live spec in your default editor, applies your changes on save, and shows the diff. Kubernetes validates the edited object before applying. For scripted changes prefer kubectl patch or kubectl set image.

commands.desc: Patch a deployment's replicas
commands.tooltip: Applies a surgical JSON patch to the live deployment, here scaling replicas to 5 without editing the whole object. Patches are ideal for single-field changes in scripts. Related: kubectl edit deploy/web for interactive edits.

commands.desc: Set up automatic pod autoscaling
commands.tooltip: Creates a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) that keeps the deployment between 2 and 10 replicas based on CPU usage. The cluster needs the metrics server installed, for example minikube addons enable metrics-server. Check kubectl get hpa to see the current target and actual replicas.

commands.desc: Expose a deployment as a service
commands.tooltip: Creates a service (stable network endpoint for a set of pods) of type NodePort that publishes the deployment on a cluster-wide port. On local clusters, minikube service web opens the URL in a browser. For HTTP routing, consider an ingress instead.

commands.desc: List all kubeconfig contexts
commands.tooltip: Shows every context defined in your kubeconfig (the file that maps cluster addresses to credentials), with an asterisk marking the current one. Contexts bundle a cluster, user, and namespace. Switch with kubectl config use-context prod.

commands.desc: Show the active context
commands.tooltip: Prints the name of the context (which cluster kubeconfig currently points at) that kubectl will use. Confirm it before destructive commands so you do not hit the wrong cluster. Related: kubectl config view.

commands.desc: Switch to another context
commands.tooltip: Makes the prod context the active one, so all subsequent kubectl commands target the prod cluster. Switching contexts does not touch the clusters themselves. Verify with kubectl config current-context.

commands.desc: Set the default namespace
commands.tooltip: Updates the current context so every kubectl command runs against the staging namespace unless you override with -n. This only changes your kubeconfig, not the cluster. Undo with the same command and --namespace=default.

commands.desc: Show the merged kubeconfig
commands.tooltip: Prints the merged contents of your kubeconfig file: clusters, users, and contexts. Combine with --minify to show only the current context, or --raw to include certificate data. Redact credentials by omitting --raw.

commands.desc: Delete a context from kubeconfig
commands.tooltip: Removes the staging context entry from your kubeconfig, leaving clusters and users intact. The cluster itself keeps running; only your local pointer disappears. Re-add contexts via kubeconfig edits or tools like kind and minikube.

commands.desc: Show node CPU and memory usage
commands.tooltip: Prints live CPU and memory usage per node, provided the metrics server is running in the cluster. Numbers come from the Metrics API, so they lag a few seconds behind reality. Related: kubectl top pods for per-pod usage.

commands.desc: Show pod CPU and memory usage
commands.tooltip: Prints live CPU and memory usage for pods in the current namespace, useful for spotting runaway containers. Requires the metrics server addon, for example minikube addons enable metrics-server. Add -A to cover all namespaces.

commands.desc: Mark a node unschedulable
commands.tooltip: Marks node-a as unschedulable, so no new pods are placed on it while existing pods keep running. Prepares a node for maintenance before draining it. Reverse with kubectl uncordon node-a.

commands.desc: Make a node schedulable again
commands.tooltip: Removes the unschedulable marker set by kubectl cordon node-a, allowing new pods onto the node. Pending pods will be scheduled there as capacity allows. Use after maintenance finishes.

commands.desc: Evict pods from a node
commands.tooltip: Evicts every pod from node-a so the node can be rebooted or removed, keeping daemonset pods in place with --ignore-daemonsets. This is disruptive: it terminates workloads, so do it during maintenance windows. Add --delete-emptydir-data for pods using emptyDir volumes, and undo with kubectl uncordon node-a.

commands.desc: Add a label to a node
commands.tooltip: Labels node-a with disktype=ssd, a key-value pair that schedulers and selectors can match. Deployments can then target labeled nodes via nodeSelector or affinity. List existing labels with kubectl get nodes --show-labels.

commands.desc: Add a taint to a node
commands.tooltip: Taints node-a so the scheduler refuses to place pods there unless they tolerate the taint. Taints and tolerations keep dedicated workloads off shared nodes. Remove the taint by re-running with a trailing minus, key=value:NoSchedule-, and note that tainting an active node can strand pods.

commands.desc: Check if you can perform an action
commands.tooltip: Asks the API server whether your current credentials may create pods, honoring role bindings and impersonation. Useful for debugging permission errors before they hit your workflow. List everything you can do with kubectl auth can-i --list -n staging.

commands.desc: List all permitted actions
commands.tooltip: Prints every verb and resource you are allowed to touch in the staging namespace, based on your roles and bindings. A fast way to audit your permissions. Pair with kubectl auth whoami to see which identity is being checked.

commands.desc: Show the current authenticated user
commands.tooltip: Reports the user and groups your kubeconfig credentials resolve to on the current cluster. Useful when the same kubeconfig file is shared across contexts. Combine with kubectl auth can-i create pods to test permissions.

commands.desc: Create a secret from a literal value
commands.tooltip: Creates a secret named db-pass holding the key password, stored base64-encoded in etcd. Secrets are meant for sensitive values like passwords and API tokens. Read it back with kubectl get secret db-pass -o yaml.

commands.desc: Create a secret from a file
commands.tooltip: Loads the entire creds.json file into the secret as a key named after the filename. Multiple --from-file flags can pack several files into one secret. Mount the result into pods as files or environment variables.

commands.desc: Create a registry pull secret
commands.tooltip: Creates a secret of type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson so nodes can pull images from a private registry. Reference it in a pod spec via imagePullSecrets. The password sits in the secret base64-encoded, so rotate it if it leaks.

commands.desc: Create a configmap from a file
commands.tooltip: Creates a configmap named app-config whose key config.yaml holds the file's contents, mountable into pods as a file. Configmaps keep configuration out of container images so you can change it without rebuilding. Update pods to pick up changes with kubectl rollout restart deploy/web.

commands.desc: Show a secret's encoded values
commands.tooltip: Prints the secret object with its values base64-encoded, not plain text. Decode a value with echo <value> | base64 -d. Prefer tools like kubectl create secret over committing secrets to git.

commands.desc: Generate bash completion for kubectl
commands.tooltip: Writes the bash completion script so kubectl tab-completes resources, flags, and names. Load it by adding source ~/.kube/completion.bash to your .bashrc. Other shells use kubectl completion zsh or fish.

commands.desc: Proxy the Kubernetes API to localhost
commands.tooltip: Starts a local HTTP proxy on 127.0.0.1:8001 that forwards requests to the cluster API server, with authentication handled for you. Handy for browsing API endpoints in a browser or with curl. Stop with Ctrl-C.

commands.desc: Wait for a resource condition
commands.tooltip: Blocks until the pod reports Ready or the 60 second timeout passes, returning a non-zero exit code on timeout. Scripts use this to sequence dependent deployments. Conditions vary by resource, for example available for deployments.

commands.desc: Print the Helm client version
commands.tooltip: Shows the installed Helm client version. In Helm 3 there is no server-side component, so only client info is printed, unlike Helm 2's tiller. Useful for confirming you are on Helm 3.x. Related: helm list shows what you have installed.

commands.desc: Search Artifact Hub for charts
commands.tooltip: Searches Artifact Hub, the public catalog of distributed Helm charts, for charts matching nginx. Results link back to each chart's repository and maintainer. Once you pick one, add its repository with helm repo add and search locally.

commands.desc: Search your added repositories
commands.tooltip: Looks for charts named nginx inside the repositories you have added locally, using the cached index. The repo/chart form narrows the search to one repository. Refresh the index first with helm repo update if results look stale.

commands.desc: Add a chart repository
commands.tooltip: Registers the Bitnami chart repository under the short name bitnami, so you can install charts with helm install my-web bitnami/nginx. Repository metadata is stored in ~/.config/helm/repositories.yaml. List what you have with helm repo list.

commands.desc: Refresh local repository indexes
commands.tooltip: Downloads the latest index files for every configured repository, so helm search repo finds newly published chart versions. Run it after adding a repo or when a chart version seems missing. There is no harm in running it often.

commands.desc: List configured chart repositories
commands.tooltip: Prints the short names and URLs of every repository you have added. The short name is the prefix used when installing, such as bitnami in bitnami/nginx. Remove an entry with helm repo remove bitnami.

commands.desc: Remove a chart repository
commands.tooltip: Forgets the bitnami repository, so its charts stop appearing in helm search repo and installs must use a full URL or another repo. Installed releases keep working after removal. Re-add later with helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami.

commands.desc: Install a chart as a release
commands.tooltip: Installs the bitnami/nginx chart under the release name my-web, creating the Kubernetes resources the chart templates. A release (an installed instance of a chart) can be upgraded, rolled back, and uninstalled independently. Watch the printed status and notes for next steps.

commands.desc: Install a chart with custom values
commands.tooltip: Installs the chart while overriding defaults with the settings in values.yaml, which is how you customize size, resources, and features per environment. Values files are YAML and can be chained with repeated --values flags. See the available keys with helm show values bitnami/nginx.

commands.desc: Upgrade a release with overrides
commands.tooltip: Upgrades the my-web release to the latest chart while setting replicaCount to 3, overriding the default without editing a file. In Helm 3, upgrades create a new revision while the old one stays restorable. Roll back with helm rollback my-web 2.

commands.desc: Roll back a release to a revision
commands.tooltip: Reverts the my-web release to revision 2, reapplying the manifests that revision used. Find revision numbers with helm history my-web. Rolling back creates a new revision itself, so the current state is never lost.

commands.desc: List release revisions
commands.tooltip: Shows every revision of the my-web release with its status, chart version, and when it was deployed. Revision numbers feed helm rollback my-web 2 and tell you which state to restore. Prune old revisions with --max on upgrade.

commands.desc: List installed releases
commands.tooltip: Prints the releases installed in the current namespace with their chart, version, and status. Filter by namespace with -n or use -A for all namespaces. Add -a to include failed and uninstalled releases.

commands.desc: List releases in one namespace
commands.tooltip: Shows only the releases installed in the monitoring namespace, keeping multi-tenant clusters readable. The namespace flag works the same way on helm install and helm uninstall. Pair with helm status my-web for details of one release.

commands.desc: Show a release's status and notes
commands.tooltip: Prints the my-web release's current status, revision, and the notes the chart author wrote, which often contain the admin password or access URLs. A failed status points at a broken upgrade, so check helm history my-web next. Related: helm list for the summary view.

commands.desc: Remove a release
commands.tooltip: Deletes every resource created by the my-web release, including its secrets and volumes unless they are protected. There is no undo, so export what you need first with helm get manifest my-web. Use --keep-history to preserve the release record for auditing.

commands.desc: Render chart manifests locally
commands.tooltip: Renders the chart's Kubernetes manifests to stdout without installing anything or contacting the cluster. Pipe to a file to review exactly what helm would create. Use --values values.yaml to render with your overrides.

commands.desc: Validate a chart's structure and values
commands.tooltip: Checks the chart in ./chart for common errors such as malformed Chart.yaml, invalid templates, and bad values references. Lint errors usually mean the chart will fail to install. Run it in CI before publishing charts.

commands.desc: Download and unpack a chart
commands.tooltip: Downloads the latest bitnami/nginx chart as a tgz and unpacks it into a directory of the same name. The source lets you inspect templates or vendor the chart into your repo. Add --version to pin a specific chart version.

commands.desc: Fetch a chart's dependencies
commands.tooltip: Downloads the charts declared in ./chart's Chart.yaml dependencies into its charts/ directory, honoring the versions and repositories listed. Run it after editing dependencies or checking out a chart that omits vendor files. Related: helm dependency list shows what is expected.

commands.desc: Scaffold a new chart
commands.tooltip: Generates a complete starter chart in ./mychart with Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates, and a sample deployment and service. Edit the metadata and templates to fit your app. Validate the result with helm lint ./mychart.

commands.desc: Show a chart's default values
commands.tooltip: Prints every configurable value of the chart with its default, the reference for writing your own values.yaml overrides. Keys seen here can be set with --set or --values at install time. Related: helm show chart for metadata.

commands.desc: Show a release's installed manifests
commands.tooltip: Prints the exact Kubernetes manifests Helm applied for the my-web release, useful before uninstalling or when auditing what is live. Compare with helm template to spot drift. Values used are visible with helm get values my-web.

commands.desc: Launch the k9s terminal UI
commands.tooltip: Starts the interactive terminal dashboard for Kubernetes, showing pods in the current context with keyboard shortcuts for describe, logs, edit, and delete. It reads the same kubeconfig as kubectl. Press ? inside for the key binding reference.

commands.desc: Launch k9s in a namespace
commands.tooltip: Starts k9s scoped to the staging namespace, so resource views only show that namespace's objects. Switch namespaces later from inside the UI with the :ns command. Equivalent to kubectl -n staging.

commands.desc: Launch k9s into a resource view
commands.tooltip: Opens k9s directly in the pod view instead of the default start screen, skipping a few keystrokes. The -c flag accepts any resource name, short name, or alias such as deploy or svc. Related: k9s -n staging -c deploy.

commands.desc: Launch k9s against a context
commands.tooltip: Starts k9s using the prod context from your kubeconfig, which selects the cluster and credentials to talk to. The running UI lets you hop contexts with the :ctx command. Verify the active context with k9s info.

commands.desc: Launch k9s with changes disabled
commands.tooltip: Starts k9s in read-only mode, so delete, edit, and scale actions are blocked in the UI. Useful when a developer should only observe a production cluster. The flag also works per context in the k9s config.

commands.desc: Show k9s runtime and config paths
commands.tooltip: Prints the k9s version, current context and namespace, and where k9s reads its configuration files. Run it first when k9s behaves unexpectedly, since it reveals which config directory is active. Related: k9s --help lists all startup flags.

commands.desc: List all containers, running or stopped
commands.tooltip: Shows every container on this machine, including exited ones, with their names, images, and status. The plain podman ps lists only running containers. Remove old ones with podman rm <name>.

commands.desc: List local container images
commands.tooltip: Prints all images stored locally with their repository, tag, size, and creation date. Images are the templates that containers run from, fetched with podman pull. Reclaim space with podman image prune.

commands.desc: Search registries for images
commands.tooltip: Searches container registries for images matching nginx, showing official and community results with star counts. Registries are servers that store container images, such as Docker Hub. Pull a result with podman pull nginx:1.25.

commands.desc: Pull an image from a registry
commands.tooltip: Downloads the nginx:1.25 image (a container image is the template containers run from) from its registry into local storage. Tagged versions like 1.25 are reproducible, unlike latest. See local images with podman images.

commands.desc: Run a detached container
commands.tooltip: Starts a container named web from the nginx image in the background, mapping host port 8080 to the container's port 80. The -d flag detaches, so your terminal stays free. Check it with podman ps and podman logs -f web.

commands.desc: Run an interactive throwaway container
commands.tooltip: Starts an alpine container with an interactive shell, removing the container automatically when you exit thanks to --rm. Perfect for experiments that should leave no trace. Type exit to return to your host shell.

commands.desc: Open a shell in a running container
commands.tooltip: Runs sh inside the running web container, giving you a shell for inspecting processes, files, and network state. The container must be running, so start it first with podman start web. Changes inside are lost when the container is removed.

commands.desc: Stream a container's logs
commands.tooltip: Follows the stdout and stderr output of the web container, printing new lines as they appear. Drop -f to print the existing log once. Pair with podman ps to find the container name first.

commands.desc: Stop a running container
commands.tooltip: Sends SIGTERM to the web container's main process and waits for it to exit, letting the app shut down cleanly. The container stays on disk and can be restarted with podman start web. A hung container can be killed with podman stop -t 0 web.

commands.desc: Start a stopped container
commands.tooltip: Restarts the stopped web container, preserving its filesystem and configuration. The container must already exist, so run podman run once first. Verify it is running again with podman ps.

commands.desc: Restart a container
commands.tooltip: Stops and starts the web container in one step, useful after changing its host files or when it misbehaves. Restart time counts against the container's restart policy. For clean shutdowns prefer podman stop and podman start.

commands.desc: Remove a stopped container
commands.tooltip: Deletes the web container and its writable layer, so all filesystem changes inside are gone. The container must be stopped first, or add -f to force it. Removing an image with podman rmi nginx still fails while a container uses it.

commands.desc: Remove an image
commands.tooltip: Deletes the nginx image from local storage, freeing disk space, but fails if a container still references it. There is no undo, and the image must be pulled again to recreate it. List images with podman images and remove unused ones in bulk with podman image prune -a.

commands.desc: Build an image from a Dockerfile
commands.tooltip: Builds a container image named myapp from the Dockerfile in the current directory, using the same syntax as docker build. Podman builds run rootless and unprivileged by default. Tag another version with podman tag myapp myapp:1.0.

commands.desc: Show storage usage by object type
commands.tooltip: Summarizes disk space used by images, containers, volumes, and build cache, like docker system df. Use --verbose for per-object detail. Reclaim space with podman system prune.

commands.desc: Remove unused images, containers, and cache
commands.tooltip: Deletes every stopped container, dangling and unused image, and cached build data, which can free gigabytes but is not undoable. Add --volumes to also drop unused named volumes. Double-check what would go with podman system df first.

commands.desc: Create a named volume
commands.tooltip: Creates a volume called data, a piece of persistent storage that survives container removal and can be shared between containers. Mount it with -v data:/app/data on podman run. List volumes with podman volume ls.

commands.desc: List named volumes
commands.tooltip: Shows every named volume on the host with its driver. Volumes persist independently of containers, so they survive podman rm and podman system prune unless --volumes is passed. Inspect one with podman volume inspect data.

commands.desc: Create a user-defined network
commands.tooltip: Creates a bridge network called web-net that containers can join with --network web-net on podman run. User-defined networks give containers DNS resolution by name. List networks with podman network ls.

commands.desc: Show live container resource usage
commands.tooltip: Prints CPU, memory, and network usage for all running containers, updating continuously like a container-aware top. Press Ctrl-C to stop. Pair with podman ps -a to spot containers to prune.

commands.desc: Show container details as JSON
commands.tooltip: Dumps the web container's full configuration, including mounts, environment, and network settings, as JSON. Grep the output or use --format to pull one field, for example podman inspect -f '{{.State.Status}}' web.

commands.desc: Log in to a container registry
commands.tooltip: Saves credentials for the ghcr.io registry so podman push and pull can authenticate, storing them in ~/.config/containers/auth.json. The same file is shared with buildah and skopeo. Log out with podman logout ghcr.io.

commands.desc: Build an image from a Dockerfile
commands.tooltip: Builds a container image named myapp from the Dockerfile in the current directory. The older spelling buildah bud -t app:latest . still works but is deprecated. Podman's podman build wraps the same engine.

commands.desc: Create a working container from a base image
commands.tooltip: Pulls the alpine base image and creates a working container from it, printing its name, typically alpine-working-container. Working containers are scratch spaces for assembling images without a Dockerfile. List them with buildah containers.

commands.desc: Run a command in a working container
commands.tooltip: Executes sh inside the working container, where you can install packages and lay down files for the final image. Unlike container runtimes, no long-lived process is started, so the container stays buildable. Commit the result with buildah commit alpine-working-container myapp.

commands.desc: Save a working container as an image
commands.tooltip: Converts the alpine-working-container's filesystem into an image named myapp, ready to run or push. This is the buildah equivalent of docker commit. Verify the result with buildah images.

commands.desc: Push an image to a registry
commands.tooltip: Uploads the myapp image to the registry.example.com registry using the docker:// transport, after buildah login for private registries. The destination form is transport://location, and other transports include docker-archive and oci. Confirm the remote copy with skopeo inspect docker://registry.example.com/myapp:latest.

commands.desc: List local images
commands.tooltip: Shows every image in local storage with its repository, tag, and size, including ones committed by buildah and pulled by podman. Both tools share the same storage. Remove images with buildah rmi.

commands.desc: List working containers
commands.tooltip: Prints every working container created with buildah from, with their base image and status. Working containers are build-time scratch spaces, not running services. Clean up with buildah rm alpine-working-container.

commands.desc: Show image configuration as JSON
commands.tooltip: Prints the myapp image's config, layers, and history as JSON, useful for auditing what an image contains. Extract one field with --format. Related: skopeo inspect does the same for images in a registry without pulling them.

commands.desc: Tag an image with another name
commands.tooltip: Adds the myapp:1.0 tag to the myapp image, letting you version images without duplicating data. Tags are references, so many tags can point at one image. Push a specific tag with buildah push myapp:1.0 docker://registry.example.com/myapp:1.0.

commands.desc: Inspect an image without pulling it
commands.tooltip: Reads metadata for the nginx:1.25 image directly from its registry, reporting architecture, layers, and digest without downloading the image. The docker:// prefix is the registry transport. Compare with buildah inspect, which works on local images.

commands.desc: Show an image's config blob
commands.tooltip: Prints the image's config blob, the JSON describing environment variables, entrypoint, and exposed ports, straight from the registry. Useful for checking what an image runs without pulling it. Add --raw to see the raw manifest instead.

commands.desc: List the tags of a repository
commands.tooltip: Queries the registry for every tag attached to the nginx repository, handy for finding the exact version to pin. The repository is identified with the docker:// transport. Verify a chosen tag with skopeo inspect docker://nginx:<tag>.

commands.desc: Copy an image between registries
commands.tooltip: Copies the image from one registry to another without a local pull, streaming layers directly between them. This is the fastest way to mirror images. For private registries, pass credentials with --src-creds and --dest-creds.

commands.desc: Delete an image from a registry
commands.tooltip: Marks the image for deletion in the registry, which is destructive and often requires the registry to support the operation. Deleting by digest can remove every tag pointing at that manifest, so delete by tag carefully. Confirm what exists first with skopeo list-tags docker://registry.example.com/nginx.

commands.desc: List running containers via CRI
commands.tooltip: Lists the containers running on this node as the container runtime (containerd, for example) sees them, the same view the kubelet uses. crictl talks to the CRI (Container Runtime Interface) socket, so it works even when the kubelet is down. Add -a for stopped containers.

commands.desc: List all containers, including stopped
commands.tooltip: Shows every container on the node with its status, image, and the pod sandbox it belongs to. Stopped containers linger until the kubelet's garbage collection runs. Pair with crictl logs <container-id> to inspect a failed one.

commands.desc: List images on the node
commands.tooltip: Lists the container images present in the node's runtime storage, tagged by repository and digest. Compare with kubectl get nodes -o wide to see which runtime is in use. Remove unused ones with crictl rmi <image>.

commands.desc: List pod sandboxes
commands.tooltip: Shows the pod sandboxes on the node, which are the pause containers that hold the pod's namespaces. Each sandbox maps to one Kubernetes pod scheduled on this node. Dig into one with crictl inspectp <sandbox-id>.

commands.desc: Pull an image with the CRI runtime
commands.tooltip: Downloads the nginx:1.25 image into the node's runtime storage, equivalent to what the kubelet does before starting a pod. Useful when debugging image pulls without the kubelet. Confirm with crictl images.

commands.desc: Show a container's logs
commands.tooltip: Prints the logs of the container identified by the shortened ID 3f8d9c2a1b4e, which you find with crictl ps -a. This is the runtime-level view, available even if Kubernetes is unreachable. Follow with -f for live output.

commands.desc: Exec into a container on the node
commands.tooltip: Runs sh inside the container directly through the runtime, bypassing the API server and kubelet. A lifesaver when the node is not registered with the cluster. List container IDs with crictl ps.

commands.desc: Show container resource usage
commands.tooltip: Prints CPU and memory usage per container from the runtime, similar to kubectl top pods but node-local and working without the metrics server. Press Ctrl-C to stop the live view. Related: crictl ps -a for the container list.

commands.desc: Remove an image from the node
commands.tooltip: Deletes the image from the runtime's storage, freeing disk space on the node. There is no undo, and the kubelet will repull it when a pod needs it. Removing images still in use by a running container fails.

commands.desc: Show runtime and client versions
commands.tooltip: Prints the crictl client version and the CRI runtime version and name (for example containerd) on the node. Run it first when crictl cannot reach the runtime socket, since it surfaces connection errors. The default socket path is /run/containerd/containerd.sock.

commands.desc: List instances as JSON
commands.tooltip: Lists every LXD instance (container or VM) as machine-readable JSON instead of the default table, handy for scripting and jq. The plain lxc list is covered in the master glossary. Add filters, for example lxc list type=container status=running.

commands.desc: Create and start a container
commands.tooltip: Pulls the ubuntu:24.04 image and starts a container named web01 in one step, the LXD equivalent of docker run. Images come from remotes like ubuntu:, and LXD caches them locally. Connect with lxc exec web01 bash.

commands.desc: Launch a virtual machine instead of a container
commands.tooltip: Starts an LXD virtual machine from the ubuntu:24.04 image with a 2GiB memory limit, using the --vm flag to choose VMs over containers. VMs give kernel isolation at the cost of more overhead. The -c flag sets instance configuration at launch.

commands.cmd: lxc exec web01 -- systemctl status nginx
commands.desc: Run a command inside an instance
commands.tooltip: Executes systemctl status nginx inside the web01 container, the way to manage services or inspect state from the host. The double dash separates lxc flags from the remote command. For an interactive shell use lxc exec web01 bash.

commands.desc: Show instance details
commands.tooltip: Prints web01's configuration, resource usage, IP addresses, and snapshot list in one view. It is the first stop when an instance misbehaves. Snapshots created with lxc snapshot web01 snap1 show up here too.

commands.desc: Restart an instance
commands.tooltip: Stops and starts web01 in one step, applying changes made to its configuration. Add --force to skip graceful shutdown if it hangs. For scheduled maintenance, lxc stop and lxc start give you finer control.

commands.desc: Delete an instance
commands.tooltip: Removes web01 and everything on its root disk, which cannot be undone unless a snapshot exists. Running instances refuse deletion, so stop them first or pass --force. Restore a snapshot beforehand with lxc restore web01 snap1.

commands.desc: Snapshot an instance
commands.tooltip: Captures web01's filesystem (and optionally memory with --stateful) as snap1, giving you a restore point before risky changes. Snapshots are cheap and stored with the instance. Revert with lxc restore web01 snap1.

commands.desc: Restore an instance from a snapshot
commands.tooltip: Replaces web01's current state with the snap1 snapshot, discarding every change since the snapshot was taken. Data written after the snapshot is lost, so confirm before running. List snapshots with lxc info web01.

commands.desc: Copy a file into an instance
commands.tooltip: Uploads config.yaml from your machine into web01's filesystem at /etc/config.yaml, the LXD equivalent of scp. Add -p to create missing parent directories. Pull files back with lxc file pull web01/etc/config.yaml ./config.yaml.

commands.desc: Copy a file out of an instance
commands.tooltip: Downloads nginx.conf from inside web01 to your current directory, handy for backing up configs or inspecting them on the host. Use lxc file push for the reverse direction. Directories work too with --recursive.

commands.desc: List locally cached images
commands.tooltip: Shows the images cached on your LXD server, which are the base templates instances are created from. Images from remotes like ubuntu: are cached automatically. Import your own with lxc image import ./myimage.tar.gz --alias myapp.

commands.desc: Set an instance resource limit
commands.tooltip: Limits web01's memory to 512MB, one of many limits.* keys that constrain CPU, memory, and processes. Changes apply after a restart. See the current config with lxc config show web01.

commands.cmd: lxc config device add web01 www proxy listen=tcp:0.0.0.0:8080 connect=tcp:127.0.0.1:80
commands.desc: Add a proxy device to an instance
commands.tooltip: Forwards host port 8080 to port 80 inside web01 via a proxy device, the LXD way to publish services without touching iptables. The device survives restarts and is managed with lxc config device. Remove it with lxc config device remove web01 www.

commands.desc: List LXD networks
commands.tooltip: Shows the networks managed by LXD, including the default lxdbr0 bridge most instances attach to. Create isolated networks with lxc network create and attach instances with --network on launch. Check usage with lxc network show <name>.

commands.desc: Show an instance's full config
commands.tooltip: Prints web01's complete configuration as YAML, including limits, devices, and profiles. Edit values with lxc config set web01 <key> <value>. The output is also what lxc edit would open for changes.

commands.desc: Start a local Kubernetes cluster
commands.tooltip: Creates and starts a single-node Kubernetes cluster on your machine using the default driver (Docker on Linux). The first run downloads a VM image or container, so it can take a while. Check readiness with minikube status.

commands.desc: Show cluster status
commands.tooltip: Reports whether the minikube cluster's host, kubelet, and API server components are running. If something is down, the output names which part failed. Start or repair with minikube start and minikube delete.

commands.desc: Stop the local cluster
commands.tooltip: Shuts down the minikube VM or container, pausing the cluster while preserving its state. Start it again later with minikube start, and the same workloads come back. To remove the cluster entirely, use minikube delete.

commands.desc: Open the Kubernetes web dashboard
commands.tooltip: Launches the Kubernetes dashboard in your browser, showing cluster resources in a UI. It starts a proxy automatically and prints the URL in the terminal. Combine with kubectl port-forward for services you want to browse.

commands.desc: Expose LoadBalancer services locally
commands.tooltip: Runs a network tunnel so services of type LoadBalancer get reachable IPs on your machine, which minikube otherwise cannot provide. Keep the command running in its own terminal. Use it after kubectl expose deployment web --type=LoadBalancer --port=80.

commands.desc: Delete the local cluster
commands.tooltip: Destroys the minikube cluster and its data, including everything you deployed, with no undo. The same minikube start later creates a fresh empty cluster. Use minikube stop instead when you just want to pause work.

commands.desc: List available minikube addons
commands.tooltip: Shows every addon (optional bundled component like ingress, dashboard, or metrics-server) with its enabled status. Addons extend what a local cluster can do without manual installs. Enable one with minikube addons enable ingress.

commands.desc: Enable an addon
commands.tooltip: Turns on the ingress addon, installing the nginx ingress controller so ingress resources route traffic on the local cluster. The same pattern enables metrics-server for kubectl top. Confirm with minikube addons list.

commands.desc: Enable the metrics-server addon
commands.tooltip: Installs the metrics server, the component that powers kubectl top nodes and pod autoscaling. Without it, kubectl top reports an error about the Metrics API. Enable it before setting up HorizontalPodAutoscalers.

commands.desc: Show the cluster's IP address
commands.tooltip: Prints the IP of the minikube VM or container, which you need to reach NodePort services from your machine. Combine with the node port, for example curl http://$(minikube ip):30080. For LoadBalancer services, use minikube tunnel.

commands.desc: Open a service's URL in the browser
commands.tooltip: Finds the web service's URL and opens it in your default browser, or prints it with --url. It handles NodePort and LoadBalancer services for you. Pair with minikube tunnel for LoadBalancer types.

commands.desc: Create a default kind cluster
commands.tooltip: Creates a Kubernetes cluster named kind running entirely in Docker containers, with one control-plane node. kind (Kubernetes in Docker) is the fastest way to spin up a local cluster for testing. Point kubectl at it with kubectl config use-context kind-kind.

commands.desc: Create a named kind cluster
commands.tooltip: Creates a second cluster named dev, letting you run several isolated clusters side by side. Each cluster gets its own context named kind-dev. List them with kind get clusters.

commands.desc: Create a cluster from a config file
commands.tooltip: Creates a cluster using the multi-node topology in kind-config.yaml, such as one control-plane and two workers, or custom ports. Config files unlock realistic test setups that the default single-node cluster cannot provide. Delete with kind delete cluster --name <name>.

commands.desc: List kind clusters
commands.tooltip: Prints the name of every kind cluster currently running on your machine. Each name maps to a kubectl context of the form kind-<name>. Remove one with kind delete cluster --name dev.

commands.desc: Delete the default kind cluster
commands.tooltip: Destroys the kind cluster and its Docker containers, deleting everything deployed in it with no undo. Running containers are removed too, so export anything important first. Use --name to target a specific cluster.

commands.desc: Load a local image into the cluster
commands.tooltip: Copies the myapp:latest image from your local Docker daemon into every node of the cluster, making it available to pods without a registry. kind nodes do not share your Docker images, so loading is required for local builds. Reference the image as myapp:latest in your manifests.

commands.desc: Export a cluster's kubeconfig
commands.tooltip: Writes the dev cluster's kubeconfig so other tools can reach it, defaulting to updating your main kubeconfig when no --kubeconfig flag is passed. Useful for pointing kubectl or k9s at a specific kind cluster. Related: kind get clusters lists the names.

commands.desc: Validate Prometheus config files for syntax errors
commands.tooltip: Parses every scrape_config, rule file reference, and global setting in your prometheus.yml and reports problems with file and line numbers. Add config paths as arguments, for example promtool check config /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml. Run it before restarting the server to avoid a broken scrape setup.

commands.desc: Validate Prometheus recording and alerting rules
commands.tooltip: Checks rule files for valid PromQL expressions, correct YAML, and sane structure. It flags rules that never fire and expressions that reference missing metrics. Run it in CI before deploying new alerting rules.

commands.desc: Validate the Prometheus web server config
commands.tooltip: Verifies the YAML passed to --web.config.file, covering TLS certificates, basic auth, and HTTP header settings for the web UI and API. It catches expired certificate paths and malformed bcrypt hashes before the server fails at startup.

commands.desc: Check a running Prometheus health endpoint
commands.tooltip: Queries the /-/healthy endpoint of a Prometheus server and reports whether it is alive. The server must be running and reachable. It returns a non-zero exit code when the server is down, which makes it useful in monitoring probes.

commands.desc: Check that Prometheus is ready for queries
commands.tooltip: Queries the /-/ready endpoint, which only reports ready after the server has finished loading TSDB data following a restart. Use it in load balancer checks to avoid querying a server that is still warming up.

commands.desc: Lint Prometheus metric names from stdin
commands.tooltip: Reads a metrics exposition file from standard input and flags metric and label names that break Prometheus naming rules. Pipe an exported file to it, for example cat metrics.prom | promtool check metrics. Add --extended for deeper consistency checks.

commands.desc: Deep-lint an exported metrics file
commands.tooltip: Runs the extended metric checks against a text-format metrics dump, validating naming conventions and unit consistency. The --extended mode also flags names whose _total or _seconds suffixes suggest unit mistakes. Feed it output from any exporter, such as a curl of a /metrics endpoint.

commands.desc: Run an instant PromQL query against a server
commands.tooltip: Evaluates a PromQL expression at the current time against the server given as the positional argument and prints the resulting series. The expression up returns one series per scrape target, where 1 means healthy and 0 means down. Add --time with an RFC3339 timestamp to evaluate at a past moment.

commands.desc: Evaluate a PromQL expression over a time range
commands.tooltip: Samples a PromQL expression between --start and --end at intervals of --step, letting you preview what a graph will show without opening the UI. rate(cpu[5m]) computes the per-second increase of a counter averaged over five-minute windows. Times accept RFC3339 or Unix epoch seconds.

commands.desc: List blocks in the Prometheus TSDB
commands.tooltip: Shows the time series blocks on disk in the TSDB (time series database), including each block's time range, series count, and size. Point it at the data directory with promtool tsdb list /var/lib/prometheus when the server uses a non-default path. Add -r for human-readable sizes.

commands.desc: Analyze TSDB blocks for cardinality
commands.tooltip: Reports which metric names and label pairs consume the most storage, helping you find high-cardinality series that bloat the TSDB. High cardinality from labels like user_id or pod names is the most common cause of Prometheus memory growth. Point it at the data directory, for example promtool tsdb analyze /var/lib/prometheus.

commands.desc: Dry-run service discovery against a config
commands.tooltip: Runs the service discovery and relabeling steps from your scrape config and prints the targets that would be scraped, without scraping them. It takes the config file and job name as arguments, for example promtool check service-discovery /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml node. Invaluable for debugging relabel rules.

commands.desc: Capture pprof profiles from a running Prometheus
commands.tooltip: Collects Go runtime performance profiles such as heap, CPU, and goroutines from a running server and stores them locally for analysis. The server URL is the required argument, for example promtool debug pprof http://localhost:9090. Use it when investigating memory growth or slow queries.

commands.desc: Dump self-metrics from a running Prometheus
commands.tooltip: Exports every metric the Prometheus server exposes about itself into a file for offline inspection. The server URL is the required argument. Combined with promtool debug all, this gives a full snapshot for debugging server performance problems.

commands.desc: Collect a full debug bundle from Prometheus
commands.tooltip: Bundles pprof profiles, self-metrics, and config into one archive for support and debugging sessions. It requires only the server URL. Prefer it when you are not sure which individual debug command you need.

commands.desc: Pretty-print a PromQL expression
commands.tooltip: Reformats a PromQL expression with consistent spacing and indentation so complex queries become readable. It is handy for cleaning up expressions pasted from dashboards. The formatted query prints to standard output without being evaluated.

commands.desc: Dump raw samples from a TSDB block
commands.tooltip: Prints the raw sample data stored in the TSDB at the given path, useful for low-level debugging of what exactly is on disk. Output can be enormous on production databases, so prefer tsdb analyze for cardinality questions.

commands.desc: Start the Prometheus server with a config file
commands.tooltip: Launches the Prometheus server reading its scrape and alerting configuration from the given file. The main config holds scrape_configs, rule file references, and alertmanager settings. Most distributions ship a systemd unit that already passes this flag, so run the binary directly only for test instances.

commands.desc: Start Prometheus bound to a specific address
commands.tooltip: Sets the address and port the web UI and API listen on, defaulting to 0.0.0.0:9090 on all interfaces. Bind to 127.0.0.1:9090 to keep the API private. Combine with --web.external-url when serving behind a reverse proxy.

commands.desc: Start Prometheus bound to localhost only
commands.tooltip: Restricts the web UI and API to the loopback interface so only local processes can reach port 9090. Useful for test instances or when a reverse proxy terminates TLS on the same host. The API is unauthenticated by default, so binding it to a public interface exposes full query and admin access.

commands.desc: Limit how long Prometheus keeps samples
commands.tooltip: Configures the retention window for samples in the TSDB (time series database); data older than 30 days is deleted in the background. Disk usage grows with retention, scrape frequency, and series count, so size the volume accordingly. Lower it on small disks and raise it when you need long-range queries.

commands.desc: Set the TSDB data directory for Prometheus
commands.tooltip: Points the TSDB (time series database) at a specific directory, defaulting to ./data in the working directory. Put it on a fast disk with room for at least two blocks plus head block headroom. Keep the path consistent across restarts or Prometheus starts a fresh empty database.

commands.desc: Advertise an external URL for the web UI
commands.tooltip: Tells Prometheus the public URL users and other systems use to reach it, which matters when it sits behind a reverse proxy or load balancer. Links in the web UI, alert notifications, and generated configs use this URL. Also pass --web.route-prefix when serving under a subpath.

commands.desc: Fetch the first metrics from the node exporter
commands.tooltip: Pulls the OpenMetrics text exposition from the node exporter's /metrics endpoint, which listens on port 9100 by default. Every line is one metric: name, labels in braces, and the current value. The head -20 shows the header, HELP and TYPE lines, and the first metrics.

commands.desc: Grep one metric from the node exporter
commands.tooltip: Filters the node exporter output for the node_cpu_seconds_total metric, which counts CPU time per core and per mode such as user or idle. It is a counter that only increases, so dashboards normally apply rate() to it in PromQL. Add the caret form '^node_cpu_seconds_total' to skip the HELP and TYPE lines.

commands.desc: Show status of the node exporter service
commands.tooltip: Displays whether the prometheus-node-exporter systemd unit is running, its PID, recent log lines, and the listen address. A failed state usually means a bad flag in the unit file. Follow with journalctl -u prometheus-node-exporter -f to watch live output.

commands.desc: Enable the node exporter textfile collector
commands.tooltip: Enables the textfile collector, which serves metrics from .prom files dropped into the given directory. Cron jobs write custom metrics there, such as backup duration or pending update counts, and the exporter exposes them alongside its built-in ones. The directory must exist and be readable by the exporter user.

commands.desc: Bind the node exporter to an address
commands.tooltip: Sets the address and port the node exporter listens on, defaulting to :9100 on all interfaces. Bind to 127.0.0.1:9100 when only a local Prometheus scrapes it, or to a private IP when Prometheus runs elsewhere. Change it in the systemd unit, then restart the service.

commands.desc: Enable the node exporter systemd collector
commands.tooltip: Activates the systemd collector, which exposes metrics about every unit on the host: active state, restart counts, and recent start times. It is opt-in because it is expensive on machines with hundreds of units. Filter which units are tracked with the --collector.systemd.unit-whitelist and --collector.systemd.unit-blacklist flags.

commands.desc: Start node exporter with only chosen collectors
commands.tooltip: Disables all default collectors so only the ones you enable explicitly run, cutting overhead on specialized hosts. Combine it with flags such as --collector.systemd to build a minimal collector set. Re-enable anything you still need, for example --collector.textfile.directory for custom metrics.

commands.desc: Query active alerts from Alertmanager
commands.tooltip: Lists the alerts currently firing or resolved in Alertmanager, using the server from --alertmanager.url or your amtool config file. Add label matchers to filter, for example amtool alert query alertname=HighCPU. Use -o json for machine-readable output in scripts.

commands.desc: Query alerts matching a label matcher
commands.tooltip: Filters Alertmanager's active alerts by label matchers, here any alert whose alertname label equals HighCPU. Matchers support regex and negation, so alertname=~'High.*' also works. Add -i or -s to include inhibited or silenced alerts in the listing.

commands.desc: Export active alerts as JSON
commands.tooltip: Prints Alertmanager's current alerts as a JSON array, ideal for piping into jq or other tooling. The simple output mode is the default; extended adds annotation fields. The alertmanager URL comes from --alertmanager.url or the amtool config file.

commands.desc: Create a silence for a fixed duration
commands.tooltip: Suppresses alert notifications for the given duration, here two hours, until it expires on its own. You must also pass label matchers to select which alerts are silenced, for example alertname=HighCPU. The --comment and --author fields are required by default and show up in the Alertmanager UI.

commands.cmd: amtool silence add alertname=HighCPU -d 1h -c 'scheduled maintenance' -a alice
commands.desc: Silence alerts matching a label matcher
commands.tooltip: Short-form silence creation: match alerts with alertname=HighCPU and mute them for one hour (-d). -c sets the comment and -a the author, both shown in the Alertmanager web UI. The flag is -d/--duration, not the --expires form older documentation shows.

commands.desc: Expire a silence by its ID
commands.tooltip: Immediately ends a silence identified by its UUID, which you can copy from the Alertmanager UI. Expiring is instant and cannot be undone, so confirm the ID first. Use it when a maintenance window ends early and you want notifications flowing again.

commands.desc: Validate an Alertmanager config file
commands.tooltip: Parses alertmanager.yml and reports problems with routes, receivers, and inhibit rules before you load it. Run it in CI or before restarting Alertmanager to avoid a config that silently drops notifications. Pass multiple files to check them together.

commands.desc: Point amtool at a specific Alertmanager
commands.tooltip: Overrides the Alertmanager endpoint for this invocation, here the default local address on port 9093. Without it amtool reads the URL from its config file or the AMTOOL_URL environment variable. Useful when several Alertmanager instances run on one host.

commands.desc: Install a Grafana plugin from the catalog
commands.tooltip: Downloads and installs a plugin from the Grafana catalog; grafana-clock-panel adds a live clock visualization. Bundled panels such as piechart are already built in, so pick a community plugin for install examples. Restart grafana-server afterwards so the plugin is picked up.

commands.desc: List plugins in the Grafana catalog
commands.tooltip: Shows every plugin in the remote Grafana catalog with its version, useful for finding plugin IDs before installing. Output is long, so pipe it through grep for a keyword. Note the subcommand form: the canonical syntax is grafana cli followed by the action.

commands.desc: List locally installed Grafana plugins
commands.tooltip: Prints the plugins installed on this Grafana instance with their versions and whether updates exist. Compare it against list-remote to spot outdated plugins. Plugins live under the data/plugins directory of the Grafana install.

commands.desc: Update one installed Grafana plugin
commands.tooltip: Upgrades a single plugin to the latest version from the catalog. Restart grafana-server afterwards so the new version is loaded. For plugins installed from a local zip, reinstall the zip instead.

commands.desc: Update every installed Grafana plugin
commands.tooltip: Upgrades all plugins on the instance to their latest versions in one pass. Useful after major Grafana upgrades, though plugin authors occasionally break compatibility, so check the release notes. Restart grafana-server after the update completes.

commands.desc: Uninstall a Grafana plugin
commands.tooltip: Removes a plugin from the Grafana installation, freeing space and hiding it from the panel list. Dashboard panels that used the removed plugin show an error until replaced. Restart grafana-server to complete the removal.

commands.desc: Reset the Grafana admin password from the CLI
commands.tooltip: Sets the admin user's password directly, bypassing the web UI login flow. On Debian packages add --homepath /usr/share/grafana or you get 'Could not find config defaults'. Restart grafana-server afterwards so the new password takes effect.

commands.desc: Show status of the Grafana server service
commands.tooltip: Reports whether the grafana-server systemd unit is running, its PID, memory use, and the last log lines. The web UI listens on port 3000 by default, so a healthy unit should answer on http://localhost:3000. Follow with journalctl -u grafana-server -f for live logs.

commands.desc: Follow Grafana server logs live
commands.tooltip: Streams new log lines from the grafana-server systemd unit as they are written, ideal for watching a startup or debugging a login issue. Press Ctrl+C to stop following. Add --since '10 min ago' to replay recent lines before following.

commands.desc: Check the Grafana health API endpoint
commands.tooltip: Returns the Grafana health status as JSON, including database connectivity, without requiring authentication. A response of database ok means the server is up and its backend store is reachable. Useful as a load balancer or monitoring probe.

commands.desc: Call the Grafana API with a service account token
commands.tooltip: Authenticates to the Grafana HTTP API using a service account token from Administration, Service accounts. The token travels as a Bearer token in the Authorization header; $GRAFANA_TOKEN expands from your environment. Authenticated calls can reach user-scoped endpoints such as /api/users.

commands.desc: Run Uptime Kuma in a Docker container
commands.tooltip: Starts Uptime Kuma, a self-hosted uptime monitor, detached (-d) with its web UI on port 3001. The named volume uptime-kuma-data persists monitors and settings, so data survives container recreation. Use image tag :2 for the current v2 release, not :1. Open http://localhost:3001 to create the admin account.

commands.desc: Run Uptime Kuma bound to localhost only
commands.tooltip: Same as the default run but binds the web UI to 127.0.0.1, so only the local machine can reach port 3001. Pair it with a reverse proxy like Caddy or nginx to serve Kuma over HTTPS. The monitor data volume and image tag :2 are unchanged.

commands.desc: Open the btop system monitor
commands.tooltip: Launches the btop TUI (terminal user interface) showing CPU, memory, disks, network, and process tables. Mouse and arrow-key navigation work out of the box. Press ? for the help overlay and q to quit.

commands.desc: Start btop with a saved preset layout
commands.tooltip: Loads preset layout number 1, one of ten saved box arrangements that persist between sessions. Presets are useful when you like a specific arrangement of CPU, memory, and process panes. Save your own layouts and cycle them with the p key.

commands.desc: Set the btop refresh interval in milliseconds
commands.tooltip: Sets the UI update interval to 500 milliseconds, down from the default 1000, for smoother graphs on fast machines. Lower values cost more CPU, so raise it on loaded servers or slow SSH links. The interval is also adjustable live with the plus and minus keys.

commands.desc: Start btop with a process filter applied
commands.tooltip: Pre-filters the process list to entries matching nginx, so only matching processes appear at startup. The filter is a substring match against process names. You can also press f while btop runs to filter interactively.

commands.desc: Start btop with a specific config file
commands.tooltip: Tells btop to read its configuration from the given path instead of the default ~/.config/btop/btop.conf. Useful for shipping a team-standard layout or testing theme changes without touching your real config. Generate a fresh default file with btop --default-config.

commands.desc: Analyze disk usage interactively starting at /home
commands.tooltip: Scans /home and opens an interactive TUI where you navigate directories with arrow keys and delete files with d. Sizes update progressively as the scan proceeds. Quit with q; nothing is deleted unless you confirm.

commands.desc: Print disk usage non-interactively
commands.tooltip: Runs a single non-interactive scan and prints a text table of the largest directories, suitable for scripts and SSH sessions. gdu is much faster than du because it reads the filesystem in parallel. Pair it with -o to write the result to a file for later analysis.

commands.desc: Analyze root without crossing filesystems
commands.tooltip: Scans / but does not descend into mounted filesystems like /proc, /sys, or other disks, mirroring du -x. Without it gdu would count kernel pseudo-files and remote mounts, inflating the total. Use it to measure a single filesystem's real usage.

commands.desc: Ignore hidden files in the gdu scan
commands.tooltip: Excludes dot-directories such as .cache and .config from the gdu scan, giving a clearer view of visible disk usage. The flag is -H/--no-hidden; current gdu has no --show-hidden option. Combine with -n for scripted output.

commands.desc: Show disk usage as a treemap bar chart
commands.tooltip: Renders directory sizes as an inverted treemap where the widest bar is the largest consumer, making outliers obvious at a glance. The current directory is scanned when no path is given. Use arrow keys or the mouse to navigate into subdirectories.

commands.desc: Limit dust output to the top 20 entries
commands.tooltip: Restricts the listing to the 20 largest entries, trimming the long tail of small directories. Useful when a scan produces hundreds of rows. The order still reflects size unless you add -r to reverse it.

commands.desc: Limit dust recursion to three levels deep
commands.tooltip: Stops the tree at depth 3, so only top-level, second-level, and third-level directories are shown. Deeper nesting is collapsed, which speeds up scans of large trees. Raise the depth when the real space hog sits far down the tree.

commands.desc: Sort dust output by apparent size
commands.tooltip: Sorts directories by apparent size, the sum of file lengths, instead of actual disk usage including filesystem block overhead. The two differ most on filesystems with large block sizes or many small files.

commands.desc: Hide bars and percentages in dust
commands.tooltip: Removes the size bars and percentage columns, leaving a compact plain listing of sizes. Useful for piping dust output into other commands or when the bars wrap on narrow terminals.

commands.desc: Restrict dust to a single filesystem
commands.tooltip: Prevents dust from crossing into other mounted filesystems while scanning /, so /proc, /sys, and external mounts are excluded. This mirrors the -x flag of du. Use it to measure one disk's usage without noise from pseudo-filesystems.

commands.desc: Show disk usage across mounted filesystems
commands.tooltip: Lists every mounted filesystem with size, used, available, and usage percentage in a color-coded table. It groups local disks, network mounts, and special filesystems into separate sections. The default view hides some pseudo-filesystems to reduce noise.

commands.desc: Show usage for filesystems under a path
commands.tooltip: Filters the duf output to the filesystem containing the given path, here /home. Pass multiple paths to see several at once. The filter also works with mount points such as duf /var/lib/docker.

commands.desc: Sort duf output by filesystem size
commands.tooltip: Orders the duf table by total size, largest first, so the biggest volumes stand out. Other sort keys such as usage or mountpoint are available. Combine with --only or --hide to restrict which filesystem types appear.

commands.desc: Emit duf output as JSON
commands.tooltip: Prints the filesystem table as JSON for scripting and monitoring integrations. Each entry carries device, mount point, and size fields in both human-readable and byte values. Pipe it through jq for custom formatting.

commands.desc: Show every filesystem including pseudo mounts
commands.tooltip: Includes pseudo, loop, and bind filesystems that duf hides by default, such as tmpfs, squashfs, and loop devices. Useful when tracking down container or snap storage. The output gets long, so combine with --sort size and grep for what you need.

commands.desc: Choose which columns duf prints
commands.tooltip: Restricts the table to the named columns, here mountpoint, size, and usage, in that order. Available fields include device, type, used, avail, and inodes. Useful for keeping the table narrow in scripts.

commands.desc: Show live per-process network usage
commands.tooltip: Displays which processes, connections, and remote hosts consume bandwidth in real time, with per-interface totals. It sniffs packets, so it usually needs root. Quit with q; press h for help. The default view shows local ports and remote addresses.

commands.desc: Monitor bandwidth on one interface
commands.tooltip: Limits packet capture to the given interface, here eth0, instead of sniffing all interfaces. Useful on machines with many virtual interfaces where the default view is noisy. Other flags such as -n cut further noise.

commands.desc: Disable DNS resolution in bandwhich
commands.tooltip: Skips reverse DNS lookups so remote hosts appear as raw IP addresses, speeding up the display and reducing network chatter. Handy on servers where DNS lookups are slow or blocked. Combine with -i to scope the capture to one interface.

commands.desc: Show total utilization instead of per process
commands.tooltip: Switches the display to overall interface utilization rather than per-process breakdowns, a cleaner view for spotting saturation. The total includes traffic bandwhich cannot attribute to a process. Use it with -i eth0 to watch a single uplink.

commands.desc: Show DNS queries in bandwhich
commands.tooltip: Adds a section listing DNS queries as they happen, showing which hosts are being resolved and by which process. Useful for spotting leaky or unexpected DNS traffic. It is off by default to keep the view compact.

commands.desc: Show GPU utilization and memory per process
commands.tooltip: Prints a one-screen summary of every GPU: utilization, memory used, temperature, and the processes using it. Think of it as nvidia-smi condensed to the essentials. Requires an NVIDIA driver and nvidia-smi on the PATH.

commands.desc: Continuously refresh the GPU status view
commands.tooltip: Re-renders the gpustat output every second by default, like watch for GPUs. Adjust the interval with -i, for example gpustat -i 2 for two-second updates. Press Ctrl+C to stop. Use it while training jobs run to watch utilization swing.

commands.desc: Refresh gpustat every two seconds
commands.tooltip: Sets the watch interval to two seconds instead of the default one. Longer intervals lower the CPU cost of the loop on busy machines. Combine with --watch or use it standalone for a periodic snapshot.

commands.desc: Dump GPU status as JSON
commands.tooltip: Emits GPU utilization, memory, and process data as JSON for scripts and dashboards. Pipe it into jq to extract a single field such as memory per GPU. The JSON contains one entry per GPU, keyed by index.

commands.desc: Show all GPU details including processes
commands.tooltip: Adds command lines, PIDs, and power draw to the standard gpustat summary. Useful when several jobs share one GPU and you need to see which process owns the memory. Combine with -P for power usage in watts.

commands.desc: Show live network traffic graphs
commands.tooltip: Renders incoming and outgoing traffic as moving bar graphs, with current, average, min, and max rates in the corner. By default it shows the first available interface; cycle through devices with the left and right arrow keys. Quit with q or Ctrl+C.

commands.desc: Monitor a specific network interface
commands.tooltip: Targets a single interface by name, passed positionally rather than with a flag. Pass several names to monitor multiple devices at once, and use -m to show them side by side. The device list is also cyclable with arrow keys.

commands.desc: Show nload rates in megabytes per second
commands.tooltip: Sets the display unit for traffic rates to MB/s; other letters are k for KB/s, g for GB/s, and b or B for bits and bytes. Uppercase means bytes and lowercase means bits, so -u m differs from -u M. Use -t to also tune the refresh interval.

commands.desc: Serve the Glances web interface
commands.tooltip: Starts Glances' built-in web server so you can view the same dashboard in a browser, on port 61208 by default. Add -B 127.0.0.1 to restrict the bind address when no reverse proxy is in front. The web mode shares the terminal dashboard's data.

commands.desc: Run Glances in server mode
commands.tooltip: Starts Glances as a server that clients attach to with glances -c, exporting all metrics over the network. By default it listens on 0.0.0.0:61209 with no authentication, so firewall it or add -P for a password. Server and client versions should match.

commands.desc: Connect a Glances client to a server
commands.tooltip: Attaches this Glances instance to a remote Glances server at the given address, showing the server's dashboard as if it were local. The server must run with glances -s. Use -p to override the default port 61209 and -P to supply a password.

commands.desc: Set the Glances refresh interval in seconds
commands.tooltip: Changes how often Glances refreshes its data, here every 5 seconds instead of the default 2. Longer intervals lower CPU and network overhead, handy over slow links or on busy hosts. The interval also applies to exported data.

commands.desc: Export Glances metrics to a CSV file
commands.tooltip: Writes sampled metrics to a CSV file in the current directory while Glances runs, one row per interval. Other exporters include json, influxdb, statsd, and prometheus. For Prometheus output, configure host and port in the [prometheus] section of glances.conf instead of CLI flags.

commands.desc: Show Glances network rates in bytes
commands.tooltip: Forces byte-based units for network and disk rates instead of the auto-scaled human format. Handy when you want exact numbers for scripts or comparisons. The dashboard layout stays the same otherwise.

commands.desc: Show per-CPU usage in Glances
commands.tooltip: Splits the CPU section into one line per core instead of a single aggregate, revealing one saturated core on an otherwise idle machine. It matches the 1 key inside the UI. Combine with -t for a slower refresh on big machines.

commands.desc: Bind Glances services to an address
commands.tooltip: Restricts the web and server listeners to the given address, here the loopback interface, so remote hosts cannot connect. Pair it with -w or -s to control exactly where the service is reachable. Leave it off when clients on other hosts must connect.

commands.desc: Show status of the netdata service
commands.tooltip: Reports whether the netdata systemd unit is running and serving metrics on port 19999, plus recent log lines. A healthy instance answers on http://localhost:19999. Watch the agent logs with journalctl -u netdata -f.

commands.desc: Export netdata metrics in Prometheus format
commands.tooltip: Pulls every metric netdata collects, rewritten as Prometheus exposition text so a Prometheus server can scrape it directly. The format parameter also accepts json and shell. This endpoint is how you wire netdata into an existing Prometheus setup.

commands.desc: Export netdata metrics as JSON
commands.tooltip: Returns all collected metrics as a JSON object, useful for scripts and custom dashboards. The format parameter switches between json, prometheus, and shell output. Pipe it through jq to extract a single chart's values.

commands.desc: List all netdata charts as JSON
commands.tooltip: Returns the full catalog of charts netdata maintains, each with its id, title, units, and dimensions. Use jq to pretty-print and filter, for example .charts | keys to see the names. Chart ids feed the /api/v1/data endpoint for raw samples.

commands.desc: List netdata alarms and their states
commands.tooltip: Shows every configured alarm with its current status, from OK through WARNING and CRITICAL, plus the triggering value. The output is a flat list of alarm objects, so filter with jq for just the critical ones. Notifications still go through the configured channels.

commands.desc: Show netdata version and build info
commands.tooltip: Returns the netdata version, host details, and collection configuration as JSON. A cheap way to confirm which release is running and whether the agent sees its host correctly. The same info appears in the dashboard footer.

commands.desc: Fetch raw samples for one netdata chart
commands.tooltip: Queries the samples behind a chart, here system.cpu for the last 60 seconds, with dimension names and values in JSON. The after parameter accepts negative offsets from now. This is the API behind the dashboard graphs, useful for scripting custom checks.

commands.desc: Print netdata build and version details
commands.tooltip: Prints compile-time options, the version, and plugin configuration of the netdata binary. Run it to confirm feature flags before enabling a plugin or filing a bug. The -W prefix is netdata's generic way to pass internal commands.

commands.desc: Reload netdata health configuration
commands.tooltip: Sends the USR2 signal to the netdata process, which reloads alarm definitions from health.d without a full restart. Sending HUP instead reopens log files. Use it after editing alarm files so new checks apply immediately.

commands.desc: Show per-process disk I/O usage
commands.tooltip: Lists processes sorted by their current disk read and write throughput, with cumulative totals. It needs root to see other users' processes and to read kernel I/O counters. Quit with q; the display refreshes every second by default.

commands.desc: Show only processes doing active I/O
commands.tooltip: Filters the listing to processes that performed I/O during the last refresh, hiding the idle ones. This is the standard flag for finding what is hammering the disk right now. Combine with -b -n 3 for a three-shot batch snapshot in scripts.

commands.desc: Run iotop in batch mode for three samples
commands.tooltip: Non-interactive mode prints the current I/O table, then exits after -n 3 samples, suitable for cron jobs and log files. Each batch line carries a timestamp. Add -k to display sizes in kilobytes.

commands.desc: Show I/O per process, not per thread
commands.tooltip: Aggregates I/O at the process level instead of listing each thread separately, cutting noise on multi-threaded applications. The default view shows threads, which can look like duplicated entries. Combine with -o to keep only the busy ones.

commands.desc: Show iotop rates in kilobytes
commands.tooltip: Displays I/O throughput in kilobytes instead of the default human-readable units. Useful when you want exact numbers for scripts or comparisons. It pairs well with batch mode for logged output.

commands.desc: Show NVIDIA GPU status summary
commands.tooltip: Prints every NVIDIA GPU: name, driver and CUDA version, utilization, memory, temperature, and running processes. The table updates once, so pair it with watch for a live view. Requires the NVIDIA driver and CUDA toolkit libraries.

commands.desc: Refresh nvidia-smi every five seconds
commands.tooltip: Re-runs the GPU summary every 5 seconds, equivalent to watch -n 5 nvidia-smi. The loop keeps running until Ctrl+C. Newer drivers also accept -lms for millisecond intervals during benchmarks.

commands.desc: Query specific GPU fields as CSV
commands.tooltip: Selects only the requested fields, here name, utilization, and memory used, and prints them as CSV for scripts. Add --format=csv,noheader to skip the header row. Queryable fields include temperature, power.draw, and clocks.

commands.desc: Trim journal files to a maximum size
commands.tooltip: Deletes the oldest journal files until the remaining ones total at most 500 MB. This permanently removes those logs, so archive anything you need first. Run it when journald's disk usage creeps up; the counterpart --vacuum-time keeps only recent days.

commands.desc: Delete journal entries older than 30 days
commands.tooltip: Removes journal files whose contents are all older than 30 days, freeing space while keeping recent history. The oldest files go first, so recent logs are never touched. Combine it with --vacuum-size if you also want a hard size cap.

commands.desc: Rotate journal files immediately
commands.tooltip: Tells journald to close the current journal file and start a new one, which helps when a file is corrupted or you need clean rotation before shipping logs. New entries go to the fresh file. Usually follow it with --vacuum-size to actually reclaim space.

commands.desc: Check journal files for corruption
commands.tooltip: Scans all journal files for structural damage and missing entries, reporting per-file status. Run it if timestamps jump or entries vanish, then rotate and vacuum to rebuild if problems appear. The scan is read-only and safe on a live system.

commands.desc: Print journal entries as JSON objects
commands.tooltip: Formats each log entry as a JSON object with fields like __REALTIME_TIMESTAMP, _PID, and MESSAGE, ideal for piping into jq or a log shipper. Add -n 50 to limit the volume of JSON produced.

commands.desc: Dry-run logrotate to debug configs
commands.tooltip: Debug mode prints every decision logrotate would make, which files rotate, when, and why, without touching any log. Use it to test config changes safely, including files included from /etc/logrotate.d. Errors show exactly which directive is misconfigured.

commands.desc: Force logrotate to run now
commands.tooltip: Forces rotation regardless of the age or size rules, useful after editing configs or when a log must rotate immediately. Because it bypasses the schedule, files rotate even when they would not normally. Handy before compressing a directory of logs.

commands.desc: Follow Uptime Kuma container logs
commands.tooltip: Streams the logs of the uptime-kuma service defined in docker-compose.yml, tagged by container and colored per service. Press Ctrl+C to stop following. Run it from the directory containing your compose file, or pass -f path/to/docker-compose.yml.

commands.desc: Check the Prometheus health endpoint
commands.tooltip: Returns a short health message with HTTP 200 when the server is up; any other status means the process is down or restarting. This is the endpoint load balancers and monitoring probes use. Use it in monitoring checks instead of scraping metrics.

commands.desc: Query the Prometheus HTTP API for instant results
commands.tooltip: Evaluates the PromQL expression up against the Prometheus API and pretty-prints the JSON with jq. The -G flag keeps parameters in the URL while --data-urlencode encodes them safely. Results appear under .data.result, one series per scrape target.

commands.desc: Test if the fail2ban server is running
commands.tooltip: Fail2ban watches log files and bans repeated offenders with firewall rules. The ping command asks the fail2ban-server daemon to answer, confirming the client can reach it. A pong reply means the service is alive. Pair with systemctl status fail2ban to inspect service health.

commands.desc: Reload fail2ban configuration without restarting the server
commands.tooltip: Applies changes made in /etc/fail2ban/jail.conf and jail.d/*.conf while keeping the daemon and current bans intact. Use it after editing jail settings or filter definitions. For a full restart of one jail, fail2ban-client restart sshd restarts just that jail.
