commands.desc: Cap CPU and memory for a service
commands.tooltip: Limits each task to half a CPU and 512 MB of memory; exceeding memory kills the task. Limits apply per task, not per service. Reserve values guarantee capacity with --reserve-cpu and --reserve-memory.

commands.desc: Show full task details of a service
commands.tooltip: Lists every task (replica instance) of the web service with state, node, and error columns. --no-trunc stops Docker abbreviating long fields like image digests. Errors from failed tasks appear here.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 log lines of a service
commands.tooltip: Aggregates logs from all tasks of the web service, newest first with --tail 100. --follow streams live output. Requires the json-file or journald logging driver.

commands.desc: List services as a custom table
commands.tooltip: Enumerates swarm services with name and replica counts; --format trims the columns via Go templates. The Replicas column shows ready versus desired counts. Filter with --filter name=web.

commands.desc: Scale multiple services at once
commands.tooltip: Adjusts replica counts for several services in one call, starting or stopping tasks as needed. Each service is scaled independently. The same as docker service update --replicas per service.

commands.desc: Deploy a stack from a compose file
commands.tooltip: Creates or updates the mystack stack from stack.yml, converting services into swarm services and networks into overlay networks. Stacks are the production deployment unit of swarm mode. Redeploy to apply changes.

commands.desc: Deploy a stack forwarding registry credentials
commands.tooltip: Passes the local registry login to the swarm nodes so they can pull private images. Without it, workers hit auth errors on private registries. The credentials are sent to nodes at deploy time.

commands.desc: Render a stack's merged configuration
commands.tooltip: Prints the fully resolved stack config after merging files and interpolation, without deploying. Use it to validate stack.yml before docker stack deploy. The -c flag selects the compose file.

commands.desc: Show full task details of a stack
commands.tooltip: Lists every task across the stack's services with state and node columns. --no-trunc reveals full digests and error messages. The deploy column distinguishes updates.

commands.desc: Create a swarm secret from stdin
commands.tooltip: Feeds the secret value through stdin, with - as the file argument, keeping it out of shell history. Swarm secrets mount into tasks as files at /run/secrets. Rotate by creating a new secret and updating the service.

commands.desc: Inspect a swarm secret in readable form
commands.tooltip: Shows metadata of the secret mysecret, including creation time and ID. --pretty formats the JSON for humans instead of raw output. Secret values themselves are never readable after creation.

commands.desc: Inspect a swarm config in readable form
commands.tooltip: Displays metadata of the config myconfig, which holds non-sensitive files like nginx configs distributed to tasks. Configs differ from secrets in being viewable. --pretty makes the JSON readable.

commands.desc: Print the active Docker context
commands.tooltip: Prints the name of the currently selected context, which determines which daemon docker talks to. Contexts bundle endpoints, credentials, and TLS settings. Switch with docker context use.

commands.desc: Create a context for a remote daemon
commands.tooltip: Defines a context pointing at a remote Docker daemon over TCP with TLS on port 2376. The ssh:// form tunnels through SSH instead. Select it with docker context use myremote.

commands.desc: Show disk usage by Docker resource type
commands.tooltip: Summarizes disk consumed by images, containers, volumes, and build cache, the first stop for disk-pressure debugging. --format renders a Go template per line. Add --verbose for per-item details.

commands.desc: Show the Docker server version
commands.tooltip: Prints one field of the daemon's info payload, here the server version, handy for scripts that gate on engine features. Default output is a long human report. The full JSON is available with --format '{{json .}}'.

commands.desc: Show the server version from docker version
commands.tooltip: Extracts just the server version from the version report, ideal for CI checks. Default docker version prints client and server sections. Compare with docker system info for the same value.

commands.desc: Start the Docker daemon with a config file
commands.tooltip: Launches the daemon using settings from daemon.json, where storage driver, registries, and limits live. Normally started by systemd, so validate configs before hand-running it. Run as root.

commands.desc: Run the daemon with a custom data directory
commands.tooltip: Relocates all Docker state (images, containers, volumes) to /mnt/docker-data instead of the default /var/lib/docker. Useful when the root filesystem is small. Existing data must be moved or the daemon starts empty.

commands.desc: Run the daemon with the overlay2 storage driver
commands.tooltip: Selects overlay2, the standard modern storage driver using copy-on-write layers. Most distros default to it; set it explicitly on unusual filesystems. A wrong driver can corrupt images, so prefer the default.

commands.desc: Validate a Dockerfile without building
commands.tooltip: Runs BuildKit's checker against the Dockerfile, catching syntax errors and anti-patterns without executing steps. It is shorthand for docker build --call=check. Fast feedback before slow full builds.

commands.desc: Build using the host network
commands.tooltip: Lets RUN steps reach the host's network directly, bypassing BuildKit's default sandboxed networking. Needed when builds pull from private hosts only the host can see. Slower builds and weaker isolation are the trade-off.

commands.desc: Revoke a signed image trust record
commands.tooltip: Removes the trusted signature for myapp:latest, so clients with Docker Content Trust enabled refuse to pull it. Signatures prove who built the image; revoking is permanent for that tag. Re-sign with docker trust sign.

commands.desc: List containers with name and ports only
commands.tooltip: Renders the container table with just names and port mappings via Go templates, narrow enough for wide screens. Fields like {{.Status}} and {{.Image}} are available. Omit table for headerless lines.

commands.desc: List containers created from an image
commands.tooltip: Matches containers whose image is nginx or shares its ancestry, useful after bulk image rebuilds. Other filters include name, status, and label. Combine with -q to feed IDs into cleanup loops.

commands.desc: Rebase while keeping stacked branches updated
commands.tooltip: During an interactive rebase, --update-refs also moves any branch that points at a rebased commit, so stacked branches follow their base. Without it those branches keep pointing at the old commits. It only affects local branches.

commands.desc: Rebase while preserving merge commits
commands.tooltip: Interactive rebase normally flattens merges away; --rebase-merges keeps the merge structure and re-creates the merge commits on the new base. It is essential for rebasing branches with intentional merge topology. Conflicts may need to be re-resolved at each merge.

commands.desc: Run a command after every rebased commit
commands.tooltip: Runs the given command after each commit is replayed, stopping the rebase if it fails. Use it to verify every step still passes tests during a long rebase. The -x shorthand works the same.

commands.desc: Rewrite history back to the first commit
commands.tooltip: Extends an interactive rebase to the very first commit instead of stopping at a fixed HEAD~N. Useful for fixing the root commit or its author. Rewriting the root changes every commit hash, so never do it on published history.

commands.desc: Undo a bad reset using the reflog
commands.tooltip: Resets to the state recorded one step ago in the reflog, the standard escape hatch after a destructive reset --hard. The reflog logs every HEAD movement, so the lost commit is usually still reachable. Do this before garbage collection prunes the orphaned objects.

commands.desc: Reset your branch to match the remote
commands.tooltip: Throws away all local commits and working-tree changes on the current branch, pointing it at origin/main exactly. Every local-only commit is lost, so check git log first. Prefer it only when the local branch is known to be garbage.

commands.desc: Reset while preserving local changes
commands.tooltip: Moves the branch back one commit but keeps working-tree and staged changes intact, aborting if they conflict with the reset. It is a safer middle ground between --mixed and --hard. Files touched only by the reset get updated.

commands.desc: Reset without losing overlapping changes
commands.tooltip: Resets to the given commit but refuses if the working tree has changes that overlap with the difference. It can also cancel an in-progress merge cleanly. When it fails, stash or commit before resetting.

commands.desc: Inspect the reflog five steps back
commands.tooltip: Shows the state of HEAD five moves ago, complete with the hash and what changed. Combined with git reset --hard HEAD@{5} it restores exactly that point. The reflog is local to your machine and expires after 90 days by default.

commands.desc: Revert a commit without committing yet
commands.tooltip: Computes the inverse of the named commit and stages it in the index and working tree, leaving the revert commit for you to make. Combine several -n reverts into one commit, or review before committing. It is the batch-friendly revert.

commands.desc: Revert a merge commit
commands.tooltip: Undoes a merge by replaying its inverse against one of its parents; -m 1 selects the first parent, usually the mainline. Reverting a merge without -m fails because the direction is ambiguous. The reverted change still exists in the merged branch's history.

commands.desc: Finish a revert after resolving conflicts
commands.tooltip: Completes a conflicted revert once the files are fixed and staged, reusing the prepared revert message. It is the revert counterpart of git rebase --continue. Resolve and git add every conflicted file first.

commands.desc: Cancel an in-progress revert
commands.tooltip: Stops the current revert and restores the branch and working tree to their pre-revert state. All conflict resolutions made during the attempt are discarded. It is the clean escape when a revert gets messy.

commands.desc: Cherry-pick and record the source commit
commands.tooltip: Applies the named commit to the current branch and appends a line noting the original commit hash in the new message. The -x trailer makes provenance traceable across branches. Use it when cherry-picking between long-lived branches.

commands.desc: Cherry-pick without committing
commands.tooltip: Applies the changes from the named commit to the index and working tree without creating a commit. It is useful for staging several picks and committing them as one. The -n shorthand stands for --no-commit.

commands.desc: Finish a cherry-pick after fixing conflicts
commands.tooltip: Completes a conflicted cherry-pick once conflicts are resolved and staged, keeping the original commit message. It is the cherry-pick counterpart of git rebase --continue. Resolve all conflicts and git add the files first.

commands.desc: Cancel an in-progress cherry-pick
commands.tooltip: Stops the current cherry-pick and restores the branch to its state before the operation began. Any conflict resolutions made along the way are discarded. Run it when a pick turns out to be more trouble than it is worth.

commands.desc: Create a GPG-signed commit
commands.tooltip: Signs the commit with your GPG key so others can verify its authorship. Configure the key with git config user.signingkey and enable signing by default with commit.gpgsign true. Verify signatures with git verify-commit.

commands.desc: Rewrite the last commit with your identity
commands.tooltip: Amends the most recent commit and resets its author to your configured identity, fixing commits made with the wrong name or email. Handy after realizing you committed with a work account. Amending changes the hash, so avoid it on pushed commits.

commands.desc: Verify a commit's GPG signature
commands.tooltip: Checks the GPG signature on the named commit against the signer's key and reports whether it is valid. Commits that are not signed produce an error, which scripts can use as a gate. The -v flag prints the full commit contents alongside.

commands.desc: Skip an unbuildable commit during bisect
commands.tooltip: Marks the current commit as un-testable and moves the search to another candidate, since a broken build would pollute the results. Use it when a commit cannot compile or the test cannot run. The search continues between the remaining good and bad boundaries.

commands.desc: Show the current bisect progress
commands.tooltip: Prints the entire bisect session: the start points and every good, bad, and skip marking so far. It lets you verify the session or replay it later with git bisect replay. Run it before git bisect reset to keep a record.

commands.desc: Remove stale worktree bookkeeping
commands.tooltip: Cleans up administrative data for worktrees whose directories were deleted behind Git's back. Git normally prunes automatically, but crashes and manual deletions leave clutter. Run git worktree list to see what remains.

commands.desc: Compare two versions of a branch
commands.tooltip: Shows how two commit ranges relate commit by commit, pairing equivalent patches and marking changed, added, or dropped ones. It is the standard tool for reviewing a rebase or a cherry-pick batch. The symmetric-difference syntax a...b is the common form.

commands.desc: Generate a patch file for the last commit
commands.tooltip: Writes the latest commit as an email-style patch file named 0001-subject.patch in the current directory. Others can apply it with git am. The -1 limits it to one commit; use -3 or a range for more.

commands.desc: Stream a patch series and apply it
commands.tooltip: The left side prints the last three commits as one patch stream; the right side applies them with three-way merging where needed. The -3 on am falls back to a three-way merge against the original blobs when a patch does not apply cleanly. This is the classic email-based contribution pipeline.

commands.desc: Package the repo into a single file
commands.tooltip: Writes the entire repository, including all branches and tags, into one portable bundle file. Transfer the file to another machine and clone or fetch from it without any network. It is the standard offline transfer and backup format.

commands.desc: Check a bundle's integrity
commands.tooltip: Validates that the bundle file is well-formed, its prerequisites are satisfied, and its commits are reachable. Run it before cloning from a bundle you received. It reports which prerequisite commits are missing.

commands.desc: List the refs inside a bundle
commands.tooltip: Shows every branch and tag contained in the bundle file without unpacking it. It is the inspection step before deciding which ref to clone or fetch. The heads are the entry points into the bundled history.

commands.desc: Strip a file from all of history
commands.tooltip: Removes the named path from every commit, rewriting all affected hashes, so the file is gone from the entire history. filter-repo is the maintained successor to filter-branch, which the Git project now recommends against. Anyone with a clone of the old history can still retrieve the file, so rotate any exposed secrets.

commands.desc: Profile repository history for cleanup
commands.tooltip: Scans the whole history and writes a report of the largest files, biggest extensions, and busiest paths into .git/filter-repo/. It is the first step before rewriting history with --strip-blobs-bigger-than or --path. The analysis itself changes nothing.

commands.desc: Enable sparse checkout with cone mode
commands.tooltip: Turns on sparse checkout, so future checkouts only materialize the directories you choose. Cone mode is the simpler, recommended pattern matching. Follow with git sparse-checkout set to pick directories.

commands.desc: Limit the working tree to one directory
commands.tooltip: Restricts the checkout to the given directory, shrinking disk use in huge monorepos. Files outside the set are removed from the working tree but stay in the repository. Add more directories with git sparse-checkout add.

commands.desc: Restore a full checkout
commands.tooltip: Turns sparse checkout off and materializes the entire working tree again. It is the undo for a limited checkout. The repository data was never missing, only the on-disk files.

commands.desc: Set up Git LFS for this machine
commands.tooltip: Registers Git LFS hooks and filters so large files tracked with LFS are handled transparently. Git LFS stores big files outside the repository and swaps in small pointer files. Run it once per machine after installing git-lfs.

commands.desc: Tell Git LFS to manage a file type
commands.tooltip: Adds a pattern to .gitattributes so matching files, here Photoshop files, are stored as LFS pointers instead of blobs. The pointer keeps the commit small while the real content lives on the LFS server. Commit the .gitattributes change.

commands.desc: List files stored in Git LFS
commands.tooltip: Shows every file the repository tracks with LFS, including its size and the commit that added it. Use it to audit how much data LFS is carrying. Add --long for full hashes and --all to include every revision.

commands.desc: Convert existing files to Git LFS
commands.tooltip: Rewrites history so matching files are stored as LFS pointers retroactively, shrinking the repository. It rewrites every affected commit hash and requires a force push, so coordinate with the whole team first. Back up the repository before running it.

commands.desc: Find objects not reachable from any ref
commands.tooltip: Lists commits, trees, and blobs that no branch, tag, or reflog reaches, often the remains of rebases and resets. These are candidates for recovery with git show or for pruning with git gc. The --lost-found option writes dangling objects to disk.

commands.desc: Force garbage collection immediately
commands.tooltip: Runs a full garbage collection and prunes unreferenced objects right away instead of respecting the default grace period. Any commit only reachable via the reflog or dangling objects is permanently deleted. Only run it after you are certain nothing needs recovery.

commands.desc: Resolve conflicts in favor of the incoming branch
commands.tooltip: The -X theirs strategy option makes merge conflicts resolve automatically to the incoming branch's version, while -X ours prefers the current branch. It removes the manual conflict step but can silently drop the losing side's changes. Reserve it for well-understood merges.

commands.desc: Push every ref to mirror a remote
commands.tooltip: Pushes all branches, tags, and remote-tracking refs, and deletes anything on the remote that is missing locally, making it an exact copy. It can destroy branches on the remote, so never point it at a shared repository. It is meant for backup and migration mirrors.

commands.desc: Search every commit for a pattern
commands.tooltip: Expands git rev-list --all into every commit hash and greps each one's tree, turning git grep into a whole-history search. It is how you hunt for secrets or deleted code across all time. Expect slow runs on large repositories.

commands.desc: Ignore local changes to a tracked file
commands.tooltip: Marks the file so Git ignores local modifications to it, keeping the committed version intact. It is designed for files that differ per machine, like local config, and is stronger than assume-unchanged. Revert with --no-skip-worktree when you want changes tracked again.

commands.desc: Stop ignoring local changes to a file
commands.tooltip: Clears the skip-worktree bit set earlier, so the file's local modifications are tracked and visible again in git status. It is the undo for --skip-worktree. Run it before editing the file if you want the change committed.

commands.desc: Find the common ancestor of two branches
commands.tooltip: Prints the merge base, the most recent commit shared by both branches. It is the reference point for diffs and rebases between them. Scripts use it to compute what each branch added.

commands.desc: Take your version of a conflicted file
commands.tooltip: Resolves the conflict in the named file by taking your side, stage two, of the merge. --theirs picks the incoming side instead. The file is then staged as resolved. Use it when one side is known to be correct.

commands.desc: Take the incoming version of a conflicted file
commands.tooltip: Resolves the conflict by keeping the branch being merged in, stage three, and discarding your local changes to that file. --ours is the opposite. After running it the file still needs a final commit to finish the merge.

commands.desc: Mark a commit to be amended into another
commands.tooltip: The amend: form of --fixup marks the new commit to be folded into the target using the combined message, which rebase --autosquash applies automatically. Plain --fixup discards the fixup message in favor of the target's. Both keep history tidy without manual todo editing.

commands.desc: Initialize an empty bare repository
commands.tooltip: A bare repository holds only Git's internal data with no working tree, so no files are ever checked out. Bare repos are the standard layout for central shared remotes and self-hosted servers. Push into one directly and clone from it like any other remote.

commands.desc: Clone a full mirror of a repository
commands.tooltip: A mirror clone is a bare copy that includes every branch, tag, and remote ref exactly as on the origin. Use it to back up a repository or migrate it to another host. Keep it in sync later with git push --mirror.

commands.desc: Clone a repository and all its submodules
commands.tooltip: A submodule is a nested Git repository pinned to a specific commit inside another repository. The --recurse-submodules flag initializes and checks out every submodule right after the clone finishes. Without it the submodule directories stay empty until you run git submodule update --init.

commands.desc: Clone history only since a given date
commands.tooltip: A shallow clone downloads only commits newer than the given date, cutting transfer size for very old histories. The commit graph is truncated, so operations like git log --follow or merging deep history may need to fetch more. Use --depth 1 for the absolute minimum history.

commands.desc: Clone a repository without file contents
commands.tooltip: A partial clone, here blobless, fetches commits and trees but defers file versions until you actually need them. Files download on demand when you check out or diff them, making huge repositories clone fast. It is a good fit for monorepos and very large codebases.

commands.desc: Clone only a single branch of a repository
commands.tooltip: The --single-branch flag fetches just the named branch instead of every branch and tag. Pair it with --branch to pin the checkout to a specific branch or tag, like a release line. It is handy for CI jobs and for exploring one version without downloading everything.

commands.desc: Show compact status with branch and tracking info
commands.tooltip: Adding --branch to the short format puts the current branch and its upstream on the first line, like main...origin/main [ahead 2]. The remaining lines use two-column shorthand, XY, for staging and working-tree state. It is the compact status most people use day to day.

commands.desc: Print status in a stable script-friendly format
commands.tooltip: The porcelain format is a guaranteed-stable variant of the short format designed for scripts and tools to parse. Its output never changes between Git versions, unlike human-oriented output. Use it in CI checks instead of parsing git status -s.

commands.desc: List ignored files alongside normal status
commands.tooltip: Shows tracked, untracked, and ignored files in one view, with ignored paths under their own section. It is useful for spotting .gitignore patterns that no longer match anything. Combine it with --short for a compact listing.

commands.desc: Summarize changed files with line counts
commands.tooltip: Prints one line per changed file with insertions and deletions drawn as plus and minus bars, plus a final total. It answers what changed and how much without any patch detail. Append it to most diff commands, such as git diff --stat origin/main.

commands.desc: Show numeric add and delete counts per file
commands.tooltip: The numstat format is a machine-friendly diff summary with tab-separated added, deleted, and filename columns. Scripts use it to compute churn or estimate review size. Binary files show a dash in both count columns.

commands.desc: List only the names of changed files
commands.tooltip: Prints just the file paths touched between the two commits, with no diff content. It is the fastest way to get the file list for a commit, a range, or your working tree. Pipe the output to tools like xargs to lint only the changed files.

commands.desc: Show changes word by word instead of line by line
commands.tooltip: A line-based diff hides small edits inside a long line, so --word-diff splits changes at word boundaries instead. Deleted words appear wrapped in [- -] and added words in {+ +}. It shines for prose, config files, and long JSON lines.

commands.desc: Flag whitespace errors in a diff
commands.tooltip: Scans the diff for trailing whitespace, space-before-tab, and blank-line-at-EOF problems and lists each occurrence. It is a common pre-commit gate in CI pipelines. The command returns a non-zero exit code when errors are found, so scripts can fail the build.

commands.desc: Show the latest changes to a single file
commands.tooltip: Diffs the named path between the previous commit and the working tree, filtering the patch to just that file. The HEAD~1 syntax means the commit one step before HEAD. Use HEAD~3 or a branch name to look further back.

commands.desc: Diff two files outside a repository
commands.tooltip: The --no-index mode compares two arbitrary files or directories with the normal diff engine, even outside any Git repository. It reports differences with the same patch formatting Git always uses. Useful for spotting drift between two config files or generated outputs.

commands.desc: Mark a new file as intent-to-add
commands.tooltip: The -N flag registers a new file so git diff and git diff --stat start showing its content before it is staged. The file appears in the index as empty rather than untracked. Follow up with git add when you are ready to stage the real content.

commands.desc: Edit the staged patch in your editor
commands.tooltip: Stages the file but opens the generated patch in your editor first, letting you hand-edit hunks before they enter the index. It is a surgical alternative to git add -p when you know exactly what belongs in the commit. Save and close the editor to apply the edited patch.

commands.desc: Preview what git add would stage
commands.tooltip: Reports which files would be added, modified, or removed without changing the index. Run it before a big git add to confirm the staging set. Add -v to see per-file verdicts in more detail.

commands.desc: Set the executable bit while staging
commands.tooltip: Stages the file and marks it executable in one step, avoiding a second commit just for the file mode. The opposite form --chmod=-x clears the executable bit. Handy for scripts added on Windows, where the bit is often wrong.

commands.desc: Commit with a different author identity
commands.tooltip: Overrides the author recorded in the new commit, useful for committing on behalf of someone else or fixing a misconfigured identity. The value is a display name plus an email in angle brackets. Git still records you as the committer.

commands.desc: Mark a commit to squash into the previous one
commands.tooltip: Creates a commit tagged as a squash target for the named commit, usually the one just before it. During an interactive rebase, git rebase -i folds squashed commits into their target. Unlike --fixup, the squash marker keeps your message so you can edit the combined one.

commands.desc: Commit with a backdated timestamp
commands.tooltip: Sets the author date of the commit instead of using the current clock. Common for keeping imported history in order or correcting an inaccurate system clock. Git accepts most date formats, including ISO dates and relative forms like 3 days ago.

commands.desc: Commit without running hooks
commands.tooltip: Bypasses the pre-commit and commit-msg hooks for this one commit, so checks like linters and spellers do not run. Use it sparingly for emergency fixes; the -n shorthand does the same. It does not affect push hooks, which need --no-verify on git push instead.

commands.desc: Show the diff while writing the commit message
commands.tooltip: Opens the editor with the staged diff appended below the message template, so you can review exactly what you are about to commit. The diff is stripped from the final message automatically. It is a great habit for writing accurate commit messages.

commands.desc: Commit using a message read from a file
commands.tooltip: Reads the commit message from the named file instead of the editor or -m. Useful for changelog-driven workflows and for long or script-generated messages. Trailing whitespace and comment lines are cleaned according to your cleanup mode.

commands.desc: Fix the author of the last commit
commands.tooltip: Rewrites the most recent commit with a corrected author line, leaving the message untouched. Useful after spotting a wrong identity or email in the last commit. Amending changes the commit hash, so avoid it once the commit has been pushed.

commands.desc: Show the last ten commits, one line each
commands.tooltip: Combines the compact one-line format with a count limit, giving the ten most recent commits as abbreviated hash and subject. The -10 is shorthand for -n 10. It is the fastest way to orient yourself in a branch.

commands.desc: Visualize all branches as an ASCII graph
commands.tooltip: Draws the commit history as a graph with branch topology, decorating each commit with its branch and tag names. The --all flag includes every ref, not just the current branch. It is the classic command behind the popular lg alias.

commands.desc: Find commits that changed a string count
commands.tooltip: The pickaxe -S option lists commits where the number of occurrences of the given string changed. It catches additions, removals, and renames of a function or constant. Add --pickaxe-regex to treat the argument as a regular expression.

commands.desc: Find commits whose diff matches a regex
commands.tooltip: The -G option lists commits whose patch adds or removes a line matching the regular expression. Unlike -S it matches line content rather than count changes, so it finds every touched line. Quote the pattern so the shell does not interpret it.

commands.desc: List commits by a specific author
commands.tooltip: Filters the log to commits whose author matches the given pattern, matched as a substring against name and email. Combine it with --since for a time window or --grep for message text. Use --committer to filter by who committed instead.

commands.desc: Track a file's history across renames
commands.tooltip: Walks the history of the named file and follows it through renames, so the log reaches back before the file changed name. Without --follow the history stops at the rename point. The double dash tells Git everything after it is a path, not a revision.

commands.desc: Show commit summaries with file stats
commands.tooltip: Prints each commit followed by a diffstat of the files it touched, like a compact per-commit report. It gives the shape of a change without the full patch. Add -p to include the actual diff.

commands.desc: List only merge commits
commands.tooltip: Filters the log to merge commits, which have two or more parents. Handy for finding where branches were integrated or spotting accidental merges. Flip it with --no-merges to see only ordinary commits.

commands.desc: List commits excluding merges
commands.tooltip: Shows only non-merge commits, useful for reviewing the actual work in a branch without the merge noise. It pairs well with --first-parent to trace the mainline. Many teams use it for changelog generation.

commands.desc: Follow only the mainline of history
commands.tooltip: Walks the first parent of every commit, so merged branches appear as single commits instead of expanding into their full history. It shows what actually happened on the branch itself. Ideal for reviewing a long-lived feature branch.

commands.desc: Print the log with a custom format
commands.tooltip: Replaces the default log layout with placeholders: %h for short hash, %an for author name, and %s for subject, among many others like %ad for date. It is the building block for custom log aliases and scripts. Quote the format string so the shell does not expand it.

commands.desc: List commits before a given date
commands.tooltip: Limits the log to commits older than the given date, the mirror of --since. Combine both to window a specific period, like --since='2024-01-01' --until='2024-03-01'. Any date Git understands works, including relative forms like 3 months ago.

commands.desc: List commits that modified files
commands.tooltip: Filters commits by the type of change in their diff: M for modified, A for added, D for deleted, R for renamed, and C for copied. A commit shows up when any of its files match. Chain letters like --diff-filter=AM to match several kinds.

commands.desc: Show the evolution of a line range
commands.tooltip: Traces every change to lines 40 through 60 of the named file, printing each commit that touched them with its patch. The range follows the lines as they move within the file. It is line-level archaeology, far more precise than file-level git log.

commands.desc: Show the latest commit in detail
commands.tooltip: Prints the most recent commit with its metadata, message, and full patch. It is the natural entry point when you want to see what just happened. Add --stat for a summary or pass a branch name like git show origin/main.

commands.desc: Show a file as of an older commit
commands.tooltip: Prints the content of the named path at the given revision without touching your working tree. The revision:path syntax works for any commit, tag, or branch. Use it to inspect an old version before deciding to check it out.

commands.desc: Summarize the latest commit's changes
commands.tooltip: Shows the newest commit with a file-by-file diffstat instead of the full patch. Add --name-only to get just the file list. It is a quick way to judge the size and shape of the last change.

commands.desc: Print the raw content of a Git object
commands.tooltip: cat-file is the low-level tool for reading Git objects: -p pretty-prints, -t prints the type, and -s prints the size. Running it on HEAD shows the commit object with its tree, parents, and message. It is the plumbing behind many higher-level commands.

commands.desc: Resolve a ref to its full commit hash
commands.tooltip: Resolves a name like HEAD, a branch, or a tag into the full 40-character object hash. Scripts use it to capture commit IDs reliably. Add --short for the abbreviated form and --abbrev-ref for branch names.

commands.desc: Print the current branch name
commands.tooltip: Resolves HEAD to the short branch name, like main, instead of the raw hash. On a detached HEAD it prints HEAD instead of a branch. It is the script-friendly way to ask which branch you are on.

commands.desc: Print the short hash of the current commit
commands.tooltip: Resolves HEAD to the abbreviated hash Git uses in log output, typically seven characters. Useful for build tags and cache keys in scripts. The length follows core.abbrev or disambiguation rules.

commands.desc: Count the commits reachable from HEAD
commands.tooltip: Counts every commit reachable from the given ref, which is the total history length of the branch. Add a range like main..feature to count only commits unique to feature. CI scripts use it for versioning and change detection.

commands.desc: Show last-touched info with short dates
commands.tooltip: Blame annotates each line with the commit and author that last changed it; --date short trims timestamps to YYYY-MM-DD for easier scanning. Useful on large files where full timestamps create noise. Combine it with -L 10,20 to limit the line range.

commands.desc: Blame while ignoring whitespace changes
commands.tooltip: The -w flag ignores whitespace-only edits, so blame attributes lines to the commit that last changed their content. It stops a reformat commit from claiming authorship of every line. Combine it with -M to follow lines moved within the file.

commands.desc: Summarize commits per author with emails
commands.tooltip: shortlog groups commits by author and sorts by count; -s keeps just the number, -n sorts numerically, and -e appends each author's email. It is the standard contributor leaderboard. Add a range like v1.0..HEAD to scope it to a release.

commands.desc: Search tracked files for a pattern
commands.tooltip: Greps the current checkout without touching untracked files, which plain grep cannot distinguish. It is faster than scanning the whole tree because only tracked files are searched. Use -i for case-insensitive matches and -n for line numbers.

commands.desc: Search only files matching a path pattern
commands.tooltip: Restricts the search to paths matching the pattern after the double dash, here JavaScript files only. The -n flag adds line numbers. The pathspec is a glob, so '*.js' hits files in any directory.

commands.desc: List files that contain a match
commands.tooltip: Prints only the filenames that contain the pattern, with no match lines, perfect for feeding into scripts. The -l flag stands for files-with-matches. Pass a revision like v1.0.0 to search a specific commit instead of the working tree.

commands.desc: Stash changes but keep the staged ones
commands.tooltip: Stashes the working-tree changes while leaving the index, the staged set, intact so you can test exactly what is staged. The -k shorthand does the same. Use it when staging one fix but wanting to set aside the rest.

commands.desc: Stash including untracked files
commands.tooltip: By default stash ignores untracked files, so -u, or --include-untracked, sweeps them in too. The -m flag names the stash for easier identification in git stash list. Use -a to also stash ignored files, though that is rarely needed.

commands.desc: Show the diff inside a stash
commands.tooltip: Displays the changes held by the named stash as a patch. Without -p it prints a short stat instead. stash@{0} is the most recent stash, stash@{1} the one before it, and so on.

commands.desc: Apply the latest stash without removing it
commands.tooltip: Restores the most recent stash, stash@{0}, into your working tree but keeps the stash in the list, unlike git stash pop which drops it. Apply is the safe choice when you might want the stash again. Give a stash id to apply an older one.

commands.desc: List branches with tracking and ahead-behind info
commands.tooltip: The doubled -v adds each branch's upstream and how many commits it is ahead of or behind that upstream. It answers whether your local branch has unpushed work at a glance. Compare with git status --short --branch for a single-branch view.

commands.desc: List branches fully merged into HEAD
commands.tooltip: Shows branches whose commits are all reachable from the current branch, meaning their work is already integrated. These are the safe candidates for deletion with git branch -d. Pass a ref like --merged origin/main to check against the remote instead.

commands.desc: List branches with unmerged commits
commands.tooltip: Lists branches that contain commits not reachable from the current branch, so their work is still outstanding. Deleting one of these needs -D instead of -d and throws those commits away. Review this list before any cleanup session.

commands.desc: Print the current branch name
commands.tooltip: Prints the name of the checked-out branch and nothing else, with no decoration. Unlike git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD it exits non-zero on a detached HEAD. Scripts prefer it when they need a clean branch name.

commands.desc: List branches matching a name pattern
commands.tooltip: Shows only branches whose names match the glob pattern, here every branch under the feature/ namespace. It is the filtering form of git branch. Combine it with -r for remote-tracking branches like 'origin/*'.

commands.desc: Set the tracking remote for a branch
commands.tooltip: Configures the local main branch to track origin/main, so pull, push, and status know the upstream. The -u shorthand is equivalent. Do this once after creating a local branch that mirrors a remote one.

commands.desc: List branches that contain a commit
commands.tooltip: Shows every branch that includes the given commit or tag in its history. It is the reverse lookup to git tag --contains. Useful for checking which branches already picked up a fix.

commands.desc: List branches by last commit date
commands.tooltip: Sorts branches by committer date, newest first when the key is negated. The bare --sort=committerdate puts oldest first. It is a quick way to spot stale branches that deserve review or deletion.

commands.desc: Delete a remote-tracking branch locally
commands.tooltip: Removes the local copy of a remote branch, origin/feature-x, without touching the remote itself. It cleans up stale tracking refs, which git fetch --prune also does automatically. The -r flag targets remote-tracking branches only.

commands.desc: Switch back to the previous branch
commands.tooltip: Checks out the branch you were on before, like cd - for directories. It reads the previous branch from the reflog, so it works across several switches. Great for toggling between two branches during review.

commands.desc: Check out a tag with a detached HEAD
commands.tooltip: Checks out the given commit or tag without creating a branch, leaving HEAD detached. Any commits made here belong to no branch and can be lost, so create a branch first if you plan to work. Use it to inspect or build an old release.

commands.desc: Create a branch with no shared history
commands.tooltip: Creates a new branch that shares no commits with the current one, as if history started fresh. The index and working tree stay as they are. It is the standard trick for gh-pages and other content-only branches.

commands.desc: Restore a file from an older commit
commands.tooltip: Replaces the working-tree copy of the file with its content from the given revision. The --source flag selects where the content comes from; without it restore uses the index. It is the modern replacement for the git checkout commit file form.

commands.desc: Restore a file in index and working tree
commands.tooltip: Resets the file in the index, unstaging it, and in the working tree, discarding local edits, in one move. It returns the file to its state in the last commit. Be careful: local changes to that file are lost.

commands.desc: Unstage everything
commands.tooltip: Moves every staged change back to the working tree, leaving files modified but unstaged. It is the modern equivalent of git reset HEAD with a dot pathspec and does not touch file contents. Run it before re-staging with a finer-grained git add.

commands.desc: Discard all uncommitted changes
commands.tooltip: Replaces every tracked file in the working tree with its staged version, throwing away all local edits. There is no undo for this, so check git status and git diff first. Untracked files survive; remove those with git clean.

commands.desc: Create a local branch tracking a remote one
commands.tooltip: Creates a local branch named after origin/feature-notifications and sets it to track that remote branch in one step. The -t flag stands for --track. It is the fastest way to start working on a branch that exists only on the remote.

commands.desc: Apply selected hunks from a file
commands.tooltip: Walks through the file's diff hunk by hunk, asking whether to apply each one to the working tree. It is the reverse of git add -p: selecting what to discard or check out. Answer y, n, or s to split a hunk and control the result.

commands.desc: Merge only if it can fast-forward
commands.tooltip: Merges the remote branch only when the merge is a pure fast-forward with no divergence, and aborts with an error otherwise. The flag makes the merge safe and predictable for scripted updates. If it fails, decide between a real merge or a rebase.

commands.desc: Finish a merge after resolving conflicts
commands.tooltip: Completes a conflicted merge once you have fixed the files and staged them, reusing the prepared merge message. It is the merge counterpart of git rebase --continue. Resolve all conflicts and git add the files before running it.

commands.desc: Merge without creating a commit
commands.tooltip: Performs the merge and stages the result but leaves the final commit for you to make or inspect. Useful for reviewing the combined tree before committing. A later plain git commit finishes the merge.

commands.desc: Skip the current commit during a rebase
commands.tooltip: Tells a conflicted rebase to drop the commit being applied and move on to the next one. Use it when the commit is no longer wanted, not when it just needs conflict fixes. Fix conflicts and run git rebase --continue instead, or --abort to bail out entirely.

commands.desc: Rebase with local changes stashed automatically
commands.tooltip: Stashes uncommitted changes before rebasing and pops them back afterwards, so a dirty working tree no longer blocks the operation. Without it Git refuses to rebase with local modifications. The stash is reapplied on top of the rebased branch.

commands.desc: Unstage a single file
commands.tooltip: Removes the named file from the index, turning it back into a modified or untracked file while keeping its content. It is the classic unstage command, now superseded by git restore --staged. Nothing in the working tree changes.

commands.desc: Remove a file from the repo and disk
commands.tooltip: Deletes the named file from the working tree and stages the removal in one step. The deletion lands in your next commit. Use --cached to keep the file on disk while untracking it, and -r for directories.

commands.desc: Untrack a file but keep it on disk
commands.tooltip: Stops tracking the file while leaving it in the working tree, so it becomes untracked. It is the right move for secrets or build artifacts you want to keep locally but stop committing. Add the file to .gitignore right after, or it will show as untracked forever.

commands.desc: Remove an entire directory recursively
commands.tooltip: Deletes the directory and everything inside it from both the repo and disk, staging all the removals. The -r flag is required for directories. Double-check the path, because the files are gone from the working tree after this.

commands.desc: Rename a file and stage the change
commands.tooltip: Moves or renames a tracked file in one step, staging both the deletion and the addition. Git detects it as a rename in diffs. For moving into a subdirectory, the target directory must already exist.

commands.desc: Remove only ignored files and directories
commands.tooltip: Deletes ignored files and directories from the working tree: -f forces, -d includes directories, and -X targets only ignored paths. Use it to purge build artifacts while keeping your own files. Run git clean -n first to preview exactly what would be removed.

commands.desc: List tags matching a name pattern
commands.tooltip: Shows tags whose names match the glob, here every tag starting with v1. Add --sort=-creatordate to order them newest first. It is the quick way to enumerate release lines.

commands.desc: Force a tag to point at another commit
commands.tooltip: Moves an existing tag to a new commit, overriding the error a plain git tag would raise. Tags pushed to a shared remote are a contract, so only do this for unpublished or broken tags. If the tag is already pushed, the remote needs a force update.

commands.desc: Push a single tag to the remote
commands.tooltip: Pushes just the named tag instead of every tag. Use it to publish one release without flooding the remote. The remote stores it under refs/tags/v1.0.0.

commands.desc: Delete a tag on the remote
commands.tooltip: The empty source before the colon tells the remote to delete refs/tags/v1.0.0, removing the tag there but not locally. Use it to unpublish a wrong release tag. Delete the local tag afterwards with git tag -d.

commands.desc: Set your global Git name
commands.tooltip: Writes the name attached to all your commits into ~/.gitconfig, so every repository on this machine uses it unless overridden locally. Git records this name in every commit you make. It is one half of the identity setup, along with user.email.

commands.desc: Set your global Git email
commands.tooltip: Writes the email used in commit authorship into ~/.gitconfig. Many hosting services attribute commits by this email, so it should match the one on your account. Check the current value with git config --global user.email.

commands.desc: Default new repositories to main
commands.tooltip: Sets the branch name that git init creates, replacing the historical master default. New repositories start on main instead of needing a rename later. It does not change existing repositories.

commands.desc: Create a shortcut for a Git command
commands.tooltip: Defines co as an alias for checkout, so git co works like git checkout. Aliases live in ~/.gitconfig under the alias section and accept arguments and flags. For complex commands, quote the whole string.

commands.desc: Create a pretty-log alias
commands.tooltip: Adds an lg alias that prints a decorated graph of all branches, one commit per line. It is the most imitated Git alias in the wild. Run git lg after defining it.

commands.desc: Set VS Code as the commit editor
commands.tooltip: Tells Git to open Visual Studio Code for commit messages and rebase todo lists. The --wait flag is required because Git needs the editor process to block until you finish. Other editors work too, like vim or nano.

commands.desc: Show all effective Git settings
commands.tooltip: Prints every configuration value in effect, merged from system, global, and repository scope, later files winning. Add --show-origin to see which file each value came from. Use it to debug mysterious Git behavior.

commands.desc: Read a single config value
commands.tooltip: Prints the value of the named key, here the URL of the origin remote. It exits non-zero if the key is unset, which scripts can detect. The general form works for any setting name.

commands.desc: Save credentials to a plaintext file
commands.tooltip: Caches your username and password in ~/.git-credentials in plain text, so future pushes and pulls skip the prompt. Anyone with access to your home directory can read those credentials. Prefer a helper like cache, libsecret, or an SSH key instead.

commands.desc: Convert CRLF line endings on commit
commands.tooltip: For Linux and macOS, the input setting converts CRLF endings to LF when committing while leaving the working tree alone. It keeps repositories consistent for teams mixing Windows and Unix. Windows users usually set true instead.

commands.desc: Enable colored output in terminals
commands.tooltip: Turns on color for Git output when writing to a terminal, and off when piping to a file or another program. The auto mode keeps scripts free of escape codes. It is a long-standing default in modern Git but can be set explicitly.

commands.desc: Make git pull rebase by default
commands.tooltip: Changes git pull to rebase local commits onto the fetched branch instead of creating merge commits. The result is a linear history without merge noise. It matches the workflow of teams that always pull with --rebase.

commands.desc: Add an upstream remote for a fork
commands.tooltip: Registers a second remote named upstream pointing at the original repository you forked. Fetching from it keeps your fork in sync with the source project. The convention is origin for your fork and upstream for the canonical repo.

commands.desc: Rename a remote
commands.tooltip: Changes the name of the remote from origin to upstream and updates every tracking branch and config that references it. Use it when restructuring remote layouts. Existing refs like origin/main move to upstream/main.

commands.desc: Inspect a remote in detail
commands.tooltip: Prints the remote's URLs plus which local branches track which remote branches, and whether pushes would fast-forward. It contacts the remote by default, so it can be slow on flaky networks. Add -n to skip the network call.

commands.desc: Delete stale remote-tracking branches
commands.tooltip: Removes local refs like origin/dead-branch whose remote counterparts no longer exist. It is the manual form of git fetch --prune. Run it when git branch -r shows branches you know were deleted upstream.

commands.desc: Print a remote's URL
commands.tooltip: Shows the URL Git uses for the named remote, useful for confirming https versus SSH endpoints. Add --push to see the push URL when it differs. Scripts use it to detect the hosting platform.

commands.desc: Fetch a single branch from a remote
commands.tooltip: Downloads the named branch's commits and updates its remote-tracking ref without merging anything. It is the surgical version of git fetch. The branch lands in origin/feature-branch, ready to inspect or merge.

commands.desc: Fetch all tags from the remote
commands.tooltip: Downloads every tag the remote has that you lack, in addition to the usual branch updates. Tags are not fetched by default unless they point at fetched commits. Use it after a release to pull in new version tags.

commands.desc: Pull and rebase local commits on top
commands.tooltip: Fetches origin/main and replays your local commits on top of it instead of merging, giving a linear history. It is the explicit form of a rebase pull for a specific remote and branch. Set pull.rebase true to make it the default.

commands.desc: Pull only when it fast-forwards cleanly
commands.tooltip: Updates the branch only if the local branch can fast-forward to the remote, and aborts otherwise. A failure means your local commits diverge from the remote, so a merge or rebase is needed. It prevents surprise merge commits in automated pulls.

commands.desc: Pull with local changes stashed first
commands.tooltip: Stashes uncommitted working-tree changes before pulling and restores them afterwards. Without it a dirty tree can block the pull. Conflicts between the stash and the new commits need manual resolution.

commands.desc: Preview a push without sending it
commands.tooltip: Shows exactly which commits and refs would be pushed, then stops without transferring anything. Use it to sanity-check what an unpushed branch contains. The -n shorthand does the same.

commands.desc: Push commits and their annotated tags
commands.tooltip: Pushes the branch and any annotated tags pointing at commits in the pushed range. Lightweight tags are not included. It keeps release tags in sync with the code that introduced them.

commands.desc: Push every local branch
commands.tooltip: Pushes all local branches to the named remote, not just the current one. New branches appear on the remote automatically. It never deletes remote branches; use --prune for that.

commands.desc: Show the pinned commit of each submodule
commands.tooltip: Lists every submodule with the commit it is pinned to, plus a prefix: a space for up to date, a dash for not initialized, and a plus for a different commit than recorded. It is the first stop when submodule content looks wrong.

commands.desc: Unregister a submodule from the repo
commands.tooltip: Removes the submodule's entry from the configuration and clears its working tree, so it no longer appears in git submodule status. The -f flag is needed when the submodule has local changes. The gitlink entry in the index stays until you commit.

commands.desc: Export the repo as a zip with a prefix
commands.tooltip: Bundles the current commit's tree into a zip file without any .git history. The --prefix option nests everything under myapp/ so unzipping into a directory does not scatter files. Use it for source drops and releases.

commands.desc: Show the size of the object database
commands.tooltip: Reports how many loose objects and packs exist and how much disk the repository uses. The -H flag prints sizes in human-readable units like MiB. Run it before and after git gc to see the cleanup effect.

commands.desc: Run housekeeping only when needed
commands.tooltip: Runs garbage collection only if Git estimates the repository needs it, based on loose object and pack counts. Git calls it automatically after many operations. Run the full git gc manually when you want a forced cleanup.

commands.desc: Run scheduled repository maintenance
commands.tooltip: Executes the maintenance tasks Git considers due, which on modern Git replaces most manual gc invocations. The --auto form is what Git triggers after fetch and commit operations. Configure recurring runs with git maintenance start.

commands.desc: Check the entire object database
commands.tooltip: Verifies every object's integrity, connectivity, and format, reporting dangling or corrupt objects. The --full flag scans all packs and loose objects. Run it after crashes or disk issues to assess repository health.

commands.desc: Test whether a path is ignored
commands.tooltip: Prints the path if .gitignore rules ignore it and exits zero, or exits non-zero if the file would be tracked. Scripts use it to verify ignore patterns. Add -v to see which specific rule matched.

commands.desc: List every file in a commit
commands.tooltip: Lists the full file tree of HEAD recursively, one path per line, without touching the working tree. The -r flag recurses into directories and --name-only suppresses hashes and modes. It answers what files a commit contains, not just the checkout.

commands.desc: Get the nearest tag name only
commands.tooltip: Prints the most recent tag reachable from HEAD without the commit-count and hash suffix git describe normally appends. CI scripts use it as a clean version number. Fall back to --always for repositories with no tags.

commands.desc: Print the installed Git version
commands.tooltip: Shows the Git version plus platform details, like git version 2.43.0. Scripts parse it to gate features that need newer Git. The short form git -v prints the same output.

commands.desc: List all local branch refs
commands.tooltip: Prints every local branch as a full hash plus refs/heads/name pair. It is the plumbing-level view of what git branch shows. Add --tags to include tags, or no flag to list every ref in the repository.

commands.desc: Open a diff in an external tool
commands.tooltip: Launches your configured diff tool, like meld, vimdiff, or VS Code, for the given range instead of printing a text patch. Configure the tool with git config diff.tool. It is best for large or visual review sessions.

commands.desc: Open a merge tool for conflict resolution
commands.tooltip: Starts your configured merge tool on each file with unresolved conflicts, one after another. Configure the tool with git config merge.tool. After resolving a file it asks whether the resolution is correct before moving on.

commands.desc: Generate the lockfile without installing packages
commands.tooltip: Writes package-lock.json, the file that records the exact resolved version of every dependency, without touching node_modules. Use it to update the lockfile after editing package.json, then commit it so teammates and CI install identical trees. Pair with npm ci to install from that lockfile.

commands.desc: Install dependencies while skipping the audit
commands.tooltip: Disables the security vulnerability check npm runs after every install, which speeds up large installs. The audit finds packages with known vulnerabilities, so only skip it when you run npm audit separately or in CI. Combine with --no-fund to silence funding prompts too.

commands.desc: Install dependencies without funding messages
commands.tooltip: Stops npm from printing the funding notices that some packages attach to their metadata after install. Useful for keeping CI logs clean. Funding info is still visible via npm fund when you want to support a project.

commands.desc: Install dependencies without optional packages
commands.tooltip: Skips optionalDependencies, the packages that may fail to install on some platforms without breaking the build (platform-specific binaries like esbuild are typical examples). Speeds up installs and avoids errors on unsupported systems. npm install --omit=dev is the sibling form used for production.

commands.desc: Preview an install without changing anything
commands.tooltip: Reports what npm would download, add, or remove without writing to node_modules or package.json. The fastest way to check how a dependency change would affect the tree. Pair with --json for machine-readable output.

commands.desc: Install dependencies from the local cache only
commands.tooltip: Forces npm to resolve everything from its cache and fail if any package is missing, instead of hitting the registry. Ideal for air-gapped machines or when the network is flaky. Prime the cache beforehand with npm install --prefer-offline.

commands.desc: Install a package as an optional dependency
commands.tooltip: Adds the package to optionalDependencies in package.json, meaning installs proceed even if it fails to build or download. Optional packages typically supply platform-specific binaries, and the main package falls back to another build. Remove with npm uninstall as usual.

commands.desc: Install a package as a peer dependency
commands.tooltip: Writes the package into peerDependencies, the section that tells consumers which versions of another library your package expects to share. Peer deps are not installed automatically for the package author, only for its users. Common for plugins that must match a host library version.

commands.desc: Install dependencies for a single workspace
commands.tooltip: Runs install scoped to the apps/web workspace only (workspace = one of several packages developed together in a monorepo). The -w flag takes the workspace folder path or package name and must run from the repository root. Omit -w to install every workspace at once.

commands.desc: Install all workspaces plus the root package
commands.tooltip: Installs dependencies for every workspace in the monorepo and also for the root package, which normally is skipped. The --include-workspace-root flag matters when the root has its own scripts and dev tooling. The reverse, skipping dev dependencies, is npm install --omit=dev.

commands.desc: Clean install without running lifecycle scripts
commands.tooltip: Deletes node_modules and reinstalls from package-lock.json while skipping the postinstall and prepare scripts that packages declare. Lifecycle scripts can compile native code or download binaries, so skipping them yields a faster, safer CI build. npm ci requires a lockfile to exist.

commands.desc: Preview a clean CI install without changes
commands.tooltip: Reports exactly what a clean install would do, including the full dependency tree, without deleting node_modules or downloading anything. Useful to sanity-check a lockfile before committing to a slow CI run. Add --no-audit to silence the vulnerability check.

commands.desc: List installed packages as JSON
commands.tooltip: Prints the dependency tree of the project as machine-readable JSON, including extraneous or missing packages flagged as errors. Handy for scripting or feeding into jq. The tree can be huge, so filter with npm ls --depth=0 or npm ls <package>.

commands.desc: Show outdated packages in JSON format
commands.tooltip: Reports every dependency whose installed version is behind the latest release, as JSON for scripting. Each entry lists current, wanted, and latest versions, where wanted respects the semver range in package.json. Combine with npm update to apply the changes.

commands.desc: Show outdated globally installed packages
commands.tooltip: Checks the packages you installed with npm install -g against the registry and lists those with newer releases. Global tools often lag behind because updates are manual. Apply updates with npm update -g.

commands.desc: Update all globally installed packages
commands.tooltip: Bumps every globally installed package to the newest version that satisfies its saved range, so command-line tools you installed with npm install -g stay current. Runs the same update logic as the project-level npm update. Review changes with npm outdated -g first.

commands.desc: Show why a package is installed
commands.tooltip: Traces every dependency path that pulls lodash into the project, from direct dependencies down to transitive ones. Indispensable for deciding whether a package is safe to remove with npm uninstall. npm why is the older alias for the same command.

commands.desc: Show the latest version of a package
commands.tooltip: Queries the registry for the newest published version of lodash without installing anything. npm view is the same command as npm info and accepts dotted field names to drill into metadata. Append @4.17.21 to inspect a specific version instead.

commands.desc: Show the distribution tags of a package
commands.tooltip: Lists the tags the publisher attached to published versions, like latest and next. Tags are how npm knows which version to install for a bare package name or @latest. Read them to see what the next release line looks like before it goes stable.

commands.desc: Show the Node version requirements of a package
commands.tooltip: Prints the engines field, which declares which Node and npm versions the package supports. Comparing this to your node --version output tells you whether an install or upgrade will work. npm also enforces engines when the engine-strict config is enabled.

commands.desc: Show the peer dependencies of a package version
commands.tooltip: Inspects the peerDependencies of one published version of react, the libraries its consumers must provide themselves. Pin a version after the @ to compare how requirements changed between releases. Useful before upgrading a framework.

commands.desc: Show the latest version of a scoped package
commands.tooltip: Fetches the newest release of the scoped @types/node package, which ships TypeScript type definitions for the Node runtime. Scoped package names always start with @ and are how npm namespaces packages to an owner. Works for any registry metadata field.

commands.desc: Search the npm registry for a package
commands.tooltip: Looks up package names and descriptions that match express, returning name, version, and description lines. Useful when you only half-remember a package name. Add --json or --parseable for script-friendly output.

commands.desc: List cached files for a package
commands.tooltip: Shows every cache entry npm holds for lodash, including tarballs and metadata, by matching the package name against the cache index. The cache lives under the directory reported by npm config get cache. Clean it with npm cache clean --force only if it is corrupted.

commands.desc: Rebuild all native modules in the project
commands.tooltip: Recompiles every package with native code against the current Node version and toolchain. Run it after switching Node versions with nvm or after system libraries change, when modules fail with ABI errors. To rebuild a single package, name it, for example npm rebuild bcrypt.

commands.desc: Rebuild one native module from source
commands.tooltip: Recompiles just the bcrypt package, whose C++ bindings must match the running Node version. Fixes errors like NODE_MODULE_VERSION mismatches that appear after upgrading Node. The bare npm rebuild recompiles all native modules in the project.

commands.desc: Lock dependency versions for publication
commands.tooltip: Creates npm-shrinkwrap.json, a lockfile that pins the exact versions of every dependency and is respected by consumers who install your published package. Unlike package-lock.json, it ships inside the tarball. Regenerate it whenever dependencies change.

commands.desc: Run a script only if it exists
commands.tooltip: Executes the lint script when package.json defines one and exits silently when it does not. Useful for shared commands across projects that may lack a script. npm run without arguments lists every available script.

commands.desc: Print the environment variables of npm scripts
commands.tooltip: Shows the environment that npm injects into lifecycle scripts, including npm_package_name, npm_lifecycle_event, and PATH entries for local binaries. Great for debugging why a script behaves differently from your shell. Run it inside the project directory.

commands.desc: Run a package script by its long name
commands.tooltip: Executes the build script exactly like npm run build, using the canonical run-script command name. Useful in documentation and scripts where the explicit form is clearer. npm run remains the everyday shorthand.

commands.desc: Add a start script to package.json
commands.tooltip: Writes or replaces the scripts.start field in package.json without opening an editor, then npm start runs the new script. npm pkg set accepts any dotted key, so it can also set version, private, or engines. Quote values that contain spaces.

commands.desc: Set the minimum Node version for a project
commands.tooltip: Adds an engines.node field that declares the project needs Node 20 or newer, which helps teammates and CI pick a compatible runtime. The engine-strict config turns this declaration into a hard install failure. Check what is already declared with npm pkg get engines.

commands.desc: Mark the package as private
commands.tooltip: Sets the private field so npm publish refuses to upload the package accidentally, which is essential for app repositories that are not meant to be libraries. Internal-only packages should always carry this flag. npm pkg get private shows the current value.

commands.desc: Auto-fix common package.json problems
commands.tooltip: Repairs malformed fields, normalizes values, and resolves inconsistencies npm detects in package.json, writing corrections back to the file. Run it after hand-editing the manifest or when npm warns about the file. Review the diff in git before committing.

commands.desc: Set an explicit package version
commands.tooltip: Writes version 1.2.3 into package.json and creates a matching git tag named v1.2.3, instead of computing a bump from the current version. Use it to align the package with an external release plan. Add --no-git-tag-version to skip the tag.

commands.desc: Bump the version from the latest git tag
commands.tooltip: Reads the most recent git tag, treats it as the package version, and writes it into package.json. Keeps the manifest in sync when tags are the source of truth for releases. Requires the tag to look like a version, such as v2.1.0.

commands.desc: Bump the minor version in every workspace
commands.tooltip: Increments the minor version of all workspaces in a monorepo at once and tags the release, keeping sibling packages in lockstep. The --workspaces flag applies the bump project-wide instead of to one package. Use --workspace=packages/ui to target a single one.

commands.desc: Publish a built folder as a package
commands.tooltip: Uploads the contents of the dist folder to the registry as the current package version. Publishing is permanent: fixing a mistake means publishing a new version, so run npm publish --dry-run first. Folders named in .npmignore are excluded from the tarball.

commands.desc: Publish without running lifecycle scripts
commands.tooltip: Uploads the package while skipping the prepublishOnly, prepack, and postpack scripts that normally run before publish. Useful when build steps already ran or when scripts fail in an unusual environment. Publishing is irreversible, so prefer npm publish --dry-run to rehearse.

commands.desc: Publish using a one-time password
commands.tooltip: Sends the six-digit code from your authenticator app along with the publish request, which accounts with two-factor authentication require. The OTP value changes every 30 seconds, so generate it right before publishing. Interactive prompts ask for it anyway when omitted.

commands.desc: Remove an entire package from the registry
commands.tooltip: Deletes every version of a package from the npm registry, which is permanent and can break every project that depends on it. The --force flag is mandatory because removing a whole package is destructive; unpublishing a single version within 72 hours does not need it. Prefer npm deprecate to warn users instead.

commands.desc: Preview the tarball contents before packing
commands.tooltip: Builds the publish tarball in memory and lists every file that would be included, without writing the .tgz file. The quickest way to check that .npmignore and the files field are right. The real artifact is produced by npm pack.

commands.desc: Pack a tarball into a specific folder
commands.tooltip: Creates the package tarball, typically name-version.tgz, inside the tarballs directory instead of the project root. Tarballs are the exact artifact npm publish uploads, so inspect one before releasing. The --dry-run flag previews the contents first.

commands.desc: Mark a package as a favorite
commands.tooltip: Adds lodash to the starred packages on your npm account, which is a public signal that you find the library useful. Starred packages appear in the npm website profile of the account you are logged in as. Show all of yours with npm stars.

commands.desc: Remove a package from your favorites
commands.tooltip: Removes lodash from the starred list on your npm account, the reverse of npm star. Useful for cleaning up packages you no longer use or recommend. Requires being logged in with npm whoami.

commands.desc: List the packages you have starred
commands.tooltip: Prints every package you marked as a favorite on the npm registry, which can double as a personal reading list. Pass a username, like npm stars someone, to view another account's picks. Star packages with npm star <package>.

commands.desc: Check connectivity to the npm registry
commands.tooltip: Sends a ping request to the configured registry and reports the round-trip time, confirming that your network, proxy, and credentials path work. Fails with a clear error when the registry is unreachable or the token is rejected. A fast first step when installs hang.

commands.desc: Run health checks on the npm environment
commands.tooltip: Audits the npm setup: registry reachability, Node and npm versions, cache integrity, permissions on global directories, and git availability. Reports each check as OK or a fixable warning. Run it when installs behave oddly or after a fresh setup.

commands.desc: Print the local project prefix directory
commands.tooltip: Shows the nearest directory containing a package.json or node_modules, which is where npm considers the current project to live. Useful in scripts that need the project root. The -g flag reports the global installation prefix instead.

commands.desc: Print the global npm prefix directory
commands.tooltip: Shows where globally installed packages live, the directory whose bin folder npm adds to your PATH. On this machine it is the nvm-managed Node directory. Install tools there with npm install -g and inspect them with npm ls -g --depth=0.

commands.desc: Print the local node_modules directory
commands.tooltip: Prints the absolute path of the project's node_modules folder, handy for scripts that must locate installed binaries or modules. Runs from anywhere inside the project tree. The -g flag reports the global node_modules instead.

commands.desc: Print the global node_modules directory
commands.tooltip: Shows the folder that holds globally installed packages, normally a sibling of the npm binary itself. Binaries from those packages are linked into the global bin directory. Useful when debugging why a global tool cannot be found.

commands.desc: Show the configured registry URL
commands.tooltip: Prints which package registry npm currently uses, useful to confirm a corporate mirror or a scope-specific registry is active. The default is https://registry.npmjs.org/. Point it elsewhere with npm config set registry <url>.

commands.desc: Show the npm cache directory
commands.tooltip: Prints the folder where npm stores downloaded tarballs and metadata, which speeds up repeated installs. The cache can grow large, and npm cache verify reports its health. Move it with npm config set cache <path>.

commands.desc: Disable lockfile generation
commands.tooltip: Stops npm from creating package-lock.json on install, which trades reproducibility for simpler diffs. Lockfiles pin exact dependency versions so CI and teammates install identical trees, so disable only deliberately. Re-enable with npm config set package-lock true.

commands.desc: Fail installs on mismatched Node engines
commands.tooltip: Makes npm abort with an error when a dependency declares an engines.node range that the running Node does not satisfy, instead of warning. Enforces the requirements that packages like npm view lodash engines report. Set it per project in .npmrc.

commands.desc: Set a registry for one npm scope
commands.tooltip: Routes every @myorg scoped package to the GitHub Packages registry while everything else keeps using the default registry. The scope key syntax, @scope:registry, is how npm selects registries per namespace. Useful for private packages published to GitHub.

commands.desc: Save new dependencies with tilde ranges
commands.tooltip: Configures npm to write ~4.17.21 style ranges instead of ^4.17.21 when adding dependencies, meaning only patch updates are allowed. The tilde range is the conservative choice for libraries that must avoid breaking minors. npm set is the shorthand for npm config set.

commands.desc: Create a read-only registry token
commands.tooltip: Generates a token that can only read packages, not publish, which is the safest credential for CI pipelines that just install. Tokens replace passwords for npm registry auth. List and revoke them with npm token list and npm token revoke.

commands.desc: Create a token limited to an IP range
commands.tooltip: Issues a registry token that only works from the 192.168.1.0/24 network, limiting damage if the token leaks. The --cidr flag accepts one or several CIDR blocks. Combine it with --read-only for a hardened CI credential.

commands.desc: Revoke an npm access token
commands.tooltip: Immediately invalidates the token with the given id, cutting off every system that used it. Rotate tokens when they leak or when a developer leaves the team. Find the id with npm token list before revoking.

commands.desc: Show npm account profile settings
