commands.tooltip: Removes the role; it fails while the role owns objects or holds privileges, so clean those up first with DROP OWNED BY app. Applications using the role lose access instantly. Memberships granted to the role also block the drop.

commands.cmd: psql -d postgres -c "REASSIGN OWNED BY app TO postgres;"
commands.desc: Transfer object ownership before a role drop
commands.tooltip: Moves ownership of every object the role owns to postgres, the usual prelude to dropping a role without losing its databases and tables. Follow with DROP OWNED BY to clear the remaining privileges.

commands.desc: Drop everything a role owns
commands.tooltip: Deletes every object owned by the role in the current database and revokes its privileges, preparing a clean DROP USER. Irreversible: tables, views, and sequences owned by the role are removed. Run it in each database where the role owns things.

commands.desc: Show the size of one database
commands.tooltip: pg_database_size returns the bytes a database occupies on disk; pg_size_pretty formats it as 123 MB. The database must exist or the query errors. Compare databases by joining pg_database.

commands.cmd: psql -d postgres -c "SELECT datname, pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(datname)) FROM pg_database ORDER BY pg_database_size(datname) DESC;"
commands.desc: Rank databases by size
commands.tooltip: Ranks every database by size, largest first, in one pass over pg_database. template0 always appears; it is the pristine template and should stay untouched. A good first query when disk usage surprises you.

commands.desc: Show table size including indexes
commands.tooltip: pg_total_relation_size adds the table's heap, its TOAST table, and all indexes, giving the true footprint. Use pg_relation_size for the heap alone or pg_indexes_size for indexes alone. Names are case-sensitive if quoted at creation.

commands.desc: Show total index size of a table
commands.tooltip: Sums the bytes used by every index on the table, excluding the table data itself. Compare it with the table size to judge whether indexes are bloated; REINDEX shrinks them. Per-index sizes come from pg_indexes.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active';"
commands.desc: Show running queries
commands.tooltip: pg_stat_activity is the live view of every backend; filtering on state = 'active' isolates queries currently executing. Columns include pid, usename, query, and how long the query has run. The starting point for almost any stuck-database investigation.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT pid, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active';"
commands.desc: Show active query process IDs
commands.tooltip: Narrows pg_stat_activity to the process ID and SQL text of running queries, compact enough to eyeball during an incident. Combine with SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) to kill the offender.

commands.desc: Kill a backend connection
commands.tooltip: Forcefully ends the backend with the given pid, rolling back its current transaction and dropping its connection. Take the pid from pg_stat_activity. Prefer pg_cancel_backend when the query might still finish.

commands.desc: Cancel a running query
commands.tooltip: Requests cancellation of the query running on backend 12345, leaving the session itself connected; the query aborts with canceling statement due to user request. Softer than pg_terminate_backend, which drops the whole connection.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity;"
commands.desc: Find which sessions block others
commands.tooltip: For every backend, pg_blocking_pids returns the pids currently blocking it, empty when none. The classic way to find who holds the lock everyone is waiting on. Follow up by inspecting those pids' queries in pg_stat_activity.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT * FROM pg_locks WHERE NOT granted;"
commands.desc: Show locks waiting to be granted
commands.tooltip: pg_locks lists every lock in the cluster; rows with NOT granted are requests still waiting for another session to release a lock. Match on the same relation and lock type to find the holder, then decide whether to cancel or terminate it.

commands.desc: Reclaim dead rows in all tables
commands.tooltip: Removes dead rows and updates the visibility map so space becomes reusable; the manual counterpart of autovacuum, the background process that reclaims bloat automatically. Cheap and safe to run during quiet hours; it does not lock tables.

commands.desc: Vacuum one table verbosely
commands.tooltip: Vacuuming a single table with VERBOSE prints how many dead tuples were removed, which pages were freed, and the timing. Great for verifying autovacuum keeps up on a hot table. The parenthesized syntax is the modern form of VACUUM VERBOSE.

commands.desc: Rewrite a table to compact it
commands.tooltip: Rewrites the table into a compact form and returns space to the operating system, unlike plain VACUUM. It takes an exclusive lock for the whole run, blocking reads and writes on that table, so schedule it in a maintenance window.

commands.desc: Refresh planner statistics for all tables
commands.tooltip: Updates the planner statistics for every table, helping the optimizer choose sane plans. Cheap, non-blocking, and safe to run anytime. Autovacuum also runs analyze on its own schedule.

commands.desc: Refresh statistics for one table
commands.tooltip: Updates statistics for one table only, useful right after a bulk load or a large UPDATE before you re-run EXPLAIN. Statistics power row-count estimates; stale ones cause bad index choices.

commands.desc: Rebuild all indexes of a table
commands.tooltip: Rebuilds every index on the table from scratch, removing bloat and updating statistics. Plain REINDEX takes a lock that blocks writes; CONCURRENTLY avoids that but runs slower. Consider it after heavy deletes or a failed index build.

commands.desc: Rebuild every index in a database
commands.tooltip: Rebuilds all indexes in the database, the full sweep after a major version change or serious bloat. It takes locks per relation as it goes; REINDEX DATABASE CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking writes.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;"
commands.desc: Rank tables by dead tuples
commands.tooltip: Ranks user tables by dead tuples, the rows awaiting cleanup by autovacuum. A table with a huge dead count is a candidate for manual VACUUM and ANALYZE. Statistics are approximate until refreshed.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT indexname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'users';"
commands.desc: Show index sizes for one table
commands.tooltip: pg_indexes joins index names to their catalog OIDs, letting pg_relation_size report each index's footprint. Spot oversized or duplicate indexes before deciding what to drop.

commands.desc: Show the current work_mem setting
commands.tooltip: work_mem is the per-sort and per-hash memory budget; small values force temporary files on disk, and the default is 4 MB. SHOW prints the effective value for your session, considering the whole configuration hierarchy.

commands.desc: Show the configured connection limit
commands.tooltip: max_connections caps concurrent backends for the whole cluster; exceeding it rejects new logins with sorry, too many clients. Raising it costs shared memory and needs a restart. Compare with connection counts from pg_stat_activity.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name LIKE 'autovacuum%';"
commands.desc: Inspect autovacuum settings
commands.tooltip: pg_settings holds every run-time parameter; filtering on autovacuum% reveals the tunables (threshold, scale factor, workers) and their current values. Autovacuum is the background process that reclaims dead rows automatically. Override per table with ALTER TABLE SET (autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = ...).

commands.desc: Set work_mem cluster-wide
commands.tooltip: Writes the setting into postgresql.auto.conf, which overrides postgresql.conf, so no file editing is needed. Requires superuser. Most parameters apply after a reload, not instantly. ALTER SYSTEM RESET removes the override.

commands.desc: Raise the cluster-wide connection limit
commands.tooltip: Sets max_connections via postgresql.auto.conf. This parameter needs a full restart to take effect because shared memory is sized at startup. After restarting, confirm with SHOW max_connections.

commands.desc: Reload configuration without restart
commands.tooltip: Signals the postmaster to reread configuration files and returns true when the signal was sent. Existing sessions pick up most changes; a few parameters still require a restart. Equivalent to sudo systemctl reload postgresql.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@b.com';"
commands.desc: Show a query plan without running it
commands.tooltip: Prints the plan the optimizer would use: scan type, estimated rows, and cost. Add ANALYZE to execute the query and show actual numbers. Plans are the first tool for index decisions.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7;"
commands.desc: Execute a query and show real costs
commands.tooltip: Runs the query and reports actual timings plus buffer reads, revealing whether data came from cache or disk; BUFFERS adds the shared-hit and shared-read counts. The standard diagnostic for slow queries.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 1;"
commands.desc: Plan and execute a query
commands.tooltip: EXPLAIN ANALYZE is valid shorthand for EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) and executes the statement to collect real timings and row counts. Use it on SELECTs in production; on write statements it really modifies data.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);"
commands.desc: Create an index on a column
commands.tooltip: Builds a btree index on the email column so equality lookups skip full scans. Indexes speed reads but slow writes and consume disk, so create them for real query patterns. Check usage in pg_stat_user_indexes.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email_unique ON users (email);"
commands.desc: Create a unique index
commands.tooltip: Creates an index that also enforces uniqueness: a second row with the same email is rejected, exactly like a UNIQUE constraint. Duplicates in existing data make the creation fail, so dedupe first.

commands.desc: Remove an index
commands.tooltip: Removes the index and frees its space; queries fall back to other indexes or sequential scans. Dropping a unique index also lifts the uniqueness guarantee. Keep a migration record so it can be recreated.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders (user_id) WHERE status = 'open';"
commands.desc: Create a partial index
commands.tooltip: A partial index covers only rows matching the WHERE clause, so it is smaller and cheaper to maintain when most queries target open orders. The planner uses it when the query's conditions imply the predicate.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (id serial PRIMARY KEY, email text UNIQUE);"
commands.desc: Create a table only if missing
commands.tooltip: serial makes an auto-incrementing integer column, PRIMARY KEY adds a unique index, and UNIQUE forbids duplicate emails. IF NOT EXISTS silently skips when the table is already there. Useful in idempotent setup scripts.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN age int;"
commands.desc: Add a column to a table
commands.tooltip: Adds an age column; existing rows get NULL. In modern PostgreSQL, adding a column with a constant default is nearly instant because no rewrite happens. Dropping it later is also cheap.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN age;"
commands.desc: Remove a column from a table
commands.tooltip: Deletes the column and its data; any views or queries referencing it break until updated. The freed space is reclaimed lazily by VACUUM. There is no undo without a prior backup.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "ALTER TABLE users RENAME TO members;"
commands.desc: Rename a table
commands.tooltip: Renames the table; dependent views and functions are not automatically updated and may need ALTER. Existing indexes keep their names. Run it in a quiet window to avoid breaking running queries.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN email SET NOT NULL;"
commands.desc: Enforce NOT NULL on a column
commands.tooltip: Forbids NULL values in email from now on. PostgreSQL verifies existing rows and may rewrite the table, so test on large tables. DROP NOT NULL reverses the constraint.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "TRUNCATE TABLE users RESTART IDENTITY;"
commands.desc: Empty a table and reset its sequence
commands.tooltip: Empties the table instantly and, with RESTART IDENTITY, resets its serial sequence to 1. TRUNCATE is not undoable once committed and fires no per-row triggers. Use DELETE when you need fine-grained control.

commands.desc: Force a write-ahead log checkpoint
commands.tooltip: Forces the postmaster to flush all dirty buffers to disk and advance the write-ahead log (WAL), normally done on its own schedule. A forced checkpoint shortens recovery time before a planned shutdown.

commands.desc: Check if this server is a standby
commands.tooltip: Returns true on a standby replaying WAL and false on a primary that accepts writes. The quickest way to confirm a node's role before promoting or failing over.

commands.desc: Show replication status to standbys
commands.tooltip: Lists each standby, its WAL receive position, and lag against the primary. Empty output on a standalone server is normal. Watch the lag columns to confirm standbys are keeping up.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database;"
commands.desc: Check transaction ID age per database
commands.tooltip: age() reports how many transactions elapsed since the database's frozen XID, the wraparound counter. Values approaching two billion force emergency autovacuum; below about one billion is the alerting zone. The oldest database drives the whole cluster's vacuum load.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = 'appdb';"
commands.desc: Show per-database activity counters
commands.tooltip: Reports commits, rollbacks, cache hit ratio, deadlocks, and XID age for one database. A low blks_hit ratio hints at a small shared_buffers. The main dashboard table for capacity work.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'users';"
commands.desc: Show per-table scan and tuple stats
commands.tooltip: Per-table counters: sequential and index scans, tuples inserted, updated, deleted, and the last vacuum and analyze timestamps. seq_scan far above idx_scan hints at a missing index.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;"
commands.desc: Enable the statement statistics extension
commands.tooltip: Installs pg_stat_statements, which records every executed statement with cumulative timings. To survive restarts it must also be listed in shared_preload_libraries in postgresql.conf. Requires superuser.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "SELECT query, total_exec_time FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;"
commands.desc: Rank the slowest statements
commands.tooltip: Lists the ten statements that consumed the most server time; total_exec_time accumulates since the extension loaded. The standard first step in a query-tuning project. Requires the pg_stat_statements extension.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "\copy users TO '/tmp/users.csv' DELIMITER ',' CSV HEADER"
commands.desc: Export a table to a CSV file
commands.tooltip: psql's \copy runs on the client side and writes the CSV to the local filesystem, unlike COPY, which writes on the server. CSV mode handles quoting and HEADER emits a header row. A quick way to hand data to a spreadsheet.

commands.cmd: psql -d appdb -c "\copy users FROM '/tmp/users.csv' DELIMITER ',' CSV HEADER"
commands.desc: Import a CSV file into a table
commands.tooltip: Loads the CSV into the users table, matching columns by order, not name; the header row is skipped. An error aborts the whole import. Use COPY ... FROM for files that live on the server.

commands.desc: Vacuum a database from the shell
commands.tooltip: vacuumdb is the command-line wrapper for VACUUM, useful in cron jobs. Dead rows are removed so space can be reused, mirroring what autovacuum does in the background. Add --verbose to see per-table results.

commands.desc: Vacuum and analyze a database
commands.tooltip: Combines VACUUM with ANALYZE so dead rows are reclaimed and planner statistics refreshed in one pass. The recommended routine maintenance cycle. Add --all to cover every database.

commands.desc: Vacuum every database verbosely
commands.tooltip: Processes all databases on the cluster with per-table progress output thanks to -v. Watch for tables that repeatedly report many dead tuples, a sign their autovacuum settings need tuning. Requires a superuser or the maintenance role.

commands.desc: Fully vacuum a database
commands.tooltip: Runs VACUUM FULL, which rewrites every table to compact it and return space to the OS. It takes exclusive locks on each table, blocking reads and writes, so run it in a maintenance window. Plain vacuumdb is safe anytime.

commands.desc: Reindex a database from the shell
commands.tooltip: reindexdb wraps REINDEX for scripted maintenance, rebuilding indexes that grew bloated after heavy updates or deletes. Plain mode locks writes; --concurrently avoids that but runs slower and can fail midway.

commands.desc: Reindex all databases
commands.tooltip: Rebuilds every index in every database on the cluster, the full sweep after a major upgrade or serious bloat. It locks each relation briefly as it works. Prefer --concurrently on a live system.

commands.desc: Back up a database in custom format
commands.tooltip: -Fc writes the compressed custom format, which supports selective restore and parallel restore, unlike plain SQL dumps. -f names the output file. Restore with pg_restore; the dump is not readable as text.

commands.desc: Restore a dump with parallel workers
commands.tooltip: Restores a custom-format dump using four concurrent jobs with -j, which can speed up large restores substantially. The target database must exist first. Parallel restore cannot reorder dependent objects, so it may fail on some dumps; retry with -j 1.

commands.desc: Restore after dropping existing objects
commands.tooltip: --clean drops each object before recreating it so the restore overwrites the current database; --if-exists suppresses errors for objects that are missing. Destructive to existing data, so point it at the right database. Combine with --no-owner to avoid ownership errors.

commands.desc: Dump all databases and cluster globals
commands.tooltip: pg_dumpall produces one SQL script containing every database plus cluster-wide objects: roles, tablespaces, and global settings. Use it for full-cluster backups or before pg_dropcluster. Restore by piping into psql as a superuser.

commands.desc: Back up a single table
commands.tooltip: -t users dumps only that table, handy for moving one relation between environments. Repeat -t for several tables. Custom format keeps the restore flexible.

commands.desc: Take a base backup for a standby
commands.tooltip: Copies the whole data directory from the primary with -X stream fetching WAL as it goes, the foundation of a streaming-replica setup. -P shows progress. The replicator role needs the replication privilege in pg_hba.conf.

commands.desc: Test if PostgreSQL accepts connections
commands.tooltip: Exits 0 when the server accepts connections and nonzero otherwise, so it fits monitoring scripts and load balancer checks. Use -U to also verify a specific role, or -d to check database reachability.

commands.desc: Install only the MySQL client tools
commands.tooltip: Installs mysql, mysqldump, mysqladmin, and mysqlcheck without the server, right for admin machines that manage remote databases. Debian and Ubuntu name the metapackage mysql-client. The client works against MariaDB servers too.

commands.desc: Start MySQL now and at every boot
commands.tooltip: enable --now starts the MySQL service immediately and registers it to start at boot. The unit is named mysql on Debian and Ubuntu, mysqld on some other distributions. Confirm with sudo systemctl status mysql.

commands.desc: Show MySQL service status
commands.tooltip: Reports whether the mysql unit is active, the mysqld process IDs, and recent log lines. A nonzero exit code when the service is down makes it script-friendly. Use --no-pager for cron and CI.

commands.desc: Connect to MySQL as root via auth socket
commands.tooltip: On Debian and Ubuntu the root account authenticates through the unix_socket plugin, so sudo mysql -u root logs in without a password. Use this to bootstrap a password for root. On other systems root may need -p.

commands.desc: Connect to a MySQL database interactively
commands.tooltip: Connects as app to the appdb database; -p prompts for the password. Once inside, run SQL statements or backslash commands like SHOW DATABASES. Add -h for a remote host and -P for a non-default port.

commands.desc: List databases non-interactively
commands.tooltip: -e executes the statement and returns to the shell, ideal for scripts. SHOW DATABASES lists every database the account can see. Wrap SQL in single quotes so the shell does not interpret it.

commands.desc: List tables in a database
commands.tooltip: Shows the tables in appdb without entering the interactive shell. Related: -e 'DESCRIBE users;' for columns. The database name comes before -e.

commands.desc: Show MySQL uptime and load
commands.tooltip: mysqladmin status prints uptime, thread count, queries per second, and open-table numbers in one line. A quick health snapshot for scripts. Related: mysqladmin ping for a pure alive check.

commands.desc: Check whether MySQL responds
commands.tooltip: Prints mysqld is alive and exits 0 when the server answers, making it the standard health probe for monitoring and failover scripts. Add -h to target a remote host.

commands.desc: Show active MySQL threads
commands.tooltip: Lists running client connections with their current statement, useful for spotting long queries and lock holders. The SQL equivalent is SHOW PROCESSLIST. Add --verbose for more detail.

commands.desc: Stop the MySQL server
commands.tooltip: Shuts down mysqld gracefully, flushing tables and closing connections. Destructive to availability, so announce it before running. The service can be restarted with sudo systemctl start mysql.

commands.cmd: sudo mysql -e "ALTER USER 'root'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED WITH caching_sha2_password BY 'secret';"
commands.desc: Set a password for the root account
commands.tooltip: Switches root to password authentication with the modern caching_sha2_password plugin, the recommended step right after a fresh install. Run it via sudo mysql while socket auth still works. Use a strong password, not the demo value.

commands.cmd: mysql -u root -p -e "CREATE DATABASE appdb CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;"
commands.desc: Create a database with explicit charset
commands.tooltip: utf8mb4 is the full Unicode character set, and utf8mb4_unicode_ci is its accent-insensitive collation; setting both explicitly avoids legacy latin1 defaults. Newer MySQL defaults already use utf8mb4, but being explicit protects MariaDB and older servers.

commands.desc: Create a MySQL user
commands.tooltip: Creates the app account limited to localhost; @'%' would allow any host. The password is hashed automatically. Grants are separate and must be issued afterwards.

commands.cmd: mysql -u root -p -e "GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON appdb.* TO 'app'@'localhost';"
commands.desc: Grant all privileges on one database
commands.tooltip: Gives the app user every privilege on appdb's tables and routines but nothing outside that database, a sensible least-privilege shape. Use appdb.* rather than *.* unless the account truly needs everything.

commands.cmd: mysql -u root -p -e "GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON appdb.* TO 'app'@'localhost';"
commands.desc: Grant limited DML privileges
commands.tooltip: Restricts the account to the four row-level operations, excluding DDL like DROP and ALTER. Tighten further with column-level grants for sensitive data. REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES ON appdb.* FROM 'app'@'localhost'; undoes it.

commands.desc: Change a MySQL user password
commands.tooltip: Updates the password for the app account, taking effect immediately for new logins; existing sessions keep running. Use SET PASSWORD for the current user. The host part must match the account exactly.

commands.desc: Delete a MySQL user
commands.tooltip: Removes the account and all of its privileges with no confirmation. Applications using it lose access immediately, so check SHOW GRANTS FOR 'app'@'localhost'; first. Related: DROP DATABASE for the data.

commands.desc: Delete a MySQL database
commands.tooltip: Drops the database and every table and row in it, irrevocably. Back up with mysqldump first unless you are certain. No confirmation prompt is offered.

commands.desc: Reload the grant tables
commands.tooltip: Forces MySQL to reread the privilege tables, needed after directly editing mysql.user with DML statements. GRANT and REVOKE take effect immediately on their own, so this is only for manual table edits.

commands.desc: Back up one database to a SQL file
commands.tooltip: Dumps appdb as CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements the mysql client can replay. The shell redirect writes the file. Add --single-transaction for a consistent snapshot on InnoDB without locking.

commands.desc: Restore a database from a SQL file
commands.tooltip: Feeds the dump file into the mysql client, which replays every statement. The target database must already exist. Check the file's CREATE DATABASE statements if you want a full rebuild.

commands.desc: Take a consistent dump with routines
commands.tooltip: --single-transaction produces a point-in-time snapshot of InnoDB without locking tables, while --routines, --triggers, and --events include stored procedures, triggers, and scheduled events that plain dumps omit. The standard online backup recipe.

commands.desc: Check tables for corruption
commands.tooltip: Runs CHECK TABLE on every table in appdb and reports errors and warnings. Run this before attempting a restore or after a crash. Use --all-databases to cover the whole server.

commands.desc: Optimize tables
commands.tooltip: Runs OPTIMIZE TABLE, which rebuilds InnoDB tables to reclaim fragmented space, the MySQL analogue of VACUUM FULL. It locks each table, so schedule it in a maintenance window.

commands.desc: Update table statistics
commands.tooltip: Runs ANALYZE TABLE so the optimizer's row estimates stay fresh after heavy changes. Cheap and non-blocking. Equivalent to ANALYZE TABLE appdb.users for one table.

commands.desc: Repair damaged tables
commands.tooltip: Attempts to fix corrupted MyISAM tables with REPAIR TABLE. InnoDB tables report that repair is not needed or use ALTER TABLE ... FORCE instead. Back up before repairing, and investigate why the table broke.

commands.cmd: mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT table_schema, ROUND(SUM(data_length + index_length) / 1024 / 1024, 2) AS size_mb FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY table_schema;"
commands.desc: Show the size of every database
commands.tooltip: Sums data_length plus index_length from information_schema.tables per schema and formats the total in megabytes. Values are approximate until flushed, but ideal for capacity reviews. Filter with WHERE table_schema NOT IN ('mysql', ...) to hide system schemas.

commands.cmd: mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT table_name, ROUND((data_length + index_length) / 1024 / 1024, 2) AS size_mb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'appdb' ORDER BY size_mb DESC;"
commands.desc: Rank tables by size
commands.tooltip: Lists appdb's tables with their data plus index footprint, largest first. Spot the tables driving disk growth before deciding what to archive or partition.

commands.desc: Show the connection limit
commands.tooltip: Reads the max_connections system variable, which caps concurrent client connections. Exceeding it produces too many connections errors. Compare with SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Threads_connected'.

commands.desc: Show the InnoDB buffer pool size
commands.tooltip: The buffer pool is InnoDB's main cache; a small value means heavy disk I/O. The classic sizing rule is 70 to 80 percent of available RAM on dedicated servers. Changing it requires a restart unless resized online.

commands.desc: Raise the connection limit at runtime
commands.tooltip: Raises max_connections immediately for new connections, but the change is not persisted and reverts on restart. Use SET PERSIST max_connections = 200 to write it to mysqld-auto.cnf as well.

commands.desc: Show InnoDB internals
commands.tooltip: Prints the InnoDB status report: transactions, lock waits, buffer pool, and I/O activity. The \G terminator switches to vertical output so the long text is readable. The first stop for deadlock and lock-wait investigations.

commands.cmd: mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT user, host, plugin FROM mysql.user;"
commands.desc: List users with auth plugins
commands.tooltip: Shows every account with the host it may connect from and the authentication plugin it uses, including the default root entries. A quick security audit of who can log in and how.

commands.desc: Show the privileges of one user
commands.tooltip: Prints every privilege the app account holds, one GRANT statement per line. The definitive answer to what an account can do before you tighten or hand out permissions.

commands.desc: Rebuild and defragment a table
commands.tooltip: Rebuilds the users table, reclaiming fragmented space and refreshing statistics. It locks the table during the rebuild, so run it in a maintenance window. InnoDB tables usually need this only after heavy churn.

commands.cmd: mysql -u root -p -e "PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE NOW() - INTERVAL 7 DAY;"
commands.desc: Delete binary logs older than a week
commands.tooltip: Removes binlog files older than seven days, freeing disk on servers that keep binary logging for replication or point-in-time recovery. Only the oldest files are purged; active ones stay. Verify the replica has consumed the logs first, or replication breaks.

commands.desc: Show Redis server details
commands.tooltip: The INFO server section reports the Redis version, process ID, uptime, and configured mode. INFO splits the same data into sections; pick server, persistence, clients, or replication as needed. Useful for verifying which node you reached.

commands.desc: Show RDB and AOF persistence status
commands.tooltip: Reports last successful RDB snapshot, AOF enablement and rewrite state, and whether a save is in progress. RDB is Redis's periodic snapshot file and AOF is the append-only log; both are persistence mechanisms. Check this after changing save policies.

commands.desc: Show replication role and state
commands.tooltip: Lists the node's role (master or slave), connected replicas, and replication offset. A growing master_repl_offset confirms replicas are keeping up. The first check during failover debugging.

commands.desc: Show connected client counts
commands.tooltip: Reports connected_clients, blocked clients, and the client-limit high-water mark. Pair with CLIENT LIST to see who the clients are. Spikes here often point to connection leaks in applications.

commands.desc: Show hit rates and command counters
commands.tooltip: Contains total_commands_processed, keyspace hits and misses, and expired keys. The ratio of hits to misses hints whether the cache is effective. Also shows rejected connections.

commands.desc: Delete all keys in every database
commands.tooltip: Removes every key on the server instantly; ASYNC defers the work to a background thread so the server stays responsive, but the data is still gone. There is no undo, so this is a last resort or a fresh-environment step.

commands.desc: Scan keys matching a pattern
commands.tooltip: --scan iterates keys without blocking the server, unlike KEYS, and --count tunes the batch size. session:* matches all keys in that namespace. Feed the output to a script for targeted deletion with DEL.

commands.desc: Show the ten slowest commands
commands.tooltip: Prints the most recent slow entries: timestamp, duration in microseconds, and the command, as logged by Redis's slowlog, which captures commands over the slowlog-log-slower-than threshold. The first stop when latency climbs.

commands.desc: Clear the slow command log
commands.tooltip: Empties the slowlog so future measurements start from a clean slate, useful before reproducing a latency issue. Only affects the in-memory log, not performance.

commands.desc: Disconnect a client by ID
commands.tooltip: Terminates the connection whose ID comes from CLIENT LIST. The client's next command fails and the application reconnects, so use it for stuck or abusive connections. CLIENT KILL supports filters like ADDR and TYPE too.

commands.desc: Ping with password without warning
commands.tooltip: -a passes the password on the command line, which prints a warning because it leaks via process listings; --no-auth-warning silences it. Prefer REDISCLI_AUTH for scripts. PING returns PONG when the server is reachable and authenticated.

commands.desc: Validate a Redis RDB dump file
commands.tooltip: Parses the snapshot file and reports whether the checksum and structure are valid, the check to run after copying a dump between machines. A corrupted file fails loudly instead of being loaded silently. Ships with the redis-server package.

commands.desc: Start Redis now and at every boot
commands.tooltip: enable --now starts the redis-server service immediately and registers it for boot. The unit name is redis-server on Debian and Ubuntu. Verify with sudo systemctl status redis-server.

commands.desc: Show Redis service status
commands.tooltip: Reports whether redis-server is active, its process ID, and recent log lines. Use --no-pager in scripts. The exit code is nonzero when the service is down.

commands.desc: Show the RDB snapshot schedule
commands.tooltip: Returns the save points that trigger background snapshots, pairs of seconds and change counts. Empty output means snapshots are disabled. CONFIG GET accepts glob patterns, so CONFIG GET max* covers several settings at once.

commands.desc: Change the eviction policy at runtime
commands.tooltip: Sets which keys Redis evicts when maxmemory is reached; allkeys-lru evicts least-recently-used keys from any database. The change is runtime-only until CONFIG REWRITE persists it. Wrong policies can evict important keys, so test first.

commands.desc: Persist runtime config to redis.conf
commands.tooltip: Writes the current effective configuration back to the config file, locking in CONFIG SET changes across restarts. Only parameters that differ from defaults are saved. Requires a writable config file.

commands.desc: Stop Redis without saving data
commands.tooltip: Shuts the server down immediately and skips the RDB snapshot, discarding any changes since the last save. Destructive to unsaved data, so only for emergency stops. Plain SHUTDOWN or SHUTDOWN SAVE flushes first.

commands.desc: Show memory used by one key
commands.tooltip: Returns the bytes a single key occupies, including its value and overhead. Great for finding oversized keys that blow up the memory budget. Add SAMPLES for more precise estimates on big collections.

commands.desc: Download the RDB snapshot to a file
commands.tooltip: Triggers a background save and streams the resulting dump.rdb to the local file, giving you a consistent snapshot without touching the server's filesystem. Restore by placing the file in the configured dir and restarting.

commands.desc: Move a key to another Redis server
commands.tooltip: Transfers the key atomically to the host and port given, database 0, with 5000 milliseconds as the connection timeout. The key is deleted from the source on success. The destination must be reachable and must not already hold the key.

commands.desc: Show all ACL users and rules
commands.tooltip: Prints every ACL user with its permission rules, the default user included. ACLs (access control lists) govern which commands and key patterns each user may use. Audit this before opening Redis to the network.

commands.desc: Create an ACL user with scoped access
commands.tooltip: Creates user app, enabled (on), with password secret (>secret), access limited to keys matching app:* (~app:*), and only the GET and SET commands allowed. The quotes stop the shell from interpreting > and *. Revoke with ACL DELUSER.

commands.desc: Delete an ACL user
commands.tooltip: Removes the ACL user and its rules; clients authenticated as that user are disconnected on their next command. Keep at least one admin user outside the deletion, or you can lock yourself out.

commands.desc: Start MongoDB now and at every boot
commands.tooltip: enable --now starts the mongod service immediately and registers it for boot. The unit name is mongod for MongoDB Community installed from the official repo. Confirm with sudo systemctl status mongod.

commands.desc: Show MongoDB service status
commands.tooltip: Reports whether mongod is active, its process ID, and recent log lines. Logs also live in /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log. Use --no-pager in scripts; the exit code is nonzero when the service is down.

commands.desc: Ping MongoDB to test connectivity
commands.tooltip: The ping command returns { ok: 1 } when the server is reachable, the standard health probe for mongosh and drivers alike. --eval runs the script and exits. Add --quiet to suppress banner noise in scripts.

commands.desc: Query documents from a collection
commands.tooltip: Connects to appdb and prints the first five documents of users; .limit(5) caps the output. find() returns a cursor, and mongosh prints up to 20 documents interactively. Add .pretty() for formatted output.

commands.desc: Create a unique index
commands.tooltip: Builds an ascending index on email that rejects duplicate values, enforcing uniqueness at the database level. Indexes are created asynchronously; the command returns when the build finishes. Duplicate documents make the build fail.

commands.desc: Show database statistics
commands.tooltip: Reports data size, index size, document counts, and storage engine for the current database. The admin equivalent is db.adminCommand({dbStats: 1}). A first look at whether a database is growing as expected.

commands.desc: Show server status and metrics
commands.tooltip: Returns uptime, version, connections, memory, and operation counters for the whole server. The main dashboard for capacity and health checks. Requires a user with the hostInfo or serverStatus privilege.

commands.desc: Back up one database to a directory
commands.tooltip: Writes appdb's collections as BSON files under /backups/mongo, the standard logical backup for MongoDB. The dump is consistent per collection; for a fully consistent snapshot use --oplog or a filesystem snapshot. Restore with mongorestore.

commands.desc: Back up a database to a gzip archive
commands.tooltip: --archive writes a single file instead of a directory tree, and --gzip compresses it, cutting backup size dramatically. Restore the archive with mongorestore --gzip --archive=/backups/appdb.archive.

commands.desc: Restore and replace existing collections
commands.tooltip: Loads the BSON files back into appdb; --drop removes each collection before restoring it, so the target mirrors the backup exactly. Destructive to current data, so verify the target database first. Omit --drop to merge.

commands.desc: Export a collection to JSON
commands.tooltip: Writes the users collection as newline-delimited JSON, ideal for moving data into other systems or archives. mongoexport is part of the database-tools package, separate from mongosh. Import the file back with mongoimport.

commands.desc: Export a collection to CSV
commands.tooltip: Exports only the email and name fields as CSV; --fields names the columns and must be supplied for CSV output. Rows with missing fields get empty values. Handy for spreadsheet workflows.

commands.desc: Import JSON documents into a collection
commands.tooltip: Loads the JSON file into the users collection, creating the collection if needed and inserting documents alongside existing ones. Use --drop to replace the collection first. The file format must match what mongoexport writes.

commands.desc: List indexes on a collection
commands.tooltip: Prints every index on users, including the automatic _id index, with its keys and options. Review this before creating new indexes to avoid duplicates. Related: db.users.dropIndex().

commands.desc: Drop an index from a collection
commands.tooltip: Removes the index on email, freeing space and write overhead. Queries that relied on it fall back to collection scans until a replacement exists. Dropping the _id index is not allowed.

commands.desc: Show collection storage statistics
commands.tooltip: Reports the collection's size, document count, index sizes, and average object size. Compare with db.stats() for database-level totals. Useful before deciding whether a collection needs compaction.

commands.desc: Show operations currently running
commands.tooltip: Lists in-progress operations with their IDs, durations, and query shapes, the equivalent of SHOW PROCESSLIST. Filter with db.currentOp({active: true}) to skip idle sessions. Copy an opid to pass to db.killOp().

commands.desc: Terminate a running operation
commands.tooltip: Kills the operation with the given opid, rolling back its work. Only terminate operations initiated by clients; killing internal operations can destabilize the server. Confirm the opid with db.currentOp() first.

commands.desc: Explain a query with execution stats
commands.tooltip: Runs the query in explain mode and reports the winning plan, documents examined, and execution time. Documents examined far above documents returned usually means a missing index. The core tool for query tuning.

commands.desc: Connect with explicit credentials
commands.tooltip: Authenticates as app against the admin database, where MongoDB stores user definitions, then connects to appdb. The same flags work for mongodump and mongoexport. Prefer environment variables or a config file over visible passwords.

commands.desc: Create a database user
commands.tooltip: Creates user app with the readWrite role scoped to appdb, so it can read and write that database only. Roles are the MongoDB privilege model; add more roles for broader access. The user record lives in admin.

commands.desc: Delete a database user
commands.tooltip: Removes the app user and all of its roles; clients authenticated as it lose access on their next operation. There is no undo, so confirm with db.getUsers() first.

commands.desc: List loaded kernel modules
commands.tooltip: Shows every kernel module currently loaded, one line each, with its size and how many other modules depend on it. A module is a driver or feature compiled separately from the kernel and loadable on demand. The first column is the name you pass to modprobe. Combine with grep to find a specific driver, for example lsmod | grep nvme.

commands.desc: Show details about the i915 kernel module
commands.tooltip: Prints metadata for the i915 Intel graphics driver module: description, license, version, and the file it loads from. Useful to confirm a driver is present before loading it or to identify the correct module name for modprobe. The -p flag lists the module parameters instead.

commands.desc: List tunable parameters of the i915 module
commands.tooltip: Shows the parameters the i915 driver accepts at load time, such as enable_guc for the graphics execution unit. Parameters listed here can be set through modprobe options or files under /etc/modprobe.d. Pair with modinfo i915 for the module metadata.

commands.desc: Load the nf_tables kernel module
commands.tooltip: Loads nf_tables, the module behind the nftables firewall framework. modprobe also resolves and loads every module nf_tables depends on, so you rarely load dependencies by hand. Modules are looked up under /lib/modules. Verify the load with lsmod or dmesg.

commands.desc: Unload the nf_tables kernel module
commands.tooltip: Removes nf_tables and its now-unused dependencies from the running kernel. Removal fails if another module still depends on it or a process holds a reference, which is normal safety behavior. Only unload modules you are certain are unused, since active firewall rules may vanish with it.

commands.desc: Load the drm module and its dependencies
commands.tooltip: Loads drm plus every module it requires, which for display servers includes the graphics driver stack. The -a flag stands for --all and accepts several module names at once. A module is a loadable kernel component, so this enables optional hardware support without rebooting.

commands.desc: Show module dependencies without loading
commands.tooltip: Prints exactly which modules and options modprobe would load for nf_tables, without loading anything. This dry-run inspection explains why a module pulls in others or helps debug load failures. The output lists insmod commands with full paths under /lib/modules.

commands.desc: Rebuild the kernel module dependency database
commands.tooltip: Scans all modules under /lib/modules and regenerates modules.dep, the index modprobe uses to resolve dependencies. Run it after installing new kernel modules or a new kernel so modprobe can find them. Without a current index, modprobe reports modules missing even when the files exist.

commands.desc: Regenerate the GRUB boot menu configuration
commands.tooltip: Rebuilds /boot/grub/grub.cfg from the scripts in /etc/grub.d and the settings in /etc/default/grub. Run it after editing those files or installing a kernel so the boot menu reflects the change. GRUB is the bootloader that presents the menu and loads the kernel. On Debian systems the wrapper update-grub does the same job.

commands.desc: Regenerate the GRUB menu on Debian systems
commands.tooltip: Debian and Ubuntu wrapper around grub-mkconfig that writes a fresh /boot/grub/grub.cfg using the current kernel and /etc/default/grub settings. Run it after kernel updates, fstab changes, or editing GRUB options. It must run as root and prints the kernels and initrd images it detects.

commands.desc: Install the GRUB bootloader to a disk
commands.tooltip: Writes the GRUB boot code to the master boot record of /dev/sda so the firmware can start it. This is destructive and low-level: a wrong target disk can leave a system unbootable. Normally you only re-run it after replacing a disk or installing a new bootloader. Use the --efi-directory form on UEFI machines.

commands.desc: Generate a PBKDF2 hash for GRUB authentication
commands.tooltip: Prompts for a password and prints a PBKDF2 hash you can paste into /etc/grub.d/00_header to protect GRUB menu editing. PBKDF2 is a deliberately slow key-derivation algorithm that makes the stored hash resistant to brute force. Regenerate the menu with update-grub afterwards and test the lockout on reboot.

commands.desc: Show the GRUB environment block variables
commands.tooltip: Prints variables stored in the GRUB environment block, such as saved_entry which records the last chosen menu entry. The environment block is a small file that survives reboots and lets GRUB scripts persist state. Use it with grub-reboot or grub-set-default to control which entry boots.

commands.desc: Boot a specific GRUB entry once
commands.tooltip: Sets saved_entry so the next reboot uses menu entry 2, then reverts to the default after that single boot. Useful to test an older kernel or a rescue entry without permanently changing the default. Confirm entry numbers against the menuentry lines in /boot/grub/grub.cfg.

commands.desc: Rebuild the current initramfs image
commands.tooltip: Recreates the initramfs for the running kernel, packing the drivers and scripts needed in early boot into /boot/initrd.img. The initramfs is the early userspace the kernel loads before the real root filesystem is mounted. Run it after changing filesystem, LVM, or encryption settings so the boot image matches. Requires root.

commands.desc: Create an initramfs for a specific kernel
commands.tooltip: Builds a fresh initramfs image for kernel 6.8.0-45-generic even if one exists, overwriting it. The -k flag selects the kernel version and -c forces creation. Use this after upgrading a kernel manually or restoring a damaged initrd.img. An initramfs is the early userspace used to find and mount the real root filesystem.

commands.desc: Delete the initramfs for a kernel version
commands.tooltip: Removes the initramfs image belonging to kernel 6.8.0-45-generic. Only do this when that kernel is no longer needed, because the system cannot boot it without its initramfs. Keep the image for the running kernel at all times. The initramfs holds the drivers needed before the root filesystem is available.

commands.desc: Build a custom initramfs image by hand
commands.tooltip: Creates an initramfs for kernel 6.8.0-45-generic and writes it to the path after -o, bypassing the normal update-initramfs flow. This is the underlying Debian tool for packing early-boot drivers and scripts into initrd.img. Useful for testing custom configurations or repairing a broken image. Run as root.

commands.desc: Rebuild the initramfs on RHEL-family systems
commands.tooltip: Regenerates the initramfs images managed by dracut, the initramfs generator used on Fedora, RHEL, and derivatives. The --force flag overwrites existing images even when dracut thinks nothing changed. Run it after changing storage or encryption configuration so early boot matches the new setup. Equivalent in purpose to update-initramfs -u on Debian.

commands.desc: List UEFI boot entries with details
commands.tooltip: Shows every entry in the UEFI boot manager, including the boot number, active flag, and the EFI file each entry loads. The -v flag adds verbose detail such as the full device path. Use the boot numbers shown here with efibootmgr -b to modify or delete entries. Requires access to EFI variables, so run as root.

commands.desc: Delete a UEFI boot entry
commands.tooltip: Removes boot entry 0001 from the UEFI boot manager permanently. Deleting the wrong entry can make the system fail to boot, so list entries with efibootmgr -v first and double-check the number. There is no undo, and a deleted entry must be recreated by hand with efibootmgr -c.

commands.desc: Create a UEFI boot entry for Ubuntu
commands.tooltip: Adds a new boot entry labeled Ubuntu that loads \EFI\ubuntu\shimx64.efi from partition 1 of /dev/sda. The shim is the signed first-stage loader that chains into GRUB, so this is how you re-register a distro after its entry disappears. UEFI paths use backslashes. Run as root and verify with efibootmgr -v.

commands.desc: Set the UEFI boot order
commands.tooltip: Reorders boot entries so 0001 is tried first and 0002 second, controlling which OS or loader the firmware starts. The comma-separated list can include any subset of existing boot numbers. Use efibootmgr -v to see the current numbers. This only changes firmware boot order, not the GRUB menu.

commands.desc: Restart the systemd manager process
commands.tooltip: Re-executes systemd itself, reloading the manager binary and its configuration while keeping all units and their state intact. A unit is systemd's definition of a service, socket, timer, or other managed object. Use this after upgrading systemd or editing manager-level settings in daemon.conf. Your services are not restarted.

commands.desc: Clear the failed state of a unit
commands.tooltip: Forgets that the nginx service previously failed, removing it from the failed list and resetting its failure counters. A unit stays in failed state until reset, which matters for automation that watches systemctl is-failed. The bare form systemctl reset-failed clears every failed unit at once.

commands.desc: Display one property of a unit
commands.tooltip: Prints a single property, ExecStart, of the nginx unit, showing the exact command line systemd uses to start it. The -p flag selects one property instead of the full dump plain systemctl show returns. Useful to confirm which binary and arguments a unit really runs.

commands.desc: Show units ordered before sshd
commands.tooltip: Lists the units systemd starts before sshd.service because of ordering dependencies, giving a view of that service's boot chain. The --after flag shows what must be up first, while --before shows what comes later. This helps debug services that fail because a dependency is missing.

commands.desc: Change a unit property at runtime
commands.tooltip: Applies a runtime property, here a 50 percent CPU quota, to the nginx service without editing its unit file. The change persists under /etc/systemd/system.control and can be read back with systemctl show. Not all properties support runtime assignment.

commands.desc: Edit a unit file with a full override copy
commands.tooltip: Opens the complete unit file of nginx in your editor so you can rewrite it wholesale, saving the copy as an override under /etc/systemd/system. Plain systemctl edit only opens a small drop-in snippet. Use the full form when you want to restructure the whole unit rather than patch it.

commands.desc: Remove all overrides for a unit
commands.tooltip: Deletes every drop-in override and symlink that customizes the nginx unit, returning it to the version shipped by the package. Use this to undo systemctl edit changes or accidental masking. The shipped unit file itself is not touched, only local modifications.

commands.desc: List units enabled at boot
commands.tooltip: Shows every unit file whose state is enabled, meaning systemd will start it during boot. The --state filter narrows the full list-unit-files output to one status. Combined with --type=service you get only the enabled services, a quick audit of what runs at startup.

commands.desc: List active systemd targets
commands.tooltip: Shows the currently active targets, which are named groups of units representing boot levels such as multi-user.target or graphical.target. A target is systemd's replacement for the old runlevel concept. Use this to see which groups are up and which target systemctl isolate would switch to.

commands.desc: List all systemd timers including inactive
commands.tooltip: Shows every timer unit with its next and last trigger times, including timers that are not currently running thanks to --all. Timers are systemd's replacement for cron, scheduling services by calendar or monotonic time. The output also names the service each timer activates.

commands.desc: Check a unit file for errors
commands.tooltip: Parses the nginx unit file and its dependencies, reporting syntax errors, unknown settings, and missing binaries without starting anything. It follows included files and drop-ins, so it validates the real effective configuration. A clean run prints nothing, while warnings and errors name the offending lines.

commands.desc: Audit a unit's security exposure
commands.tooltip: Scores the nginx service against hardening properties such as PrivateTmp, NoNewPrivileges, and capability restrictions, printing a risk level from 0.0 to 9.9. Use the printed suggestions to add hardening directives to the unit. The form without a unit name analyzes the whole system.

commands.desc: Show boot time breakdown by unit
commands.tooltip: Prints how long each unit took to start during the last boot, sorted by time, with a total at the end. This is the fastest way to find what slows boot. Add --boot-id or use systemd-analyze blame for a flatter list.

commands.desc: Validate a calendar timer expression
commands.tooltip: Parses a calendar specification like 'Mon 02:00' and prints the next few times it will fire, confirming the syntax before you put it in a timer unit. This catches mistakes such as wrong weekday names or impossible times. The same expression syntax is used by the OnCalendar setting in timer units.

commands.desc: Run a command on a schedule as a timer
commands.tooltip: Creates a transient timer named myjob that triggers /usr/local/bin/backup.sh every Monday at 02:00, plus the matching service unit. Transient units live only until reboot unless created with --system. This is a quick way to schedule jobs without writing timer files by hand.

commands.desc: Send command output to the journal
commands.tooltip: Runs echo hello with its output captured and written into the systemd journal tagged with the identifier myapp. The -t flag sets the tag shown in the journal. Use this to funnel scripts that normally log to stdout into journalctl, keeping all logs in one place.

commands.desc: Create missing tmpfiles entries
commands.tooltip: Processes the tmpfiles.d configuration files, creating directories, symlinks, and files that should exist on the system. Directories such as /run are defined this way. Run it manually after adding a new tmpfiles.d snippet, though systemd also runs it at boot.

commands.desc: Remove stale files per tmpfiles rules
commands.tooltip: Deletes files and directories marked with the age-based cleanup directives in tmpfiles.d configuration, such as old files under /tmp or /var/tmp. The rules specify how long entries may survive. Run with --dry-run first to preview what would be removed.

commands.desc: Escape a string for use in unit names
commands.tooltip: Converts a human-readable name like 'nginx service' into the escaped form nginx\x20service that systemd unit names require. Spaces and special characters must be escaped because unit names become file names. Use it in the other direction to decode unit names back to readable text.

commands.desc: Show kernel messages from the journal
commands.tooltip: Prints the kernel ring buffer messages captured by the journal, equivalent to what dmesg shows. Driver errors, hardware issues, and OOM killer events appear here. Add -b to restrict to the current boot or --since with a time to narrow the window.

commands.desc: Dump journal entries as formatted JSON
commands.tooltip: Outputs each journal entry as indented JSON with fields such as MESSAGE, _PID, and _SYSTEMD_UNIT. Machine-readable output like this is made for log pipelines and parsers. Other formats include json, short, and cat. Pipe into jq for filtering and aggregation.

commands.desc: Filter journal by systemd unit field
commands.tooltip: Shows entries whose _SYSTEMD_UNIT field exactly matches nginx.service, a lower-level filter than the -u shortcut. Field filters work on any journal field, such as _PID or _COMM. The journal is systemd's structured binary log store that journalctl reads.

commands.desc: List recorded boot sessions
commands.tooltip: Prints each boot the journal knows about with a boot ID, an offset number, and the time range. Use the negative offset with journalctl -b, for example -b -2 for two boots ago. The journal keeps this history until log rotation removes it.

commands.desc: Show details of all physical volumes
commands.tooltip: Prints verbose information for every physical volume, including its size, the volume group it belongs to, and the free space remaining. A physical volume is a disk or partition marked for LVM use with pvcreate. Use pvs for a compact one-line summary instead.

commands.desc: List all LVM physical volumes
commands.tooltip: Scans all disks for LVM physical volumes and prints a one-line summary per device, including which volume group each belongs to. Useful after adding new disks to see whether the system finds them. pvs gives the same information in a cleaner table.

commands.desc: Show details of all volume groups
commands.tooltip: Displays full information for every volume group: total physical extents, free space, and the number of logical volumes it contains. A volume group pools several physical volumes into one storage reservoir. Use vgs for a compact listing.

commands.desc: Remove a physical volume from a group
commands.tooltip: Detaches /dev/sdc from the volume group vgdata, shrinking the pool of available space. Move or remove the data first, because extents still on that disk become lost. Use pvmove to relocate data before removing the disk from the group.

commands.desc: Activate all volume groups
commands.tooltip: Makes every volume group available so its logical volumes appear as block devices under /dev. Groups are normally activated at boot, but after a rescue boot or a disk change they may need manual activation. The -a flag takes y for activate or n for deactivate.

commands.desc: Deactivate all volume groups
commands.tooltip: Takes every volume group offline, hiding its logical volumes from the system. All logical volumes must be unmounted first or the command fails. Use this before moving disks or resizing groups at the block level.

commands.desc: Create a logical volume using all free space
commands.tooltip: Creates a logical volume named lvbackup in group vgdata, consuming every remaining free extent. A logical volume is the LVM equivalent of a partition, usable directly or as a filesystem target. The -l flag counts extents, while -L takes a size such as 10G.

commands.desc: Grow a logical volume and its filesystem
commands.tooltip: Adds 10 gigabytes to logical volume lvdata and, thanks to -r, resizes the filesystem inside it to match. Without -r you would have to run resize2fs or xfs_growfs afterwards. The plus sign means add rather than set an absolute size.

commands.desc: Resize a logical volume to an absolute size
commands.tooltip: Sets logical volume lvdata to exactly 10 gigabytes, growing or shrinking as needed. This is the general resize command that lvextend and lvreduce wrap. Shrinking requires the filesystem to be shrunk first and the volume unmounted, so prefer growing.

commands.desc: Rename a logical volume
commands.tooltip: Changes the name of logical volume lvdata to lvdata2 inside group vgdata. The device path changes from /dev/vgdata/lvdata to /dev/vgdata/lvdata2, so update fstab and any mounts that reference the old name. Renaming is safe while the volume is unmounted.

commands.desc: Show details of one logical volume
commands.tooltip: Prints full metadata for the lvdata logical volume: size, stripes, and the underlying physical volumes. Specify the device path to limit output to one volume. Use lvs for a compact table of all logical volumes.

commands.desc: Remove the LVM label from a disk
commands.tooltip: Erases the physical volume label on /dev/sdb, returning the disk to a plain block device usable for anything else. This destroys the LVM metadata on that disk, so move or back up all data first. After removal the disk can be repartitioned freely.

commands.desc: Convert a logical volume to RAID 1 mirroring
commands.tooltip: Converts lvdata into a RAID 1 mirrored volume with one mirror copy, given enough free extents in the group. LVM RAID uses the kernel md driver, so the mirror survives individual disk failures. The -m 1 flag requests one additional copy of the data.

commands.desc: Back up a volume group's metadata
commands.tooltip: Saves the configuration metadata of volume group vgdata to /etc/lvm/backup. That file contains the exact layout needed to restore the group if metadata is lost. Regular backups let you recover a broken volume group with vgcfgrestore.

commands.desc: Show all active RAID arrays
commands.tooltip: Lists every running RAID array in a format suitable for the mdadm.conf configuration file. The output names the array device, level, and member disks. This is the first step when documenting arrays, since the lines can be appended to /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf.

commands.desc: Stop a RAID array
commands.tooltip: Takes the md0 RAID array offline, releasing its member disks. All filesystems on the array must be unmounted first. Stopping is safe as long as the member disks keep their superblocks, so the array can be reassembled later with mdadm --assemble.

commands.desc: Add a spare disk to a RAID array
commands.tooltip: Adds /dev/sdd1 to array md0 as a spare or, if the array is degraded, immediately starts rebuilding data onto it. This is how you replace a failed disk: fail the bad one, remove it, then add the new one. Watch the rebuild progress in /proc/mdstat.

commands.desc: Remove a disk from a RAID array
commands.tooltip: Detaches /dev/sdb1 from array md0, normally after marking it failed with mdadm --fail. A disk that still holds active data cannot be removed directly. Removing a healthy disk while the array runs is possible but degrades the array.

commands.desc: Mark a RAID disk as failed
commands.tooltip: Flags /dev/sdb1 as failed in array md0, simulating a hardware failure and letting the array switch to the remaining disks or a spare. Use this to test redundancy or before physically removing a dying disk. The array keeps running in degraded mode until the rebuild completes.

commands.desc: Erase RAID metadata from a disk
commands.tooltip: Wipes the RAID superblock on /dev/sdb1 so the disk no longer looks like an array member. This is destructive: do it only after the array is stopped and the data is no longer needed. Without this step, leftover superblocks can confuse future mdadm --create or --assemble runs.

commands.desc: Reassemble a RAID array from its disks
commands.tooltip: Puts array md0 back together from the member disks after a reboot or a stop, reading the superblocks to rebuild the layout. Use --scan to assemble every array found automatically. This is the recovery counterpart to mdadm --create.

commands.desc: Persist RAID configuration to mdadm.conf
commands.tooltip: Appends the current array definitions to /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf so the system assembles them automatically at boot. Without this file, arrays may come up under different names or not at all. Run it once after creating or changing an array, as root.

commands.desc: Enable quotas on a filesystem
commands.tooltip: Switches on quota accounting for the filesystem on /dev/mapper/vgdata-lvdata, using the quota files found there. Quotas limit how much space or how many inodes a user or group can consume. Enable them in fstab with the usrquota or grpquota mount option so they activate at boot.

commands.desc: Enable quotas on all mounted filesystems
commands.tooltip: Turns on quota accounting for every filesystem whose fstab entry carries the usrquota or grpquota option. This is the boot-time equivalent of running quotaon per filesystem. Quotas stay active until quotaoff or a remount without the quota options.

commands.desc: Disable quotas on all filesystems
commands.tooltip: Stops quota enforcement and accounting on every filesystem that has quotas enabled. Users can then exceed their limits without warnings or refusal. Run quotaon -a to re-enable, or give quotaoff a device path to target one filesystem.

commands.desc: Scan a filesystem and build quota files
commands.tooltip: Scans the filesystem to create or update the quota database, with -c to create new files, -u for user quotas, and -m to avoid forcing a read-only remount. Modern kernels maintain accounting on the fly, so this is mainly for repairing quota files or migrating systems.

commands.desc: Edit a user's quota limits interactively
commands.tooltip: Opens the quota limits for user alice in your editor, letting you set soft and hard limits for blocks and inodes. The soft limit triggers warnings, while the hard limit is absolute and refuses further writes. Hard limits must be greater than soft limits.

commands.desc: Edit a group's quota limits
commands.tooltip: Opens the quota settings for the developers group in an editor, applying the same soft and hard limits to every member through the group. Group quotas count the combined usage of all members. Use edquota -t to adjust the grace period for exceeding soft limits.

commands.desc: Edit quota grace periods
commands.tooltip: Sets the grace period, the time a user may stay over the soft limit before it is treated as a hard limit. Defaults are often seven days for both blocks and inodes. The editor shows the current grace values, which you change in days, hours, or minutes.

commands.desc: Report quota usage for all filesystems
commands.tooltip: Prints a table of every user and group on quota-enabled filesystems, showing blocks used, soft and hard limits, and files or inodes. The -a flag covers all quota filesystems in fstab. Use repquota /home to restrict the report to one filesystem.

commands.desc: Report user quotas with human-readable sizes
commands.tooltip: Shows per-user quota usage on /home with -u for users, -v for verbose detail, and -s to print sizes in human units such as megabytes instead of raw blocks. A plus sign marks users currently over their soft limit. This is the standard way to review who consumes space.

commands.desc: Set quota limits from the command line
commands.tooltip: Assigns user alice a 100 megabyte soft limit and 120 megabyte hard limit on /home without opening an editor; the zero inode limits mean unlimited files. The K, M, G, and T size suffixes are accepted. Ideal for scripting user onboarding.

commands.desc: Show a user's quota usage and limits
commands.tooltip: Reports how much space and how many inodes user alice has used on quota filesystems, alongside the soft and hard limits and grace status. Run plain quota as that user to check your own limits. A plus sign indicates the soft limit has been exceeded.

commands.desc: Report XFS quotas in human units
commands.tooltip: Prints XFS quota usage for the /mnt/data filesystem, with -x for expert mode and -c running the report command with -h for human-readable sizes. XFS manages quotas differently from ext4, storing them in the filesystem itself. The same tool enables and disables XFS quotas.

commands.desc: Mount a directory at another location
commands.tooltip: Makes the directory /var/www also appear at /mnt/site without copying anything, so both paths reference the same files. Bind mounts are handy for chroots, containers, and rearranging layouts. Use umount /mnt/site to remove the extra view, and --rbind to include sub-mounts.

commands.desc: Mount a disk image file
commands.tooltip: Attaches the file disk.img as a block device through the loop driver and mounts it at /mnt/img, letting you browse or modify an image without burning it to media. The loop option is inferred automatically on modern systems. Unmount with umount /mnt/img when finished.

commands.desc: Remount the root filesystem read-only
commands.tooltip: Changes the mount options of the root filesystem to read-only without unmounting it. This is a common safety step before filesystem checks or when taking a system down for maintenance. Use remount,rw to switch back to read-write.

commands.desc: Create a RAM-backed filesystem
commands.tooltip: Mounts a tmpfs, a filesystem stored entirely in RAM, at /mnt/ram. Everything written there vanishes on reboot and counts against available memory. Useful for scratch space, caches, and fast temporary files, but never for persistent data.

commands.desc: Force-unmount a busy filesystem
commands.tooltip: Forcefully detaches the filesystem at /mnt/stuck even when processes hold files open on it. The -f flag bypasses the normal busy check, which risks losing writes still in flight. Prefer finding the offender with lsof or fuser, or use umount -l for a lazy detach.

commands.desc: Mount an NFS export with a specific version
commands.tooltip: Mounts the NFS export /srv/nfs from server at /mnt/nfs, explicitly requesting protocol version 4.2. Pinning the version avoids negotiation surprises and enables features such as server-side copy. Other versions include vers=3 and vers=4.1. The export must be listed in the server's /etc/exports.

commands.desc: Mount a Windows SMB share
commands.tooltip: Attaches the SMB share //server/share to /mnt/windows using CIFS, authenticating as user alice. You are prompted for the password unless a credentials file is given. This is the Linux client side of Samba and Windows file servers.

commands.desc: List filesystems by type
commands.tooltip: Shows every mounted filesystem of type ext4 with its source, target, and options. The -t filter accepts comma-separated types. findmnt reads the kernel mount table, so it reflects reality rather than fstab.

commands.desc: Show how a mount point is mounted
commands.tooltip: Displays the filesystem mounted at /home with its source device, type, and options. Pass any path to find out which filesystem backs it. Adding -o SOURCE,FSTYPE limits the columns shown, handy for scripts.

commands.desc: List filesystems from fstab
commands.tooltip: Shows what /etc/fstab declares, including entries that are not currently mounted. fstab is the static table of filesystems mounted at boot. Compare with plain findmnt to spot entries that failed to mount or were added manually.

commands.desc: Activate all swap devices in fstab
commands.tooltip: Enables every swap area listed in /etc/fstab, which is what the system does at boot. Swap is disk space the kernel uses when RAM runs low. Verify the result with swapon --show.

commands.desc: Set the maximum mount count for a filesystem
commands.tooltip: Configures ext4 on /dev/sdb1 to force a filesystem check after 30 mounts. The counter resets each time a check runs. Setting the count to -1 disables count-based checks entirely.

commands.desc: Reserve five percent of a filesystem for root
commands.tooltip: Sets the reserved-blocks percentage of /dev/sdb1 to 5, space only root can use. Reserved blocks keep a full disk from locking out root and reduce fragmentation. Lower it toward 0 on large data volumes to reclaim space.

commands.desc: Automatically repair filesystem errors
commands.tooltip: Runs a filesystem check on /dev/sdb1 in preen mode, fixing problems that are safe to repair automatically and stopping on anything serious. The filesystem must be unmounted for a reliable check. Preen mode is what runs at boot when the mount count or error flag demands a check.

commands.desc: Print filesystem metadata as key-value pairs
commands.tooltip: Outputs the UUID, type, and label of /dev/sdb1 in VAR=value format, easy to source in shell scripts. The UUID identifies the filesystem regardless of device name, which is why fstab entries often use UUID= rather than /dev paths.

commands.desc: Create an ext4 filesystem with a label
commands.tooltip: Formats /dev/sdb1 as ext4 with the label data and no reserved blocks, since -m 0 sets the reserved percentage to zero. Formatting destroys everything on the device, so double-check the target before running. Use the label with mount -L or in fstab by LABEL=data.

commands.desc: Query the udev database for a device
commands.tooltip: Looks up /dev/sda in the udev database and prints its device path under /sys, with -q path selecting just that field. udev is the device manager that names devices and runs rules when hardware appears. The /sys path is the key for writing udev rules.

commands.desc: Export all device properties from udev
commands.tooltip: Dumps the full udev database, one block per device, with every property and value udev knows about. Useful for discovering which identifiers a device exposes before writing a rule. Pipe through less or grep to find a specific device.

commands.desc: Walk sysfs attributes for rule writing
commands.tooltip: Prints the sysfs attribute chain for /dev/sda, showing parent devices and their properties, which udev rules match against. Each block is prefixed with the lookup keywords such as ATTRS or KERNELS. This output is the raw material for a custom udev rule.

commands.desc: Watch kernel and udev events live
commands.tooltip: Prints device events as they happen, prefixed with KERNEL for the raw kernel event and UDEV for the processed event after rules run. Plug in a device or run udevadm trigger in another terminal to see activity. Useful for debugging why a rule did or did not fire.

commands.desc: Replay device events through the rules
commands.tooltip: Synthesizes add events for existing devices so udev runs its rules on them again. Use it after adding or editing rules to apply them without rebooting or replugging hardware. With --action=remove or a device path you can target specific devices.

commands.desc: Wait until udev finishes processing events
commands.tooltip: Blocks until the udev event queue is empty, ensuring all devices are named and rules have run. Scripts that mount or probe devices right after boot use this to avoid racing udev. Add a timeout for safety in automation.

commands.desc: Reload udev rules without rebooting
commands.tooltip: Signals systemd-udevd to reload the rules files and the module index. New or edited rules under /etc/udev/rules.d take effect without restarting the daemon or replugging devices. Follow with udevadm trigger to replay events through the fresh rules.

commands.desc: Dry-run udev rules for one device
commands.tooltip: Simulates a udev event for the eth0 network device, printing every rule that matches and the resulting actions and properties. Nothing is changed on the system, making this the safe way to debug a rule. Pass --action=add or --action=remove to test a specific event type.

commands.desc: Show temperature and voltage readings
commands.tooltip: Prints readings from hardware sensors: CPU and motherboard temperatures, fan speeds, and voltages. The lm-sensors package must be configured, usually after running sensors-detect. High temperatures here point to cooling problems worth investigating.

commands.desc: Show sensor readings in Fahrenheit
commands.tooltip: Same readings as plain sensors but converts temperatures to degrees Fahrenheit with the -f flag. Useful on systems where staff think in Fahrenheit. Celsius remains the default everywhere else.

commands.desc: Print sensor readings as JSON
commands.tooltip: Outputs all sensor data as structured JSON, easy to feed into monitoring scripts and dashboards. Fields are grouped by chip and include label, value, and unit. The -u raw format is the alternative for low-level debugging.

commands.desc: Read a single DMI string from firmware
commands.tooltip: Prints one DMI value, here the system serial number, straight from the firmware tables. DMI data describes the hardware as the BIOS reports it. The -s flag accepts other keywords such as system-product-name or bios-version.

commands.desc: List block devices with filesystem types
commands.tooltip: Shows every block device with the NAME, SIZE, TYPE, MOUNTPOINT, and FSTYPE columns, adding the filesystem type to the basic view. The TYPE column distinguishes disks, partitions, and LVM or RAID members. This is the fastest full picture of storage layout.

commands.desc: Switch to single-user rescue mode
commands.tooltip: Isolates rescue.target, bringing the system to a minimal single-user state with only essential services. This is the modern replacement for the old single-user runlevel, used for maintenance and repairs. You are asked for the root password unless already root.

commands.desc: Enter emergency shell mode
