commands.tooltip: The -x flag deletes one named entry from the ACL instead of modifying values. Here it strips the group devs entry from /srv/shared while leaving every other entry untouched. Verify the result with getfacl.

commands.desc: Set the ACL mask entry
commands.tooltip: The mask entry is the ceiling for what named users and groups can actually use, so m::rx caps every named entry at read and execute even if one was granted write. Tighten the mask to block group access without deleting the entries themselves. The mask only limits named entries, never the file owner.

commands.desc: Remove all capabilities from a file
commands.tooltip: Capabilities are fine-grained privileges like cap_net_bind_service that let a binary bind low ports without full root. The -r flag deletes every capability from the file, restoring normal execution. Audit what is set with getcap -r / 2>/dev/null.

commands.desc: Show the SELinux context of a file
commands.tooltip: The -Z flag prints the SELinux security context column, which labels each file with a type such as etc_t or shadow_t. SELinux is the mandatory access control system used on RHEL and Fedora, and Ubuntu systems show an empty column instead. Pair it with getenforce to see whether SELinux is enforcing.

commands.desc: Copy ownership from a reference file
commands.tooltip: The --reference form copies the user and group of template.txt onto report.pdf instead of typing a user:group pair. This is handy when a file was restored or extracted with the wrong owner. The same reference trick exists in chmod --reference for permissions.

commands.desc: Symlink the system timezone
commands.tooltip: This is how a Linux system selects its timezone: /etc/localtime is a symlink into the IANA zoneinfo database, so no file is copied. Read the link with readlink /etc/localtime to see the chosen zone. Prefer timedatectl set-timezone, which manages this link for you.

commands.desc: Print a symlink's target path
commands.tooltip: readlink resolves a symlink and prints where it actually points. Without -f it shows only one level, so the /etc/alternatives link reveals the real interpreter binary. Add -f to keep resolving until a final non-link path is reached.

commands.desc: Resolve a path to its absolute form
commands.tooltip: realpath prints the canonical absolute path, resolving symlinks and collapsing .. segments along the way. It answers questions like where this script really lives when launched through a symlink. Use it in scripts before cd-ing or storing paths.

commands.desc: Resolve a path without requiring existence
commands.tooltip: The -m flag canonicalizes a path purely by string logic, so the target does not need to exist on disk. This is useful for building paths that a program will create later. Symlinks are not resolved in this mode.

commands.desc: Print file type, size, and mtime
commands.tooltip: stat -c takes a custom format string: %F is the file type, %s the size in bytes, and %y the last modification time with full precision. It is the fastest way to get exactly the fields a script needs. See stat --help for the full format specifier list.

commands.desc: Show filesystem information
commands.tooltip: The -f flag switches stat from file details to the underlying filesystem: type, block size, and free blocks. It is the quick way to check what filesystem a path lives on and how much space remains. Compare with df, which shows the same data in human units.

commands.desc: Print the MIME type of a file
commands.tooltip: MIME types are the standard labels such as application/pdf that identify a file's format. The --mime-type flag prints just the type, while plain file adds a human description and -i includes the charset. file inspects magic bytes, not extensions, so it works on renamed files.

commands.desc: Identify a compressed file's contents
commands.tooltip: The -z flag makes file peek inside compressed archives and report what the decompressed data really is. It detects gzip, bzip2, zip, and other containers automatically. Useful for checking whether a download is a tarball or something else entirely.

commands.desc: Print the last path component
commands.tooltip: basename strips the directory part and prints file.txt, the final component of the path. It is the standard tool for pulling a filename out of a full path in scripts. Pair it with dirname to get the directory half.

commands.desc: Strip a suffix from the basename
commands.tooltip: The -s flag removes a trailing suffix, so this prints just file instead of file.txt. Scripts use it to derive output names from inputs, like turning report.txt into report.pdf. The suffix is matched literally at the end of the name.

commands.desc: Print the directory portion of a path
commands.tooltip: dirname prints everything before the last component, so this yields /path/to. It is the inverse of basename and together they split any path into its two halves. Scripts commonly wrap it around realpath to get an absolute directory.

commands.desc: Show every location of a command
commands.tooltip: The -a flag lists every match for python3 across PATH, not just the first one. This reveals shadowed installations where one binary hides another. Plain which stops at the first hit, which is the one the shell would actually run.

commands.desc: Show how the shell resolves a command
commands.tooltip: type tells you whether a name is an alias, a function, a builtin, or an external binary. The -a flag prints every definition in lookup order, so you see both the alias and the /usr/bin/ls it expands to. Use it before debugging why a command behaves unexpectedly.

commands.desc: Print the path a command would run
commands.tooltip: command -v is the POSIX-standard way to ask which binary the shell would execute, and unlike which it understands aliases and builtins. For a builtin like cd it prints the name itself instead of a path. Scripts use it to locate tools before calling them.

commands.desc: Clear the shell's command hash table
commands.tooltip: Bash caches the PATH lookup for every command it runs, and hash -r forgets that cache so the next call re-searches PATH. Run it after installing a new binary that shadows an old one, or after moving executables. Plain hash lists the cached entries.

commands.desc: Format a number with zero padding
commands.tooltip: printf is the shell's formatted output builtin, and %05d pads the number 42 to five digits with leading zeros, printing 00042. The same format specifiers as C and Python apply, so %x gives hex and %.2f fixes decimals. It is more predictable than echo for scripted output.

commands.desc: Raise the soft open-file limit
commands.tooltip: The -n limit controls how many file descriptors one shell session may hold, and this raises the soft limit to 4096. The soft limit can be raised only up to the hard limit, which needs root to increase. Set it in ~/.bashrc or a systemd unit for persistence.

commands.desc: Show the max user processes limit
commands.tooltip: The -u limit caps how many processes and threads a single user may run, and this prints the current value. Hitting it produces fork: Cannot allocate memory errors despite plenty of RAM. Raise it with ulimit -u or in /etc/security/limits.conf.

commands.desc: Show all resource limits
commands.tooltip: ulimit -a dumps every soft limit for the current shell: open files, core dumps, stack size, CPU time, and process count. It is the first stop when a program dies with mysterious resource errors. Each line maps to a single-letter flag like -n or -u.

commands.desc: Run a program in a new session
commands.tooltip: setsid starts the program in a fresh session with no controlling terminal, so terminal close and SIGHUP do not kill it. Unlike a plain background job, it fully detaches from the login session. Pair it with nohup or systemd-run for long-running tasks.

commands.desc: Remove all jobs from the shell's job table
commands.tooltip: disown detaches background jobs from the shell so they survive your logout without receiving SIGHUP. The -a form removes every job at once, while plain disown %1 targets one. Use it after starting a long task with the background operator.

commands.desc: Wait for the next background job to finish
commands.tooltip: wait -n blocks until any one of the shell's background jobs completes and then returns its status, available since Bash 5.1. It lets a script run several jobs in parallel and reap them as they finish. Plain wait with no argument waits for all of them.

commands.desc: Send a TERM signal to a process
commands.tooltip: The -s flag names the signal explicitly, so this politely asks process 1234 to terminate and gives it a chance to clean up. TERM is the default signal and the first choice; escalate to kill -9 only if the process ignores it. List signal names with kill -l.

commands.desc: Terminate every process owned by a user
commands.tooltip: killall -u alice sends TERM to all of alice's processes at once, effectively logging her out and discarding unsaved work. This is a blunt instrument, so check who is affected with pgrep -u alice first. Add -9 to force-kill anything that ignores TERM.

commands.desc: Kill processes by exact name match
commands.tooltip: The -x flag makes pkill match the process name exactly instead of as a substring, so nginx matches only nginx. Plain pkill nginx would also hit processes like nginx-cache. Use pgrep first to preview what will be killed.

commands.desc: Count processes matching a name
commands.tooltip: pgrep -c prints how many running processes match the name nginx instead of their PIDs. A count of zero also means pgrep exits nonzero, which is handy in script conditions. Combine with -f to match against the full command line.

commands.desc: Raise a process priority
commands.tooltip: renice changes the nice value of a running process, and negative values mean higher priority, so -5 boosts process 1234. Raising priority requires root, while lowering it is allowed for your own processes. Revert with renice -n 0 -p 1234 and watch impact with top.

commands.desc: Set a process to idle I/O class
commands.tooltip: ionice controls disk I/O priority, and class 3 means idle, so process 1234 only touches the disk when nobody else needs it. This is perfect for overnight backups that must not slow down interactive work. Classes are 0 none, 1 realtime, 2 best-effort, and 3 idle.

commands.desc: Set best-effort I/O priority level
commands.tooltip: Best-effort class 2 is the default, and the -n level from 0 to 7 tunes priority within it, where 4 sits in the middle. Lower numbers get the disk first, so a compile job at -n 0 would starve everything else. Combine with nice for CPU plus I/O tuning.

commands.desc: Pin a process to specific CPUs
commands.tooltip: taskset sets CPU affinity, and -c 0,1 restricts the new process to the first two CPU cores. Pinning improves cache locality for latency-sensitive workloads and contains noisy neighbors on shared boxes. Verify placement with taskset -pc on the PID.

commands.desc: Move a running process to a CPU
commands.tooltip: The -pc form operates on an existing process, so this migrates process 1234 onto CPU 2 without restarting it. It prints the old and new affinity lists on success. Use it when a process ends up on a busy core and you cannot stop it.

commands.desc: Sort version numbers naturally
commands.tooltip: The -V flag understands version numbers, so 1.10 sorts after 1.9 instead of before it as plain lexicographic sort would do. It handles dotted numbers and suffixes like rc1 sensibly. Use it to order release tags and package versions.

commands.desc: Sort a CSV by a numeric column
commands.tooltip: The -t, flag sets the field delimiter to a comma, and -k2,2nr sorts by field 2 with n for numeric and r for reverse order. The start,end key range form -k2,2 pins the sort to exactly one field. Extend the range like -k2,3 to break ties with a second column.

commands.desc: Extract specific fields from a file
commands.tooltip: cut -d: sets the delimiter to a colon and -f1,3 keeps only the first and third fields, so /etc/passwd yields username and UID pairs. Field lists accept ranges such as 2-5 and commas mixed with ranges. Pair with sort or uniq to analyze columnar data.

commands.desc: Strip carriage returns from a file
commands.tooltip: The -d flag deletes characters, so this removes every carriage return from a Windows CRLF file, leaving clean Unix line endings. Feed the result to a new file with a redirect instead of printing it. The same trick fixes files that show ^M in editors.

commands.desc: Lowercase text using character classes
commands.tooltip: POSIX character classes in brackets handle locale-aware ranges, so [:upper:] maps cleanly to [:lower:] for any alphabet. This is more reliable than tr A-Z a-z for accented letters. Read from a file with the input redirect and write with an output redirect.

commands.desc: Join two CSVs keeping unmatched rows
commands.tooltip: join merges two sorted files on a key column, here field 1 of both, and -a 1 keeps every row from the first file even without a match in the second. The process substitution runs each sort as a virtual file, satisfying join's sorted-input requirement. Without -a, unmatched rows are dropped silently.

commands.desc: Show lines unique to the second file
commands.tooltip: comm compares two sorted files and prints three columns: lines only in the first, only in the second, and in both. The -13 flag suppresses the first two columns so only lines unique to b.txt remain. The reverse filter comm -23 shows lines only in a.txt.

commands.desc: Split a file into fixed-size chunks
commands.tooltip: The -b flag splits by size, producing part_aa, part_ab, and so on, each 10 megabytes except the last. Splitting helps upload large files through size-limited channels. Reassemble in order with cat part_* > bigfile.

commands.desc: Split a file at matching lines
commands.tooltip: csplit cuts a file wherever a line matches the pattern, so '/^Chapter/' starts a new part at each chapter heading and '{*}' repeats the split for every match. The -f flag sets the prefix and -b '%02d.txt' formats the numeric suffixes. Unlike split, the parts differ in size.

commands.desc: Print the longest line length
commands.tooltip: The -L flag reports the length of the longest line in characters instead of counting lines or words. It is handy for checking whether any line overflows a fixed-width report or terminal column. Combine with sort -n to rank line lengths across many files.

commands.desc: Print all but the last five lines
commands.tooltip: A negative count flips head around, so -n -5 prints every line except the final five. This is the mirror of tail -n -5 and handy when the end of a file contains a footer you want to exclude. The feature needs the explicit -n form.

commands.desc: Print a sequence with zero padding
commands.tooltip: seq prints consecutive numbers, and -w pads them to equal width, giving 01 through 10 instead of 1 through 10. This keeps filenames and columns sorting correctly in scripts. Add a step like seq 1 2 99 to count odd numbers.

commands.desc: Pick random numbers from a range
commands.tooltip: The -i flag turns shuf into a random number generator for the inclusive range 1 to 100, and -n 5 prints five distinct picks. Without -n it shuffles the whole range. For random lines from a file, pass the filename instead of -i.

commands.desc: Number all lines including blanks
commands.tooltip: nl prepends line numbers in the classic cat -n style, and -ba numbers every line, including empty ones, instead of skipping them. The default skips blank lines unless -ba is given. Tune the format with -w for width and -s for the separator.

commands.desc: Dump binary with hex offsets and ASCII
commands.tooltip: od is the octal dump utility, and -A x switches addresses to hex while -t x1z prints each byte in hex followed by printable ASCII in the margin. This is the fastest way to eyeball binary file contents. Plain od -c shows bytes as escaped characters.

commands.desc: Export a file as a C array
commands.tooltip: The -i flag formats the file as an initialized C array named after the input, ready to embed in source code. This is the standard way to bundle small assets like icons into a binary. Add a length variable with -i plus -l to cap the size.

commands.desc: Show a canonical hex and ASCII dump
commands.tooltip: The -C flag is the canonical hexdump layout, showing offset, sixteen hex bytes, and the printable ASCII column. It is the tool of choice for inspecting binary files and network captures. Compare with od -A x -t x1z, which produces a similar view.

commands.desc: Compute a SHA-256 checksum
commands.tooltip: sha256sum prints the 64-character SHA-256 digest of a file, the standard way to verify a download matches the publisher's checksum. Compare the output against the value on the official download page. The same digest confirms two files are identical.

commands.desc: Verify checksums from a manifest
commands.tooltip: The -c flag reads a manifest of hash plus filename lines and verifies each file, printing OK or FAILED per line. A FAILED line means the file was corrupted or tampered with. Generate the manifest itself with sha256sum file > SHA256SUMS.

commands.desc: Compute an MD5 checksum
commands.tooltip: md5sum prints the 32-character MD5 digest of a file. MD5 is fast but cryptographically broken, so use it only for quick integrity checks, never for security. Prefer sha256sum whenever authenticity matters.

commands.desc: Encode a file as base64
commands.tooltip: base64 converts binary data into the printable base64 alphabet so it survives email and JSON transport. It prints the encoded text to stdout, ready to redirect to a file. The encoding inflates size by roughly a third.

commands.desc: Decode base64 back to binary
commands.tooltip: The -d flag reverses the encoding and restores the original bytes, so a file encoded with base64 comes back intact. Add -i to ignore invalid characters in sloppy input. This is how base64-encoded attachments and config blobs are unpacked.

commands.desc: Wrap long lines at spaces
commands.tooltip: fold wraps lines longer than the width, and -s breaks at spaces instead of splitting words in half. The -w flag sets the width, here 40 columns. This formats plain text for narrow terminals or email without a full text formatter.

commands.desc: Reverse each line character-wise
commands.tooltip: rev mirrors every line, so hello becomes olleh, useful for right-aligning text or trick questions. It is often chained with sort to find lines that share reversed endings. Character order reverses but lines stay in place.

commands.desc: Format text into two columns
commands.tooltip: pr paginates and columns text for printing, and the -2 flag lays the file out in two side-by-side columns. The -t flag suppresses the page headers and footers, keeping only the data. Column counts like -4 work for wide listings.

commands.desc: Read a GNOME settings key
commands.tooltip: gsettings reads and writes the DConf settings database through the session's DBus, and this fetches the current wallpaper URI. Keys are addressed as schema plus key name, here the background schema's picture-uri. The value prints in GVariant syntax with quotes.

commands.desc: Change the desktop wallpaper
commands.tooltip: This sets the wallpaper by writing the picture-uri key, and single quotes protect the file URI from shell expansion. The change applies to the running session immediately with no restart. Use dconf read to confirm the stored value.

commands.desc: Dump all keys in a schema
commands.tooltip: list-recursively prints every key in the interface schema with its current value, one per line. A schema is a named group of related settings, and this is the fastest way to discover what is configurable. Pair it with gsettings range to see a key's allowed values.

commands.desc: Switch the GTK theme
commands.tooltip: This sets the GTK theme for GNOME applications, with Adwaita-dark being the built-in dark theme. Installed third-party themes appear as new options in the same key. The change applies live to most running GTK apps.

commands.desc: Scale up interface text
commands.tooltip: The text-scaling-factor key multiplies all on-screen text, and 1.25 enlarges it by a quarter for easier reading. The valid range is 0.5 to 3.0, checkable with gsettings range. This is the accessibility-friendly alternative to lowering the whole display resolution.

commands.desc: Watch for live settings changes
commands.tooltip: monitor subscribes to a schema and prints every key change as it happens, ideal for seeing what an app or setting dialog modifies. It runs until Ctrl+C. The same trick works on a single key path for narrower output.

commands.desc: Back up GNOME settings to a file
commands.tooltip: dconf is the low-level settings database behind gsettings, and dump writes an entire subtree as readable keyfile text. The redirect saves it to gnome-backup.conf for later restore. Dump the whole /org/gnome/ tree to capture every GNOME app's settings.

commands.desc: Restore GNOME settings from a backup
commands.tooltip: load reads a keyfile from stdin and writes every key back into the database, the exact inverse of dconf dump. Keys present in the file are overwritten, so this restores a full backup in one shot. Run it while logged into the same session so apps pick up the changes.

commands.desc: Watch a settings path for changes
commands.tooltip: watch prints every write to keys under the given path as it happens, showing the key and its new value. It is the raw DConf-level equivalent of gsettings monitor and catches changes from any source. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

commands.desc: Reset an entire settings subtree
commands.tooltip: The -f flag makes reset recurse, returning every key under /org/gnome/desktop/ to its factory default in one command. This is irreversible for custom settings, so dump a backup first. The same flag resets whole apps when pointed at their paths.

commands.desc: Read one settings value
commands.tooltip: dconf read prints a single key's value using the raw path form, with slash-separated schema and key names. It is the direct database access behind gsettings get. The output uses GVariant syntax, so strings appear quoted.

commands.desc: List enabled GNOME Shell extensions
commands.tooltip: GNOME Shell extensions are JavaScript add-ons that alter the desktop, identified by UUIDs like ubuntu-appindicators@ubuntu.com. The --enabled filter shows only active ones, while plain list shows everything installed. Pipe to grep for a specific extension.

commands.desc: Disable a Shell extension
commands.tooltip: This turns off the Ubuntu AppIndicators extension by its UUID, and the desktop reacts immediately without a shell restart. Disabling keeps the files installed, so the extension can be enabled again later. Use gnome-extensions list --enabled first to confirm the UUID.

commands.desc: Enable a Shell extension
commands.tooltip: This reactivates a disabled or freshly installed extension by UUID. The change applies to the current session at once. If it still does not appear, log out and back in so the shell reloads its extension set.

commands.desc: Show details of a Shell extension
commands.tooltip: info prints an extension's name, version, description, and current state such as enabled or error. The state field is the first place to check when an extension misbehaves. A broken extension shows ERROR here and may need a reset.

commands.desc: Move a file to the trash
commands.tooltip: gio is the GLib command-line front end to GVfs, and trash moves a file into the desktop trash instead of deleting it. The file can be restored from the file manager's trash view, so this is the safe delete. Trash lives in ~/.local/share/Trash.

commands.desc: Empty the trash permanently
commands.tooltip: This deletes every file in the trash for good, freeing the disk space they occupied. There is no undo, so check the trash first. The flag is --empty, not --empty-trash.

commands.desc: Open a file with the default application
commands.tooltip: gio open launches the default application registered for the file's MIME type, exactly like double-clicking in the file manager. It respects the same associations as xdg-open. From a terminal it works with any MIME-registered file type.

commands.desc: Show metadata about a file
commands.tooltip: gio info prints attributes such as size, type, permissions, and modification time, plus trash status for trashed files. It reads the same GVfs metadata layer the file manager uses. Add -a with attribute names to filter the output.

commands.desc: List a directory like ls
commands.tooltip: gio list prints the contents of a location through the GVfs layer, which also understands remote schemes like sftp:// and trash://. It is ls for anything the file manager can open. Use -a attributes to request metadata columns.

commands.desc: List connected displays and modes
commands.tooltip: xrandr is the X11 RandR extension client, and running it bare lists every output with its supported resolutions and refresh rates. Output names like HDMI-1 and eDP-1 come from the left column. It only works on X11 sessions, not Wayland.

commands.desc: Set a display resolution
commands.tooltip: The --output flag names a display and --mode picks one of its supported resolutions, so this switches HDMI-1 to 1080p. The mode must appear in the plain xrandr listing. Add --rate to also set the refresh rate.

commands.desc: Set a display refresh rate
commands.tooltip: The --rate flag sets the refresh in hertz, and this asks HDMI-1 to run at 144 Hz for smoother motion. The monitor must support the rate at the current resolution, or xrandr refuses. Combine it in the same command as --mode for a precise mode plus rate pair.

commands.desc: Position a display left of another
commands.tooltip: Relative position flags arrange outputs on the virtual desktop, so eDP-1 sits to the left of HDMI-1 and the mouse moves between them naturally. Siblings include --right-of, --above, and --below. The arrangement persists only for the current X session.

commands.desc: Mark a display as primary
commands.tooltip: The primary output is where new windows and panels appear by default on X11. This marks HDMI-1 as primary while the others stay secondary. Only one output can be primary at a time.

commands.desc: Turn off a display output
commands.tooltip: This disables the HDMI-1 output, mirroring the settings panel's display off toggle. Turning off the only active monitor blanks the screen, so have a fallback ready. Re-enable it with xrandr --output HDMI-1 --auto.

commands.desc: Disable the X11 screensaver
commands.tooltip: xset configures the X server directly, and the s command controls the screensaver, so s off disables it entirely. The setting lasts until the X session ends or the server restarts. Pair with xset dpms to also control display power saving.

commands.desc: Set display power-down timers
commands.tooltip: The dpms command sets the Display Power Management Signaling delays in seconds for standby, suspend, and off. This sequence powers the monitor down after ten minutes of inactivity. Pass 0 0 0 to disable power saving entirely.

commands.desc: Show current X server settings
commands.tooltip: The q flag queries the X server and prints screensaver, DPMS, keyboard, and pointer settings in one dump. It is the fastest way to see what the server is actually configured to do. Look at the DPMS and screensaver sections to confirm prior xset changes.

commands.desc: List Wayland outputs and modes
commands.tooltip: wlr-randr manages displays on wlroots-based Wayland compositors, the Wayland world's answer to xrandr. Wayland is the modern display protocol replacing X11, and this tool talks to its output-management protocol. Bare wlr-randr lists outputs, resolutions, and refresh rates.

commands.desc: Set a Wayland output mode
commands.tooltip: This configures the DP-1 output on a wlroots compositor, with the mode given as width, height, and refresh rate joined by an at sign. The @60 sets the hertz; omitting it keeps the current rate. Add --scale 1.5 for HiDPI scaling.

commands.desc: Show PulseAudio server information
commands.tooltip: pactl talks to the PulseAudio sound server, and info prints the server version, default sink, and default source. PulseAudio is the classic Linux sound daemon, now often bridged to PipeWire. The default sink name here is what set-default-sink expects.

commands.desc: List audio output devices
commands.tooltip: A sink is an audio output device, and the short form prints a terse table of sinks with names and states, perfect for scripting. The first column contains the full names used by set-default-sink. Drop short for the verbose per-sink detail dump.

commands.desc: Set the default output volume
commands.tooltip: The @DEFAULT_SINK@ token stands for whatever sink is currently the default, and 80% sets the volume as a percentage. Volumes also accept linear factors like 0.8 or decibel values. A leading plus or minus adjusts relative to the current level.

commands.desc: Change the default audio output
commands.tooltip: This makes the named ALSA sink the default, so new playback streams route there. The exact sink name comes from pactl list sinks short. Switching between speakers and headphones is the classic use.

commands.desc: Create a virtual audio device
commands.tooltip: module-null-sink creates a virtual sink that accepts audio but plays nothing, useful for recording application output or routing experiments. The command prints the new module's numeric index, which unload-module expects. Remove it with pactl unload-module followed by that index.

commands.desc: Toggle mute on the default output
commands.tooltip: This flips the mute state of the default sink between muted and unmuted, the command-line version of the volume menu's mute button. The third argument also accepts 1 for mute and 0 for unmute. The change is immediate for all streams on that sink.

commands.desc: Dump all PipeWire objects
commands.tooltip: pw-cli is the low-level admin console for PipeWire, the modern audio and video server on most desktops. info all prints every global object with its properties, from devices to link nodes. The output is dense, so grep for a specific interface type.

commands.desc: List PipeWire nodes
commands.tooltip: The ls command lists objects, and filtering by the Node interface shows audio devices, virtual sinks, and streams. Each entry carries an object id used by other pw-cli commands. PipeWire nodes are the building blocks of the audio graph.

commands.desc: List PipeWire node names as JSON
commands.tooltip: pw-dump prints the entire PipeWire state as JSON, and the jq filter extracts just the node.name property of every Node object. This is the script-friendly way to enumerate audio devices. The same dump feeds any jq query for graph inspection.

commands.desc: Show WirePlumber device graph
commands.tooltip: wpctl is the control tool for WirePlumber, the session manager that wires PipeWire devices together. status prints the audio graph with sinks, sources, and their default markers. The numbered ids shown here are what set-volume and friends accept.

commands.desc: Set the default sink volume
commands.tooltip: This sets the default audio sink's volume to 0.8, meaning 80 percent, and @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ is the magic name for the current default. The value accepts fractions, percentages like 80%, and relative adjustments with a plus or minus. The same command works with a numeric sink id.

commands.desc: Read the default sink volume
commands.tooltip: get-volume prints the current volume of the default sink, such as Volume: 0.80. It is the quick sanity check before scripting volume changes. The id argument can be the magic default name or any sink id from wpctl status.

commands.desc: Check a user service status
commands.tooltip: The --user flag targets the per-user systemd instance instead of the system-wide one, so this checks the PipeWire service running under your session. User services live in ~/.config/systemd/user and start at login. Status shows active or failed plus recent log lines.

commands.desc: Restart a user service
commands.tooltip: This restarts the PipeWire service inside your user session, picking up config changes without a reboot. Restarting audio services briefly cuts sound and can reset volume levels. The same pattern manages any user unit, from syncthing to podman socket activation.

commands.desc: Show recent logs for a user service
commands.tooltip: journalctl --user restricts the log view to your session's services, and -u pipewire filters to that unit while -n 20 keeps the last twenty lines. This is the first stop when a desktop service misbehaves. Add -f to follow new messages live.

commands.desc: Show details of an installed Flatpak
commands.tooltip: Flatpak distributes sandboxed apps identified by reverse-DNS ids like org.gimp.GIMP, and info prints the installed version, origin remote, and runtime. The runtime line shows which shared platform the app depends on. Compare with flatpak list for a summary table.

commands.desc: List running Flatpak applications
commands.tooltip: flatpak ps shows every Flatpak app currently running, with its instance id and application id. The instance id is what flatpak kill expects. If nothing is listed, no sandboxed apps are open.

commands.desc: Remove unused Flatpak runtimes
commands.tooltip: Runtimes are the shared dependency platforms that Flatpak apps are built against, and this removes every runtime no installed app needs anymore. It is the single best disk-space reclaim for Flatpak systems. The command lists what it would remove and asks before deleting.

commands.desc: Stop a running Flatpak app
commands.tooltip: This politely terminates the running GIMP instance managed by Flatpak, equivalent to closing the app normally. Unlike killing the process tree by hand, it goes through the sandbox instance. Use flatpak ps to confirm the app is actually running first.

commands.desc: List snap service status
commands.tooltip: Snaps can bundle background daemons, and snap services prints each one with its startup setting and current state. Service names follow the snap name, like nextcloud.nextcloud-cron. Control them with snap start, stop, and restart.

commands.desc: Show snap task history
commands.tooltip: snap changes lists every snap operation with an id, status, and timestamp, from installs to refreshes. A long-running change can be followed with snap change followed by its id. Failed changes show a red error status worth investigating.

commands.desc: Keep only two snap revisions
commands.tooltip: This tells snapd to keep just two revisions of each snap, down from the default three, freeing disk space on snap-heavy systems. Older revisions are what snap revert rolls back to, so a smaller retain window means fewer rollback options. Read the current value with snap get system refresh.retain.

commands.desc: Read a snap system setting
commands.tooltip: snap get reads configuration keys from the snapd store, and this prints the current refresh.retain value. It confirms whether a snap set change actually took effect. Other useful keys live under the refresh and proxy namespaces.

commands.desc: Force a default alternative
commands.tooltip: update-alternatives manages symlink groups where several programs compete, like the editor group pointing /etc/alternatives/editor at one binary. The --set form pins the choice non-interactively, ideal for scripts and image builds. List the group's candidates with --list first.

commands.desc: Restore automatic alternative selection
commands.tooltip: The --auto flag returns the editor group to automatic mode, where the alternative with the highest priority wins. This undoes a manual --set choice and lets package upgrades re-decide the default. Automatic status shows as auto in --display output.

commands.desc: Pick an alternative interactively
commands.tooltip: --config shows a numbered menu of every candidate in the editor group and applies the one you choose. It is the interactive counterpart to --set. The menu also reveals the current selection and each candidate's priority.

commands.desc: List candidates for an alternative
commands.tooltip: --list prints every binary registered in the editor group, one path per line, without needing root. It is the read-only way to see what a --config menu would offer. Each entry is a real executable registered via --install.

commands.desc: Create a user interactively
commands.tooltip: adduser is the friendly Debian wrapper around useradd, prompting for a password and full name as it creates the account. It also builds the home directory and copies in the default skeleton files. The interactive prompts can be skipped with flags like --disabled-password.

commands.desc: Add an existing user to a group
commands.tooltip: The adduser USER GROUP form adds an existing user to an existing group, here granting alice sudo privileges. The user must log out and back in for the new group to take effect. It is the interactive equivalent of usermod -aG.

commands.desc: Create a user without a password
commands.tooltip: The --disabled-password flag creates the account with no password, so it cannot log in interactively until one is set, and --comment '' skips the full-name prompt. This is the standard recipe for service accounts. Lock it down further with --shell /usr/sbin/nologin.

commands.desc: Delete a user account
commands.tooltip: deluser removes alice's account but leaves her home directory and files on disk. Remove those too with deluser --remove-home, or --remove-all-files for files owned elsewhere. Back up anything needed first, since group memberships and ownership records are gone for good.

commands.desc: Delete a user and their home directory
commands.tooltip: The --remove-home flag deletes the account and its home directory together, freeing the disk space immediately. This is irreversible, so confirm nothing important lives in /home/alice first. For a full sweep add --remove-all-files to catch files owned in other directories.

commands.desc: Create a new group
commands.tooltip: A group is a named set of users that shares permissions, and groupadd creates one, here developers. The system assigns the next free GID automatically. Assign users to it with usermod -aG or adduser USER GROUP.

commands.desc: Create a group with a fixed GID
commands.tooltip: The -g flag pins the group's GID to 1500 instead of letting the system choose, useful when NFS or config files expect a specific number. Check existing GIDs with getent group first to avoid collisions. The same -g flag works for useradd.

commands.desc: Look up a group in NSS
commands.tooltip: getent queries the NSS (name service switch) databases that back user and group lookups, so this shows the developers group's GID and members. It sees accounts from /etc/passwd, LDAP, and NIS alike. Use it to verify a groupadd or usermod took effect.

commands.desc: Look up a service port in NSS
commands.tooltip: The services database maps service names to port numbers, so this prints ssh 22/tcp. getent services is the reliable way to look up standard ports without guessing. The same getent command works on passwd, group, and hosts entries.

commands.desc: Force a password change at next login
commands.tooltip: chage manages password aging, and -d 0 sets the last-change date to the epoch, so alice must set a new password on her next login. It is the standard way to expire a password immediately. Peek at the full aging policy with chage -l alice.

commands.desc: Show a user's password status
commands.tooltip: The -S flag prints the account's password status: L for locked, P for a usable password, and NP for no password at all. The output also shows the last change date and aging policy. Use it before locking or unlocking accounts to see where they stand.

commands.desc: Add a user to a group
commands.tooltip: usermod -aG appends alice to the developers group, and the -a flag is essential because plain -G replaces her entire group list. New group membership needs a fresh login to apply. Verify with groups alice or getent group developers.

commands.desc: Disable shell login for a user
commands.tooltip: Setting the login shell to nologin means alice cannot open an interactive shell, though her other services and file access keep working. This is the clean way to lock down a service account without deleting it. Reverse it with usermod -s /bin/bash alice.

commands.desc: Set a user's GECOS comment
commands.tooltip: The GECOS field holds the account's real name and contact info, and -c sets it, here to Alice Smith. This is what finger and some login screens display. Quote the value so spaces survive the shell.

commands.desc: Show default useradd settings
commands.tooltip: The -D flag prints the defaults useradd applies to new accounts: base home directory, default shell, skeleton, and expiry policy. These defaults live in /etc/default/useradd. Root can override individual defaults with useradd -D -s /bin/bash.

commands.desc: Create a system service account
commands.tooltip: The -r flag creates a system account with a UID below 1000, and -s /usr/sbin/nologin blocks interactive login, the standard recipe for daemons. System accounts skip the normal home directory creation unless -m is added. Use adduser for interactive human accounts instead.

commands.desc: Show failed login attempts
commands.tooltip: lastb reads /var/log/btmp and lists failed login attempts with usernames and source addresses, so it is the first stop when investigating break-in attempts. Reading btmp needs root, hence sudo. The output can be noisy, so pipe it through sort uniq -c to spot brute-force patterns.

commands.desc: Show shutdown and runlevel records
commands.tooltip: The -x flag adds system shutdown, reboot, and runlevel-change entries to last's usual login listing. It reconstructs the machine's boot and power history at a glance. Combine with last reboot to isolate just the reboot events.

commands.desc: Show one user's sessions and activity
commands.tooltip: w with a username limits the report to that user's sessions, showing login time, idle duration, and the command each terminal runs. The WHAT column reveals whether alice is idle or actively working. Bare w covers everyone logged in.

commands.desc: Show one property of a session
commands.tooltip: loginctl talks to systemd-logind, the session manager, and show-session prints properties of session 2. The -p State filter limits output to that one property, here whether the session is active. Find session numbers with loginctl list-sessions.

commands.desc: End all sessions of a user
commands.tooltip: This force-ends every login session alice has, killing her processes and discarding unsaved work. It is the systemd-native way to log a user out, stronger than just closing terminals. Check what she runs with w or ps -u alice first.

commands.desc: List logged-in users
commands.tooltip: list-users shows every user with an active session, their UID, and whether linger is enabled. Linger lets services keep running after logout. The user list pairs with loginctl list-sessions to map sessions to users.

commands.desc: Lock the current session screen
commands.tooltip: This asks systemd-logind to lock the session, triggering the configured screen locker immediately. It is the command-line equivalent of the Super+L shortcut. No argument locks the caller's own session; a session id targets a specific one.

commands.desc: Search the timezone database
commands.tooltip: timedatectl list-timezones dumps every IANA timezone name, and the grep filters it down to matches like Europe/Madrid. Timezone names are region/city pairs that avoid the ambiguities of UTC offsets. Feed the exact result to timedatectl set-timezone.

commands.desc: Change the system locale
commands.tooltip: The locale controls language, date formats, and character encoding for system services, and this sets the primary LANG to Spanish. New sessions inherit the change while running ones keep their old locale. The locale must exist in localectl list-locales or it will be rejected.

commands.desc: List installed locales
commands.tooltip: list-locales prints every locale the system can actually use, and the grep filters for the Spanish ones. Only locales shown here can be selected with set-locale. Generate missing ones with locale-gen or dpkg-reconfigure locales.

commands.desc: Show the installed listmonk build version
commands.tooltip: Prints the version string of the compiled binary, for example 6.2.0. Run it right after downloading a release to confirm the file is intact and to match the version against release notes before upgrading. The same flag works inside a container via `docker compose exec app ./listmonk --version`.

commands.desc: Generate a sample config.toml for a new install
commands.tooltip: Writes a fully commented config.toml sample into the current directory. The file holds the database connection, app address, and SMTP settings, where SMTP is the mail-sending protocol listmonk uses to deliver campaigns. Edit it before the first run, then launch listmonk with the same --config path.

commands.desc: Generate a sample config file at a custom path
commands.tooltip: Combines --new-config with --config so the sample lands at the path you will actually use, which suits packaged installs where /etc/listmonk is the config directory. The directory must already exist and be writable. Run `listmonk --install` afterwards to create the database schema.

commands.desc: Start the listmonk server with an explicit config file
commands.tooltip: Launches the web app, API, and campaign scheduler using the given TOML file. The flag is repeatable and multiple files are merged in order, so you can layer a base config with environment-specific overrides. config.toml is already the default, so pass the flag explicitly when running from another directory.

commands.desc: Start listmonk configured entirely by environment variables
commands.tooltip: Every config.toml key maps to an env var with the LISTMONK_ prefix and double underscores for dots, so db.host becomes LISTMONK_db__host. Passing --config '' disables file config and makes environment variables the only source. This is exactly how the official docker-compose.yml configures the container.

commands.desc: Create the listmonk database schema on first run
commands.tooltip: Connects to Postgres using the current config and creates all tables, indexes, and materialized views; Postgres 12 or newer is required. Run it once against an empty database, since re-running against an existing schema errors out. The Super Admin account is created on the first visit to the admin UI, or in advance via the LISTMONK_ADMIN_USER and LISTMONK_ADMIN_PASSWORD environment variables.

commands.desc: Install the schema only when the database is not set up
commands.tooltip: --idempotent makes the install skip silently when the database already contains the schema, and --yes answers the confirmation prompts automatically. This combination is exactly what the official Docker entrypoint runs so that container restarts never re-create an existing database.

commands.desc: Run database migrations after upgrading the binary
commands.tooltip: Applies any pending schema migrations to bring an existing database in line with the new binary version. Upgrades are idempotent, so running them repeatedly has no side effects. Always back up the Postgres database before upgrading listmonk itself, as release notes warn.

commands.desc: Create the Super Admin account during install via env vars
commands.tooltip: LISTMONK_ADMIN_USER and LISTMONK_ADMIN_PASSWORD seed the Super Admin login while the schema is installed, skipping the interactive setup page. The values are honored only on the very first installation. Swap the example password for a strong one before running.

commands.desc: Run listmonk without processing campaign sends
commands.tooltip: Starts the server and admin UI but disables the campaign scheduler, so queued campaigns are not sent and subscribers are not processed. Useful for maintenance windows, upgrades, or when you only need the API. The log line 'running in passive mode' confirms the flag took effect.

commands.desc: Serve static assets from an external directory
commands.tooltip: Points the embedded file system at a directory holding email templates and public assets, overriding the files bundled inside the binary. Needed when the binary is installed somewhere the assets are not, such as /usr/bin. The packaged systemd unit uses this flag.

commands.desc: Write listmonk logs to a file instead of stdout
commands.tooltip: listmonk logs to standard output only, so redirecting into a file preserves history across restarts; the admin UI Logs page only keeps the last 1000 lines in memory. Append 2>&1 to also capture error output. Rotate the file with logrotate to avoid unbounded growth.

commands.desc: Download and extract the listmonk release binary
commands.tooltip: Fetches the prebuilt amd64 tarball from GitHub Releases and extracts the listmonk binary into the current directory. Pick the arm64 asset on ARM servers. Compare the sha256 checksums listed on the release page against the downloaded file before running the binary.

commands.desc: Fetch the official listmonk docker-compose file
commands.tooltip: Downloads the maintained compose file that defines the app service, a Postgres 17 database, and the shared network. Customize the LISTMONK_* environment and port mapping before starting it. The recommended Docker install path is compose rather than a bare docker run.

commands.desc: Clone the listmonk source repository over SSH
commands.tooltip: Fetches the master branch for building from source or contributing. The project is a single Go binary with a Vue frontend. Requires an SSH key registered on GitHub; use the https URL instead if you have no key configured.

commands.desc: Compile the listmonk binary from source
commands.tooltip: Runs the Makefile target that builds the production binary into the repo root after compiling the frontend. Requires go, nodejs, and yarn on the PATH. Run it inside the cloned repository; the resulting ./listmonk is self-contained with assets embedded.

commands.cmd: docker run -d --name listmonk -p 9000:9000 -e LISTMONK_db__host=localhost -e LISTMONK_db__user=listmonk -e LISTMONK_db__password=listmonk -e LISTMONK_db__database=listmonk -v listmonk_uploads:/listmonk/uploads listmonk/listmonk:latest
commands.desc: Run the listmonk container on port 9000
commands.tooltip: Starts the listmonk/listmonk:latest image detached with the admin UI exposed on port 9000. The LISTMONK_db__* variables point at an existing Postgres, and the named volume keeps uploaded media across container replacements. A bare container cannot reach a database on the host's localhost unless run with --network host; the official compose stack wires app and database together instead.

commands.cmd: docker run --rm -it -e LISTMONK_db__host=db -e LISTMONK_db__user=listmonk -e LISTMONK_db__password=listmonk -e LISTMONK_db__database=listmonk listmonk/listmonk:latest --install --idempotent --yes --config ''
commands.desc: Install the schema from inside a fresh container
commands.tooltip: Runs the listmonk image once to create the database schema, using environment variables for the connection and --config '' to skip file config. --idempotent and --yes make the run non-interactive and safe to repeat. The official compose file performs this automatically on first start.

commands.desc: Show the listmonk version inside the container
commands.tooltip: Executes the binary inside the running app service of the official compose stack and prints its version. Handy for confirming the deployed image matches a release. The service is named app in docker-compose.yml while its container is listmonk_app.

commands.cmd: docker compose exec db psql -U listmonk -d listmonk -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM subscribers;'
commands.desc: Count subscribers through the database container
commands.tooltip: Runs psql inside the Postgres service of the compose stack against the listmonk database. A quick way to verify data made it in after an import. Use `docker compose exec db pg_dump` for backups from inside the stack.

commands.cmd: docker compose exec db pg_dump -U listmonk -Fc listmonk > listmonk-backup.dump
commands.desc: Back up the listmonk database from the container
commands.tooltip: Runs pg_dump inside the db service and writes a compressed custom-format dump to the host shell, keeping the backup off the container filesystem. The -Fc custom format compresses well and restores with pg_restore. Replay it with `docker compose exec db pg_restore -U listmonk -d listmonk < listmonk-backup.dump`.

commands.cmd: sudo docker compose stop ; sudo docker compose up
commands.desc: Restart the compose stack after config changes
commands.tooltip: The docs-recommended way to apply time zone, volume, or media-upload changes to the compose stack: stop the services, then bring them up again with the new settings. Note the semicolon runs the second command regardless of the first one's result. sudo is only needed when Docker requires root on your host.

commands.desc: List the Docker volumes created for listmonk
commands.tooltip: Filters docker volume ls for listmonk volumes such as listmonk_listmonk-data, which holds the Postgres data directory. Compose prefixes declared volume names with the project directory name. Find the host path of one with `docker volume inspect <name>`.

commands.desc: List all tables in the listmonk database
commands.tooltip: Shows the tables listmonk manages: subscribers, lists, subscriber_lists, campaigns, campaign_views, link_clicks, bounces, templates, and settings. Use \d <table> for column details. You need the postgres client installed and the listmonk role credentials.

commands.cmd: psql -h localhost -U listmonk -d listmonk -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM subscribers;'
commands.desc: Count total subscribers in the database
commands.tooltip: Returns the number of rows in the subscribers table, the ground truth for audience size regardless of dashboard caching. Filter by status by adding WHERE status = 'enabled' to exclude blocklisted or disabled addresses.

commands.cmd: psql -h localhost -U listmonk -d listmonk -c "SELECT count(*) FROM campaigns WHERE status = 'running';"
commands.desc: Count campaigns currently in the running state
commands.tooltip: Queries the campaigns table for rows whose status is 'running'; the full status enum is draft, scheduled, running, paused, cancelled, finished. Useful to confirm a stuck campaign before restarting the app. The outer double quotes keep the single quotes for SQL intact.

commands.cmd: psql -h localhost -U listmonk -d listmonk -c "SELECT l.name, count(sl.subscriber_id) FROM lists l LEFT JOIN subscriber_lists sl ON sl.list_id = l.id GROUP BY l.name;"
commands.desc: Show subscriber counts for every list
commands.tooltip: Joins the lists and subscriber_lists tables to report how many subscribers each list holds, including lists with zero members via the LEFT JOIN. A subscriber counts once per list they are attached to. Confirm the numbers against the dashboard list stats when in doubt.

commands.desc: Dump the listmonk database to a plain SQL file
commands.tooltip: Exports the whole schema and data as SQL statements that psql can replay, taking a consistent snapshot automatically. Plain format is easy to inspect and grep but larger and slower than custom format. Keep the dump off the same disk as the database when possible.

commands.desc: Back up listmonk in compressed custom format
commands.tooltip: The -Fc custom format compresses the dump, preserves object metadata, and supports selective restore with pg_restore. Restore with `pg_restore -h localhost -U listmonk -d listmonk listmonk-backup.dump`. Pair it with a rotation scheme since nightly backups accumulate.

commands.desc: Restore a listmonk backup from a SQL dump
commands.tooltip: Feeds the plain-format dump produced by pg_dump back into the database, recreating schema and data. The database must exist and the target should be empty, otherwise you will hit duplicate-key errors. Stop the listmonk app during the restore so it does not write concurrently.

commands.desc: Restore a custom-format listmonk backup
commands.tooltip: Replays a -Fc dump into the database, re-creating tables and rows in dependency order. Add --clean --if-exists to drop existing objects first for a full overwrite. Requires the target database to exist; create it with `createdb -h localhost -U listmonk listmonk` if needed.

commands.desc: Check the listmonk API health endpoint
commands.tooltip: Returns a JSON payload whenever the API server is up, and needs no credentials, so it is ideal for uptime monitors. The admin frontend pings this route on load. A 200 response with a data key means the app is serving requests.

commands.desc: Fetch the dashboard summary statistics
commands.tooltip: Returns subscriber, list, and campaign counts served from materialized views like mat_dashboard_counts, which refresh periodically so the numbers lag slightly. The companion endpoint /api/dashboard/charts provides the click and view series. Credentials are the API user token created under Admin -> Users, or the legacy admin_username and admin_password from config.toml.

commands.desc: List subscribers with pagination via the API
commands.tooltip: Queries the first 100 subscribers with their status, attributes, and list memberships. page and per_page control paging, set per_page=all for everything, and repeat list_id parameters to filter by list. Quote the URL so the shell does not treat & as a background operator.

commands.desc: List all active subscriber lists
commands.tooltip: Returns lists whose status is active, the ones usable in campaigns and subscription forms. Add minimal=true to skip subscriber counts for faster responses, or status=archived to include hidden lists. Each list carries its optin mode, either single or double.

commands.desc: Create a new subscriber list via the API
commands.tooltip: Creates a list; name, type, and optin are required fields. type public makes it appear on subscription forms while private hides it, and optin double sends a confirmation email that new subscribers must click before they receive campaigns. The response contains the new list id for later calls.

commands.cmd: curl -u admin:admin -X POST http://localhost:9000/api/subscribers -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":"john@example.com","name":"John Doe","status":"enabled"}'
commands.desc: Create a new subscriber via the API
commands.tooltip: Adds a subscriber with the given email and name; email and name are required, status defaults to enabled. Pass lists as an array of list ids to subscribe them immediately. Duplicate emails are rejected, so check for an existing record first or expect a 422 response.

commands.cmd: curl -u admin:admin -X PUT http://localhost:9000/api/subscribers/42 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Jane Doe"}'
commands.desc: Update a subscriber's profile via the API
commands.tooltip: Updates the subscriber record; the numeric id comes from the database. PATCH on the same endpoint updates only the fields you send, while PUT is the heavier form. Custom profile data lives in the attribs JSON object, for example a city value that campaign templates can reference.

commands.desc: Blocklist a subscriber so they receive no mail
commands.tooltip: Flags the subscriber with status blocklisted, and campaigns skip blocklisted addresses entirely. This is the API form of the same action in the admin UI. There is a bulk variant PUT /api/subscribers/blocklist for banning many ids at once.

commands.desc: Re-send the opt-in confirmation email
commands.tooltip: Triggers a fresh optin confirmation message to an unconfirmed subscriber, for example after they ask for a new link or the first one expired. Only meaningful for subscribers on double opt-in lists. The email uses the system optin template.

commands.desc: Delete multiple subscribers by id
commands.tooltip: Deletes the named subscriber rows plus their list memberships, bounce records, and tracking data via cascade. Repeat the id parameter for each target and quote the URL. There is no undo, so dump the affected rows first or use blocklist when you only want to stop mailings.

commands.desc: Export one subscriber's full data profile
commands.tooltip: Returns the profile, list subscriptions, campaign views, and link clicks for a single subscriber, which is the data needed to answer GDPR access requests. Private list names are masked as 'Private list' in the export. Combine with the delete endpoint to complete an erasure request.

commands.desc: List campaigns currently running
commands.tooltip: Filters campaigns by status; repeat the parameter for multiple statuses, for example ?status=running&status=paused. Each campaign object includes sent counts, target lists, and its send_at schedule. Add no_body=true to skip message bodies and slim the response.

commands.desc: Preview a campaign's rendered message
commands.tooltip: Renders the campaign body with template placeholders like {{ .Subscriber.FirstName }} filled with sample subscriber data. Use it to check layout and personalization before sending. The response is rendered HTML or plain text depending on the campaign content type.

commands.desc: Send a campaign test to specific email addresses
commands.tooltip: Queues a test delivery of campaign 1 to arbitrary recipients, bypassing the campaign's actual list. Include the campaign's full fields when it is still a draft without saved content. Confirm the message renders in a real client before scheduling the real send.

commands.desc: Change a campaign's status via the API
commands.tooltip: Moves a campaign between draft, scheduled, running, paused, cancelled, and finished. Set status scheduled together with a send_at timestamp to queue it, or running to start immediately. Pausing a running campaign stops new sends but keeps progress.

commands.desc: Fetch campaign view counts over a date range
commands.tooltip: Returns daily tracking-pixel view counts for campaign 1 between the from and to dates. Swap views for clicks, links, or bounces for the other analytics series. Counts stay empty unless the tracking features are enabled in the privacy settings.

commands.desc: Bulk import subscribers from a CSV file
commands.tooltip: Uploads subs.csv as a multipart form with a params JSON string controlling the import: mode subscribe or blocklist, the CSV delimiter, and the target list ids. The CSV needs email and name columns. Poll GET /api/import/subscribers/logs to watch progress.

commands.desc: Watch an in-progress subscriber import
commands.tooltip: Returns the import log lines, showing each processed file and the final tally once the import finishes. Combine with the status endpoint GET /api/import/subscribers, which reports total, imported, and current status. Poll it after a bulk upload to know when the import completed.

commands.desc: List campaign and transactional templates
commands.tooltip: Returns all templates with their subject and body source, plus the is_default flag that marks the fallback template. Templates are shared across campaigns, so editing one changes every campaign that references it. The default template is used when a campaign omits template_id.

commands.desc: List public lists without authentication
commands.tooltip: Returns name and uuid for every active public list, with no credentials required, so external forms and scripts can build subscription pages. Only lists with type public and status active appear. Post the chosen uuid to POST /api/public/subscription to subscribe someone.

commands.cmd: curl -u admin:admin -X POST http://localhost:9000/api/campaigns -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"June Newsletter","subject":"Hello, world","lists":[1],"content_type":"richtext","type":"regular"}'
commands.desc: Create a campaign draft via the API
commands.tooltip: Creates a campaign in draft status; name, subject, lists, content_type, and type are required. A campaign is one newsletter send to the target lists. Add body with template markup and template_id to use a custom template, then test and schedule it before it goes out.

commands.desc: Start the n8n server
commands.tooltip: Boots the n8n instance, serving the editor UI at http://localhost:5678 and activating the triggers of published workflows. The process stays in the foreground, so run it in a terminal, a systemd unit, or a process manager. Running bare n8n with no arguments behaves the same as n8n start. Stop with Ctrl+C for a graceful shutdown.

commands.desc: Start n8n and open the editor in a browser
commands.tooltip: Starts the server and attempts to open the editor URL in your default browser. The -o flag is the only flag n8n start accepts; ports and hostnames are configured through environment variables like N8N_PORT and N8N_HOST. Press o in the running terminal to reopen the browser at any time.

commands.desc: Show the installed n8n version
commands.tooltip: Prints the version number of the n8n package, handy before reading release notes or filing a bug report. The aliases -v and -V are accepted too. Compare the output against the stable version listed in the n8n docs to see how outdated your install is.

commands.desc: List every available n8n CLI command
commands.tooltip: Prints the full command list with a one-line description of each entry, plus a pointer to the CLI reference documentation. Run n8n <command> --help to get that command's own flags and examples. The list includes export, import, execute, and maintenance helpers, though not every command appears on the docs page.

commands.desc: List workflows with IDs and names
commands.tooltip: Prints every workflow as id|name, one pair per line, using the internal IDs that export, execute, and publish commands expect. This is the fastest way to find a workflow ID when you only know its display name. Combine with --onlyId or --active to shape the output.

commands.desc: List only workflow IDs
commands.tooltip: Prints just the numeric workflow IDs, one per line, dropping the names for easy scripting. Feed the output into a loop that backs up or executes every workflow. Use --active=true or --active=false to restrict the list to published or unpublished workflows.

commands.desc: List only published workflows
commands.tooltip: Filters the listing to workflows whose active flag is true, meaning their triggers run automatically. In n8n 2.0 the active flag corresponds to the published state. The --active flag accepts only true or false and rejects any other value.

commands.desc: Run a saved workflow once
commands.tooltip: Executes workflow 123 the same way a manual run would, starting from the first trigger node, and prints the full execution result as JSON. The workflow must already exist in the n8n database, so import it first when it came from a file. The --id flag is required; the old --file flag no longer works.

commands.desc: Run a workflow and print only JSON
commands.tooltip: Executes workflow 123 and prints only the JSON execution data, with no surrounding status text, so piping into jq or another parser stays clean. Use the flag exactly as written, --rawOutput. Failed runs still exit with a non-zero code and log the error.

commands.desc: Run multiple workflows in parallel
commands.tooltip: Executes workflows 10, 13, and 15 once each, up to 10 at a time, and prints a JSON summary with the status of every run. The --ids flag also accepts a file path whose contents are comma-separated IDs. Omitting --ids runs every workflow in the instance, which can take a while.

commands.desc: Save execution snapshots for regression tests
commands.tooltip: Runs all workflows and writes one snapshot JSON file per workflow into the given directory, comparing only top-level output attributes when --shallow is set. Point --compare at the snapshot directory on a later run to diff current output against it. Deleted output fields are flagged as errors, new ones as warnings.

commands.desc: Compare executions against saved snapshots
commands.tooltip: Runs every workflow and diffs each execution against the matching snapshot file in the directory, retrying failed or warning runs up to 2 extra times. Structural removals in the output are reported as errors and additions as warnings. Add --shortOutput to print only the summary instead of full execution data.

commands.desc: Publish the draft of a workflow
commands.tooltip: Makes the current draft of workflow 123 the published version, so its scheduled triggers fire and its webhooks become live. Publishing replaced the old active toggle in n8n 2.0, and there is deliberately no --all flag to prevent accidental bulk publishes. The change takes effect after an n8n restart.

commands.desc: Unpublish a workflow
commands.tooltip: Removes workflow 123 from the published state, stopping its scheduled triggers and webhook endpoints. Third-party services may still hit a webhook URL briefly while it deregisters. Restart n8n to be certain every trigger is fully stopped.

commands.desc: Unpublish every workflow
commands.tooltip: Takes all workflows offline at once, which is handy before a maintenance window or a full instance migration. This is a bulk action: every schedule and webhook stops firing. Prefer targeting individual IDs unless you genuinely mean everything.

commands.desc: Export all workflows to stdout
commands.tooltip: Prints every workflow as a JSON array to the terminal, ready to redirect into a file with > or pipe into jq. Exactly one of --all, --id, or --projectId is required. The export is a bare array, so jq filters such as .[].name address workflows directly.

commands.desc: List workflow names from an export
commands.tooltip: Pipes the exported workflow array into jq and prints only the name field of each workflow. The export format is a plain JSON array, not an object with a workflows key, so the filter is .[] rather than .workflows[]. Add -r to strip the surrounding quotes.

commands.desc: Export one workflow to a file
commands.tooltip: Writes workflow 123 as JSON to workflow.json, with --output (short form -o) naming the file. The file holds a single workflow object with nodes, connections, and metadata, ready to import on another instance. The export keeps the workflow ID, so importing into an instance that already has ID 123 overwrites it.

commands.desc: Export all workflows to one file
commands.tooltip: Dumps every workflow into a single JSON array at workflows.json, ideal for a quick full backup or a migration between instances. Import the same file back with n8n import:workflow --input=workflows.json. For per-file, versioned backups, prefer --separate or --backup.

commands.desc: Export one JSON file per workflow
commands.tooltip: Writes each workflow to its own file named by ID inside backups/latest/, a layout that plays well with version control and single-workflow restores. The --output directory is created automatically if missing. Restore the whole set with n8n import:workflow --separate --input=backups/latest/.

commands.desc: Export workflows in backup mode
commands.tooltip: Runs the backup convenience flag, shorthand for --all --pretty --separate: pretty-printed JSON, one file per workflow, into the given directory. This is the documented one-shot backup command for workflows. Restore with n8n import:workflow --separate --input=backups/latest/.

commands.desc: Export a historical workflow version
commands.tooltip: Writes the historical version whose version ID is the version id, not the current draft, to workflow-v1.json. Version IDs come from the workflow history and are listed in the editor's version panel. The --version flag cannot be combined with --all or --published.

commands.desc: Export the published version of a workflow
commands.tooltip: Writes the currently published version of workflow 123 to published.json instead of the draft. Exporting the published version captures exactly what production is running, including its version metadata. The --published and --version flags are mutually exclusive.

commands.desc: Export all workflows of one project
commands.tooltip: Exports every workflow belonging to project Ox8O54VQrmBrb4qL into a single file, handy for team-level backups. Exactly one of --all, --id, or --projectId must be given, making this the project-scoped selector. The same selector pattern exists on export:credentials.

commands.desc: Export all credentials to stdout
commands.tooltip: Prints every credential as a JSON array with its metadata, keeping data fields encrypted so secrets stay unreadable. Use --decrypted only when you truly need the plain values. Note the plural command name, export:credentials.

commands.desc: Export one credential to a file
commands.tooltip: Writes credential 5 to credential.json using its ID, which you can find in the credentials list in the editor. The data is still encrypted, so the file is only useful on an instance that can decrypt it. Restore with n8n import:credentials --input=credential.json.

commands.desc: Export all credentials to one file
commands.tooltip: Saves every credential into a single JSON array at credentials.json, still encrypted. This pairs with n8n import:credentials for moving credentials between instances that share the same encryption key. For a plain-text migration, add --decrypted.

commands.desc: Export credentials in plain text
commands.tooltip: Writes every credential with its secrets in plain text, required when migrating to an instance with a different encryption key. Treat this file like a password vault, since anyone who reads it can use every stored API key and password. Delete it as soon as the migration finishes.

commands.desc: Export credentials in backup mode
commands.tooltip: Combines --all --pretty --separate to write one pretty-printed, still-encrypted JSON file per credential into backups/latest/. This is the credentials counterpart of the workflow backup command. Restore with n8n import:credentials --separate --input=backups/latest/.

commands.desc: Export all credentials of one project
commands.tooltip: Writes the credentials owned by project Ox8O54VQrmBrb4qL to project-creds.json, still encrypted. Useful before deleting a project or auditing what a team can access. Combine with the workflow project export for a complete team snapshot.

commands.desc: Import workflows from a file
commands.tooltip: Loads workflows.json, accepting either a single workflow object or an array, and creates the workflows in the database. Imported workflows are deactivated by default so their triggers do not fire until you publish them. Workflows whose IDs already exist in the target instance are overwritten.

commands.desc: Import workflows from a directory
commands.tooltip: Reads every .json file in backups/latest/ as one workflow each, matching the layout produced by --separate and --backup exports. Files without valid nodes and connections are skipped with a warning. Assign ownership with --userId or --projectId, but never both.

commands.desc: Import workflows keeping their active state
commands.tooltip: Imports each workflow and honours the active field from its JSON instead of deactivating everything. The fromJson value only works in queue or multi-main mode, and a regular instance rejects the flag outright. On single-instance setups, import with the default and publish afterwards.

commands.desc: Import workflows into a project
commands.tooltip: Imports the workflows and assigns them to project Ox8O54VQrmBrb4qL, which is how multi-user instances restore backups into a team space. Combining --projectId with --userId is an error. Omitting both assigns the workflows to the instance owner.

commands.desc: Import credentials from a file
commands.tooltip: Reads credentials.json, which may hold one credential or an array, and inserts them into the database, encrypting any plain-text data it finds. Credentials with the same ID as existing ones are overwritten, so rename or delete IDs first when merging exports. Ownership goes to the instance owner unless --userId or --projectId is passed.

commands.desc: Import credentials from a directory
commands.tooltip: Loads every .json file from backups/latest/, one credential per file, as produced by the --separate or --backup export. The --input value must be a real directory, and the file names do not matter. Use --projectId to assign all imported credentials to one project.

commands.desc: Export all database entities
commands.tooltip: Dumps every n8n database entity, including users, projects, settings, and more, into ./outputs so you can migrate between database engines such as SQLite and Postgres. Execution history tables are excluded by default because they can be enormous. This is the CLI-level migration path, separate from the workflow and credential exports.

commands.desc: Export entities including execution history
commands.tooltip: Adds the execution history data tables to the entity export, which the default omits to keep the dump small. Expect a much larger output directory on instances with heavy automation traffic. Import the result with n8n import:entities.

commands.desc: Import database entities
commands.tooltip: Loads an entity export back into n8n, targeting a possibly different database engine than the export source. The target database should be empty, or pass --truncateTables true to wipe the tables first. Back up the destination instance before running this.

commands.desc: Reset user management to its initial state
commands.tooltip: Removes every user account and returns user management to the pre-setup state, the recovery path when you lose the owner password and have no SMTP for password resets. This deletes all accounts, so only run it when you have another way in. You will create the owner account again at the next login.

commands.desc: Disable two-factor authentication for a user
commands.tooltip: Turns off MFA for the account with the given email, the escape hatch when a user lost their recovery codes and cannot log in. Only the named user is affected, and they can re-enable MFA from their profile afterwards. Works without the server running.

commands.desc: Clear LDAP configuration
commands.tooltip: Resets the LDAP settings so the instance falls back to its default authentication method, useful when a misconfigured LDAP server locks everyone out. User accounts are not deleted, but LDAP-managed users may need password resets. Reconfigure LDAP from the settings UI afterwards.

commands.desc: Show license details
commands.tooltip: Prints the current license information, including plan and expiry date, the first thing to check when enterprise features stop working. It runs from the CLI without the server. Paid features such as projects and SSO unlock only with a valid license.

commands.desc: Remove the license from the database
commands.tooltip: Deletes the stored license and resets n8n to default community features, releasing any floating entitlements back to the pool. Enterprise-only features become unavailable immediately. Reinstall the license to restore them.

commands.desc: Run the security audit
commands.tooltip: Scans the instance for common security issues such as missing security settings, risky node configurations, and exposed files, then prints a report. The same audit is available in the settings UI. Fix the flagged items and re-run to confirm.
